title: RFK Jr tells US families to vaccinate children against measles amid outbreak
body_text: Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, on Sunday told American parents that they should get their children vaccinated against measles, as the surge in infections has reached numbers not seen in the past 35 years. Kennedy, a leading vaccination skeptic who has spent years amplifying misinformation about vaccines, including the shot that protects against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), made his call in the course of a contentious interview with CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday morning. His remark came as the incidence of measles crossed a milestone – the US has now officially recorded 2,371 confirmed infections so far this year, surpassing 2025’s total tally of 2,289. Taken together, the past two years have seen more measles infections in the US than the rest of the 21st century combined. The last time a greater number of measles cases were recorded in a single year was in 1991. Kennedy’s statement was extracted from him by Dana Bash, CNN’s host, who invited him to use his “bully pulpit” to talk directly to parents as the new school year approached. She urged him to tell families that they should vaccinate for measles “because it is safe and it will help them save their children’s lives”. The health secretary replied: “Parents should get their children vaccinated for measles. A measles vaccine is effective, it stops measles in about 97% of the cases. People should get vaccinated.” Later in the interview he added that people should also get the combined measles, mumps and rubella vaccine, the main protection against the disease that has been a particular target of the anti-vaccination movement. The health secretary’s call for parents to vaccinate their children for measles contrasts starkly with the many years in which Kennedy has been a leading proponent of misinformation questioning the efficacy and safety of vaccinations. Even since he became the country’s top health official, he has depicted a measles vaccination as a personal choice and claimed inaccurately that the power of the inoculation is waning. The call also comes late in the day, given the rate at which measles is spreading in the US. The 37 new measles outbreaks that have already been recorded this year are putting the US in danger of losing the measles elimination status that it has held since 2000. Kennedy continues to shrug off criticism that his work as a prominent vaccine skeptic, both before and after he entered the Trump administration, has exacerbated the problem. Asked whether he took any responsibility for the measles surge, he said: “Absolutely not.” He went on to blame the outbreaks on religious communities who eschew vaccines and on global health conditions. Any hope that Kennedy’s measles statement might indicate a change of heart were dashed in the rest of the CNN interview in which he turned combative. Batting off questions from Bash, the health secretary responded with personal attacks. He accused the CNN host of “saying nonsense”, “repeating like a parrot” and “making assertions you can’t support”. In one especially demeaning remark he said Bash had become “flustered”. “I’m not flustered at all,” she asserted in a calm voice. “I am frustrated because you are the HHS secretary and you are talking about things that lead to vaccine hesitancy in this country.” In a further comment dripping with condescension, Kennedy told Bash “you probably don’t understand this because you’re not a scientist”. The journalist riposted: “But you’re not, either.” The health secretary’s belligerent approach, in which he at times appeared red-faced while frequently poking his finger towards Bash, attracted the attention of commentators. The journalist Aaron Rupar described the performance as “RFK Jr’s epic CNN crashout” and said in a post on X that Kennedy’s “yelling” sounded like “a rabid dog barking”. Andy Kim, the Democratic US senator from New Jersey, took from Kennedy’s comments that he and Donald Trump had no plans to prepare for a possible next pandemic. “The only thing they have a plan for is trying to distract you from the fact that they’ve taken away healthcare from millions,” Kim said. Kennedy used the CNN exchange to spread further misinformation about other aspects of public health. He claimed that both respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) that is a major cause of infant mortality and Lyme disease were caused by manipulation of germs in laboratories. The suggestion has been contradicted by decades of scientific evidence that suggest they both have natural roots. RSV was initially identified in the 1950s, two decades before such experimentation, known as “gain-of-function” research, started. During the interview, Kennedy repeated unfounded claims that there was a link between Tylenol use during pregnancy and autism, and poured doubt on the efficacy of vaccines to protect children against Covid-19. Speaking to CNN’s State of the Union later in the show, Ashish Jha, who advised Joe Biden’s White House on its Covid response, said he was heartened to hear Kennedy say that “every kid in America should be getting the MMR vaccine”. But he added that much else of what the health secretary had said “just isn’t true”. Jha said that the dramatic rise in measles cases on Kennedy’s watch was not coincidental. “The administration has not done enough to promote vaccines. It has not done enough to highlight the harms that come from measles.”

Jha said that the dramatic rise in measles cases on Kennedy’s watch was not coincidental. “The administration has not done enough to promote vaccines. It has not done enough to highlight the harms that come from measles.”

title: Trump meets his obstinate match in Iran’s hardball regime
body_text: The Donald Trump doctrine has always contained a tenuous relationship with the truth. It was his mentor, the infamous New York lawyer Roy Cohn, who taught the young real estate mogul always to claim victory and never to admit defeat. Unfortunately for Trump, in Iran the US president has found a counterpart just as stubborn as himself. As Trump claims new negotiations are to begin with Tehran this week, Iran has shown it can also reignite the conflict by lobbing ballistic missiles at US bases in the region and maintaining a stranglehold on the strait of Hormuz, effectively taking initiative in the stalled peace process. And time is of the essence for Trump as the clock ticks toward a global energy crisis and a painful midterm elections for him and his Republican party. But as soon as his latest attempt to hammer out a peace deal was announced, it was denied by Iran and the US president was left fuming once again. “Iranian Leadership is unbelievably duplicitous!” he posted to his social media site, Truth Social, saying that Iran had begged for a meeting and talks had already begun. “Nothing gets through to Iran, unless we want it to, and nothing will get through, unless a Deal, or Total Surrender, is accomplished.” Trump has suggested dozens of times since the beginning of the war that a deal with Iran is imminent, and his latest claim that new negotiations could produce a peace deal within days has shown the administration’s desperation to reopen the strait and find a road map out of the crisis. After promising to hit Iran “very hard”, Trump made a U-turn on Sunday and claimed that talks would continue and that the “perimeters of a deal” for the opening of Hormuz and the “denuclearization of Iran” had been agreed. Unfortunately, the Iranians don’t agree. In a statement on Monday, an Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson denied any peace negotiations were taking place. “We are not currently negotiating with the United States,” said Esmaeil Baqaei. “Our negotiations are with Oman to secure passage through the strait of Hormuz.” That may result in an agreement. But that will not result in the return of the strait of Hormuz to its prewar status, Baqaei added, in effect keeping the waterway a political football for the foreseeable future. “We must ensure that the strait of Hormuz cannot be misused by parties that have committed aggression against Iran,” said Baqaei. Little has changed since the last round of negotiations. Iran remains capable of closing the strait of Hormuz and stifling shipping – including a fifth of global oil supply – through the crucial waterway. The US remains capable of inflicting devastating strikes on Iran – despite a shortage of key munitions that could be needed for a war against key rivals like China – but has a lack of meaningful targets that could force Iran to change its policy. The Trump administration has been signalling a desire to end the conflict since April and three ceasefires have come and collapsed since then. With just over three months left until the US midterm elections, in which the Republicans are expected to lose the House and possibly even the Senate, a new Reuters/Ipsos poll last week showed that fewer than a third of Americans support the war in Iran, and 69% believe that Trump has not “clearly explained the goals of US military involvement in Iran”. For Iran, the strategic unpredictability has become a new weapon in a war that has counterintuitively strengthened its negotiating position, giving the regime new tools in slowing global oil supply and in attacking regional US allies in the Gulf. Iran has concluded that its best strategy is to “maximise the pain that they can impose on the United States and its partners in the region”, said Alex Vatanka, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute and an expert on Middle East security issues with a focus on Iran, during the institute’s podcast last week. The view there was that Trump “is not really yet ready for a deal with Iran, not a deal that would work for the Iranians anyway”. Iran is also facing a time crunch with a US blockade in effect halting trade out of the country. “They are now at a point where they don’t think just sitting back and having one round after another of diplomatic talks is the best way forward,” he added. “They’re trying to shake things up to try get Trump’s attention and see if they can get a different result.”

title: Trump accuses oil companies of ‘making too much money’ from his war on Iran
body_text: Donald Trump has criticised oil companies for “making too much money” from the global energy market disruption caused by his war on Iran. Brent crude had been trading at about $70 (£52) a barrel before the first US-Israeli strikes at the end of February, but by the end of April it had soared as high as $126 and is now trading at about $85 a barrel. The US president took aim at the windfall profits revealed last week by ExxonMobil and Chevron, and said the companies would “give some of that back to the public”. “They’re making too much money based on a shortage,” he told reporters at the White House on Monday evening. “I don’t like it.” Trump was speaking just hours before BP reported its profits had doubled in the last quarter, to $5.7bn. The US oil companies made profits totalling more than $26bn for the three months to the end of June by taking advantage of the energy market disruption triggered by the US-Israeli war on Iran. Chevron reported its highest ever quarterly profit of $12.2bn, a fivefold increase on the same period last year. ExxonMobil reported a profit of $14.5bn in the second quarter, double what it made in the same period a year ago and its highest quarterly profit since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine. “Chevron: too much money. ExxonMobil: too much money,” Trump said. “They’re going to give some of that back to the public and they better cut the retail price, the consumer price.” Asked about Trump’s comments, the BP chief executive, Meg O’Neill, told CNBC that she understood the pressures on households. “The reality is, we produce a global commodity, and the product we sell hangs off that global commodity price,” she added. Climate campaigners have also attacked big oil’s bumper quarterly earnings, condemning them as “obscene”. Clémence Dubois, a campaigns director at 350.org, an international environmental group, said: “Chevron and Exxon are profiteering from a model of distraction, leaving ordinary people to pay the price with higher bills and devastating impacts such as these fires. These profits feel almost criminal.” Trump criticised oil company profits weeks after warning energy retailers to cut their prices as he nears the November midterm elections with flagging approval ratings. He also ordered the US justice department to investigate potential price gouging in the retail energy sector. “Gasoline Retailers must get their Prices down, IMMEDIATELY,” he wrote on his Truth Social platform in late June. “If Retailers don’t do this, big problems lie ahead!” The president told journalists that the fall in oil and gas prices during the administration’s June peace talks with Iran should have caused petrol prices to fall to $2.25 a gallon. “Oil prices have come down so much and we are not seeing anything at the pump by comparison the way they should be,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office. US gasoline prices currently average $4.11 a gallon, according to data from the AAA motoring group. The Trump administration has repeatedly said it has no plans to introduce an export ban on oil or petroleum products, but some analysts say this could be revisited if prices at the pump continue to rise.

title: Asking Anthony Fauci for medical advice then calling for him to be jailed? Katie Miller is the latest Maga hypocrite
body_text: You should keep your friends close, your enemies closer, and Stephen and Katie Miller as far away from your general vicinity as humanly possible. Many people will not need to be told this. Stephen Miller, the White House deputy chief of staff, is famous for masterminding the first Trump administration’s family separation policy and Muslim ban. His wife, Katie, is similarly enthusiastic about mass deportation and has reportedly said she didn’t feel compassion for families separated at the border. Stephen met Katie when they were both working in government, but she has since left politics to start a podcast. Now she asks guests such as JD Vance important questions such as: is a hotdog a sandwich? While I may not need to inform you that the Millers are bad news, it seems Dr Anthony Fauci is only just getting the memo. The former top US government science adviser, who helped guide the country’s Covid-19 response, was forced to appear at a US Senate committee hearing last week. Senator Rand Paul of Kentucky framed the hearing as an investigation into the origins of the pandemic. Really, however, it was an opportunity for Republicans to harass Fauci, who is widely loathed among the Maga base. He has become such a target of vitriol that Biden preemptively pardoned Fauci before leaving office in case he was prosecuted by the Trump administration. While the Millers were not directly involved in the Fauci hearing, they did make an interesting cameo. Paul released more than 1,000 pages of Fauci’s diary from 2019 to 2022, which revealed that Fauci regularly talked to Katie, then a communications aide to vice-president Mike Pence, about her health concerns. “I am calling katie frequently to check on her couple time per day,” Fauci wrote in notes dated 9 May 2020. “She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone.” Fauci seemed to like Katie, who he described as “tough, smart, but great”, and she seemed on good terms with him. Fauci also sent the Millers a baby gift and, per his diary, the couple called him to say thank you. “We had a nice discussion about life after Trump,” he wrote in December 2020. I don’t think any more gifts are going to be exchanged, however, because Katie has thrown Fauci under the bus. It’s very embarrassing for a Maga bigwig like her – someone who has amplified vaccine-sceptic views and publicly called for Fauci to be jailed – to be revealed as having privately asked him for medical advice. Katie has tried to explain away the relationship by insisting that she had simply been feigning friendship as part of a cunning plan. Katie told the political news website Notus that she’d been cordial with Fauci so that he “did not leak against me or my husband”. She added that she understood “how to manage somebody like him”. Some of the information about her seems to have been redacted. Notus reports that the original Fauci journal entries released “mentioned Katie Miller 56 times, while the redacted document mentioned her 37 times”. After the diary entries became public, Katie attacked Fauci on social media and accused him of being fame-hungry. “Every man who has a journal is a narcissist,” she wrote on X on Thursday. “Dr Fauci was neither my friend nor my doctor, but a work colleague who weaponised my pregnancy and child for his gain to aggrandise himself. As they say, keep your friends close and your enemies closer … this man should be in prison.” Katie isn’t entirely wrong about Fauci enjoying fame. His journal entries contain cringeworthy details about flattering press coverage and celebs fawning over him. Julia Roberts, he wrote, “said that every time she sees me her throat gets dry and she gets nervous”. Barbra Streisand apparently also chatted to Fauci about vaccines. “Had great call with Barbra Streisand,” he wrote in February 2021. “I told her that I work listening to her songs on Alexa. She really did not know what Alexa was. I accidentally butt called her later in the evening …” Still, this was a private journal, and we’ve all been embarrassing in private haven’t we? Plus, if Roberts was gasping over me, you best believe I’d be telling dear diary. Fauci getting carried away by his sudden fame is understandable; there is no vaccine for being cringe. One day, however, I hope there will be a cure for the harm people like the Millers have inflicted on the body politic. • Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist • Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Let’s call Trump’s approach to Iran what it is: kindergarten diplomacy
body_text: On Thursday, 23 July, after weeks of escalating attacks between the US and Iran, Donald Trump told a reporter that Iran hadn’t received “enough pain yet”, and he leveled a threat. “I am considering a massive attack. Bigger than ever before,” he warned. “I am close to making a decision.” Then, on Monday 27 July, he called it off. A few days later, on Friday 31 July, Trump said: “We’ll be hitting them very hard. At some point, they’re going to say: ‘We just can’t take it any more.’” This time, it took him just one day to back down. Here we go again. Ever since the US and Israel launched their latest war on Iran on 28 February, the people of the planet have been subjected to Donald Trump’s on-again off-again relationship with raining down catastrophic destruction on the nation. It started on 21 March, when Trump promised to hit Iranian power plants (a war crime, incidentally) unless Iran opened the strait of Hormuz. He delayed that plan for five days, and then another 10 days, before issuing his next threat. That was on 7 April, when he wrote: “A whole civilization will die tonight, never to be brought back again.” A mere 10 hours later, he walked back that (genocidal) threat. On 17 May, he wrote: “For Iran, the Clock is Ticking, and they better get moving, FAST, or there won’t be anything left of them. TIME IS OF THE ESSENCE!” On 18 May, he wrote that he had been asked by Gulf leaders to “hold off on our planned Military attack of the Islamic Republic of Iran, which was scheduled for tomorrow”. The approach seems as tedious as it does childish, constantly threatening one thing only to back down in a cringey, face-saving effort shortly thereafter. Let’s call it what it is: kindergarten diplomacy. From appearances, it would seem that Trump considers this a strategy. One can only assume he holds out hope that it will achieve an end to this catastrophic conflagration he and Benjamin Netanyahu began. The war is a massive failure, plunging his popularity along with American regional dominance in the Middle East. What’s clear is that Trump hasn’t a clue about how to exit a war he never should have started in the first place. Leadership is needed when difficult decisions must be made, but Trump is not capable of such resolve. Instead, he seems primarily driven to make pronouncements based on the last person he talked to. When Netanyahu visited him in the Oval Office on 21 July, the Israeli prime minister discussed three options for the war with Trump, according to reports: “a (negotiated) deal, continuing the blockade and economic pressures, and a massive strike”, is how a senior Israeli official described the meeting to Reuters. (Let’s not forget that Netanyahu helped convince Trump to start this war back in February.) Two days later, Trump threatened a massive strike (then called it off, then threatened it again). When the president’s threat reappeared, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump on 1 August to argue for de-escalation. Guess what? To no one’s surprise, Trump backed down again. Nixon had his madman theory, in which he sought to project an image of himself as unhinged and irrational to frighten the Soviet Union into concessions. Trump, whether he knows it or not, is turning indecision into his own presidential doctrine. Such indecision is probably in part a reflection of Trump’s unflagging desire to please influential people around him. Trump’s deep-seated need to be liked by those he perceives to be powerful or popular (see: Trump’s meeting with Zohran Mamdani) is, I think, often underappreciated. But there is more behind Trump’s indecision as well. This administration cannot make any of the necessary decisions on Iran because it, along with Trump’s Maga base and the larger Republican party, has been split, as if by a lightning bolt, by the question. Vice-President JD Vance has been the most skeptical in the president’s inner circle of the war. Ever aware of the political winds, the vice-president is said to be carefully watching the rising rightwing criticism of Israel, due in part to this war. Vance went on the popular podcast The Joe Rogan Experience in mid-July and claimed that there was an Israeli government campaign to shape popular opinion in the US about the war. “There are some people within their system, we know beyond a shadow of a doubt, who are manipulating and trying to change American public opinion to keep the war going on indefinitely,” he said. “Not toward any objective, but just indefinitely.” Ever the faithful lieutenant to Trump, Marco Rubio, on the other hand, told Lara Trump on Fox News that the Iranian regime “has never faced a president like President Trump, which is someone that actually takes action”. Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner (along with Vance and their fellow negotiator Steve Witkoff) favors reducing the conflict, thereby lowering gas prices and limiting the danger to US armed forces, but just until after the midterm elections, when the war could potentially be ramped up again, according to Israel Hayom. The chairperson of the joint chiefs of staff, Gen Dan Caine, who counseled the president against the war in the first place, is now warning that stockpiles for air defense interceptors are dangerously low due to the war in Iran, putting the men and women in the US military at greater risk. Meanwhile, the Memorandum of Understanding that the US signed with Iran in June has been the subject of fierce Republican opposition, with the Louisiana Republican senator Bill Cassidy calling it “the worst foreign policy blunder in decades”. Even Trump loyalists such as the Texas senator Ted Cruz criticized the memorandum, saying: “The president is receiving some very poor advice on this deal.” And the Maga faithful have grown cold on the war, with only about a third of its voters believing the war is worth the economic cost, according to a Politico poll. Add to this the fact that CNN is now reporting that US military leadership is basically out of ideas about how to proceed with Iran at this point and is soliciting, via a crowdsourcing-type email sent to a group of military analysts, “new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran”. The report also explains that Trump “has been considering strikes akin to a ‘fireworks’ display’”, which would suggest “a symbolic victory that would allow him to exit the war without actually accomplishing one of his initial aims: ridding Iran of its nuclear program”. Charting a course through the stormy winds of political decision making is what presidents must do all the time. A debacle like the war in Iran, begun with a terrible decision and bringing much unnecessary harm to the people of the region, must eventually be followed by a brave one, however painful it is to this nation or its leadership. A responsible president would make such a choice, even when difficult, and explain the reasoning to the nation. We, unfortunately, do not have serious leaders. And so we are left with kindergarten diplomacy. Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel To Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

When the president’s threat reappeared, Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called Trump on 1 August to argue for de-escalation. Guess what? To no one’s surprise, Trump backed down again. Nixon had his madman theory, in which he sought to project an image of himself as unhinged and irrational to frighten the Soviet Union into concessions. Trump, whether he knows it or not, is turning indecision into his own presidential doctrine. Such indecision is probably in part a reflection of Trump’s unflagging desire to please influential people around him. Trump’s deep-seated need to be liked by those he perceives to be powerful or popular (see: Trump’s meeting with Zohran Mamdani) is, I think, often underappreciated. But there is more behind Trump’s indecision as well. This administration cannot make any of the necessary decisions on Iran because it, along with Trump’s Maga base and the larger Republican party, has been split, as if by a lightning bolt, by the question. Vice-President JD Vance has been the most skeptical in the president’s inner circle of the war. Ever aware of the political winds, the vice-president is said to be carefully watching the rising rightwing criticism of Israel, due in part to this war. Vance went on the popular podcast The Joe Rogan Experience in mid-July and claimed that there was an Israeli government campaign to shape popular opinion in the US about the war. “There are some people within their system, we know beyond a shadow of a doubt, who are manipulating and trying to change American public opinion to keep the war going on indefinitely,” he said. “Not toward any objective, but just indefinitely.” Ever the faithful lieutenant to Trump, Marco Rubio, on the other hand, told Lara Trump on Fox News that the Iranian regime “has never faced a president like President Trump, which is someone that actually takes action”. Trump’s son-in-law and US negotiator Jared Kushner (along with Vance and their fellow negotiator Steve Witkoff) favors reducing the conflict, thereby lowering gas prices and limiting the danger to US armed forces, but just until after the midterm elections, when the war could potentially be ramped up again, according to Israel Hayom. The chairperson of the joint chiefs of staff, Gen Dan Caine, who counseled the president against the war in the first place, is now warning that stockpiles for air defense interceptors are dangerously low due to the war in Iran, putting the men and women in the US military at greater risk. Meanwhile, the Memorandum of Understanding that the US signed with Iran in June has been the subject of fierce Republican opposition, with the Louisiana Republican senator Bill Cassidy calling it “the worst foreign policy blunder in decades”. Even Trump loyalists such as the Texas senator Ted Cruz criticized the memorandum, saying: “The president is receiving some very poor advice on this deal.” And the Maga faithful have grown cold on the war, with only about a third of its voters believing the war is worth the economic cost, according to a Politico poll. Add to this the fact that CNN is now reporting that US military leadership is basically out of ideas about how to proceed with Iran at this point and is soliciting, via a crowdsourcing-type email sent to a group of military analysts, “new creative and unconventional ways to pressure and punish Iran”. The report also explains that Trump “has been considering strikes akin to a ‘fireworks’ display’”, which would suggest “a symbolic victory that would allow him to exit the war without actually accomplishing one of his initial aims: ridding Iran of its nuclear program”. Charting a course through the stormy winds of political decision making is what presidents must do all the time. A debacle like the war in Iran, begun with a terrible decision and bringing much unnecessary harm to the people of the region, must eventually be followed by a brave one, however painful it is to this nation or its leadership. A responsible president would make such a choice, even when difficult, and explain the reasoning to the nation. We, unfortunately, do not have serious leaders. And so we are left with kindergarten diplomacy. Moustafa Bayoumi is the author of the award-winning books How Does It Feel To Be a Problem?: Being Young and Arab in America and This Muslim American Life: Dispatches from the War on Terror. He is professor of English at Brooklyn College, City University of New York, and a Guardian US columnist

title: Top Democrats accuse Trump officials over Israeli settlers’ ‘unbridled violence’
body_text: Senior Democrats have accused Donald Trump’s administration of giving a green light to violent Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, warning that its policies created “a climate of impunity and unbridled violence” that endangers both Palestinians and US citizens. In a letter seen by the Guardian, a group of 19 Democratic senators and representatives call for the restoration of sanctions against extremist settlers and demand independent US investigations into the deaths of nine US citizens killed in the West Bank since 2022. The letter, signed by the Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren among others, is addressed to Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, and Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary. It argues that Trump’s promise last year that “I will not allow Israel to annex the West Bank” has been undermined by events on the ground. “In practice,” the Democrats write, “violent settlers and the [Benjamin] Netanyahu government have proceeded to rapidly extend Israeli control over civilian populations in the region.” They urge the administration to use “all the diplomatic and economic tools at its disposal, including restoring sanctions, to end this violence and expansion of settlements”. The Democrats argue that Trump’s decision on his first day back in office to rescind sanctions imposed on more than 30 settlers and organisations linked to violence has had profound consequences. “Ending sanctions against those individuals and entities associated with West Bank extremism sent a clear message,” they write. “Settlers can use violent and deadly force with impunity against Palestinians and Americans while seizing land … and no one will face consequences.” The letter cites UN figures showing 1,835 attacks on Palestinian communities and property during 2025, the highest number since records began, and says the UN has reported that the pace of settler attacks this year is higher than in any year on record. It highlights repeated attacks on Turmus Ayya, a Palestinian town where the majority of residents are US citizens, including the burning of a family home belonging to Americans from Massachusetts and Washington state. The elected officials also focus on what they say has become an increasingly dangerous environment for Americans. Since Trump returned to office, they write, four US citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in the West Bank, bringing the total since 2022 to nine. The victims include the Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, 14-year-old Amer Mohammed Rabea, 17-year-olds Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Ahmed Mohammad Khdour and 20-year-old Sayfollah Musallet, as well as Omar Assad, a 78-year-old Palestinian American, and the Turkish American activist Aysenur Ezgi Eygi. The letter says the justice department “has the authority to independently investigate the killing of Americans abroad” but “has reportedly not opened investigations into any of the killings since 2025. Israel has yet to indict a single person involved in these incidents.” The Democrats also express concern over the detention of US citizens by the Israeli military including 20-year-old Sama Safi, whose access to vital medication was allegedly interrupted after her arrest, and Mohammed Ibrahim, who they say was detained for nine months while aged 15. They urge the administration to secure Safi’s immediate release and “push for the end of unjust and arbitrary detentions in the territory”. The senators and representatives argue that the violence extends beyond Palestinian communities, pointing to repeated attacks on Taybeh, described in the letter as “the last entirely Christian village in the West Bank”. Although the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, described an earlier attack there as “an act of terror” and pledged that those responsible would be prosecuted, the senators and representatives note that “no one has been arrested in connection with these crimes”. Huckabee is an evangelical Christian who has supported Jewish claims on the occupied land that settlers call Judea and Samaria. The letter is signed by Warren, Ed Markey, Jeff Merkley, Patty Murray, Jack Reed, Bernie Sanders, Brian Schatz, Adam Schiff, Chris Van Hollen, Peter Welch and Ron Wyden. The House of Representatives signatories are Katherine Clark, Richard Neal, Jim McGovern, Seth Moulton, Ayanna Pressley, Jake Auchincloss, Stephen Lynch and Lori Trahan. It concludes that Israeli security forces and settlers have attacked and displaced Palestinians in the West Bank “at an unprecedented rate” since the Trump administration took office and argues that Washington’s “deference to the Netanyahu government has contributed to a climate of impunity and unbridled violence towards civilian populations and religious minorities”. It demands answers by 17 August on investigations into attacks on Americans, the lifting of sanctions and the treatment of US citizens detained by the Israeli military.

title: US senators urge crackdown on wildfire betting amid warnings of arson risk
body_text: A group of US lawmakers is sounding the alarm over prediction market platforms that allow users to bet on wildfires, as experts warn the emerging trend could raise the risk of arson. Democratic senators from six states sent a letter this week to the chair of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC), an independent government agency that regulates platforms such as Polymarket, urging it to rein in the practice. “As the United States faces yet another record-breaking fire season this year, the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) cannot allow these prediction markets to offer unrestricted betting on wildfires,” said the lawmakers, who included the Oregon senator Jeff Merkley, California senators Adam Schiff and Alex Padilla, and Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada. They said such bets posed a risk that “individuals could be tempted to commit arson in order to make sure their bets are successful”. Concerns about money placed on wildfire predictions specifically stem mostly from Polymarket’s offerings during the 2025 Los Angeles fires. Kalshi, a main competitor, has not offered wildfire markets because “it creates perverse incentives”, the company’s head of communications, Elisabeth Diana, told the Guardian after publication. As the Palisades and Eaton fires devastated LA in early 2025, Polymarket gave users the chance to bet on questions such as when the wildfires would be contained, whether flames would spread to certain neighborhoods by a particular date, and how many acres of land would burn. The amounts wagered on the LA fires totalled more than $1.2m, according to Jamie L Pietruska, a historian at Rutgers University who followed those predictions. And this summer, a site called Wyldfyre, purported to be the “first prediction market for California wildfire” exclusively, has offered trades on “what fire does next”. Lawmakers’ concerns come as the US faces another brutal wildfire season. Huge fires in Washington state and Oregon have burned more than 2m acres and forced tens of thousands to evacuate. Ann Skeet, the senior director of leadership ethics at Santa Clara University’s Markkula Center for Applied Ethics, commended the senators’ demands of the CFTC, and said offering bets on how a wildfire spreads could incentivize people to commit arson. “Somebody could place a bet and then be motivated to actually start a fire,” Skeet said. “There’s just the practical reality of what it is you might be motivating people to do.” Pietruska said she was glad to see the senators’ call to regulate prediction markets, but that the demand was “year and a half late” after the Polymarket bets on the Los Angeles fires. “Gambling on the weather is not new. People have been betting informally on temperature and precipitation around the world for centuries,” Pietruska said. But it’s the “speed and scale” at which prediction markets work in a “climate-changed world” that concerns Pietruska, noting police investigations into an incident at Charles de Gaulle airport in Paris, where unusual temperature readings on weather forecasting equipment coincided with suspicious winning Polymarket bets. Neither Polymarket nor the CFTC responded to Guardian requests for comment. The US government has already launched several investigations into Polymarket, the world’s largest prediction market. The Wall Street Journal first reported in June that the agency had begun investigating Polymarket earlier this year, an investigation not publicly detailed but which is the CFTC’s third inquiry into the platform in recent years. In 2022, Polymarket was fined $1.4m for operating in the US without a license. The senators’ letter urged the CFTC to consider whether betting on wildfires was in the “public interest” and gave the agency until 14 August to respond to a list of questions. “The CFTC must lead the charge to rein in these contracts in the US and offshore and put in place commonsense guardrails to prevent people from profiting as wildfires threaten communities,” the letter demanded. • This article was amended on 12 August 2026. An earlier version incorrectly implied that Kalshi offered betting on wildfires; it does not.

title: Why making Anthony Fauci the enemy will harm US public health for years
body_text: Katie Miller, an erstwhile Trump administration official and wife of Stephen Miller, once relied on Dr Anthony Fauci to get through Covid. Now, she’s calling for his imprisonment – a reversal that illuminates the politicization of Fauci and of public health writ large, a trend that could have major repercussions for America’s preparedness for future crises. A US Senate committee will vote on Thursday morning over whether to hold Fauci in contempt of Congress after the physician and former public health official invoked his fifth amendment rights during a Senate hearing last week focused on Fauci’s actions during the Covid pandemic. The invocation of the worst days of the Covid pandemic comes as midterms loom and the administration struggles to address several infectious outbreaks, including cyclosporiasis and Ebola. Rand Paul, a senator, released contemporaneous notes that Fauci took during his time in public office, which Paul called Fauci’s diary, that reveal the confusion and fear of the time and illuminate the private episodes of a man who became known as America’s doctor. “By focusing entirely on one human being and by calling him all sorts of names, including ‘evil’, and by calling for him to be jailed, it abdicates Republicans’ own responsibility in the US response to the pandemic, which was under President Trump,” said Gavin Yamey, director of the Center for Policy Impact in Global Health at Duke University. “I think that this is all aimed at riling up the base ahead of the midterms and at washing their hands of any culpability themselves in the mass death event of Covid.” And it comes after substantial cuts to the public health infrastructure; misinformation has spread at the highest levels of the government, and growing outbreaks of measles, whooping cough, cyclosporiasis, Ebola and more. “This is an extraordinarily good way to distract people from the very deliberate destruction of the US public health system,” Yamey said. Like most Americans, Miller turned to Fauci for advice during the pandemic. As communications director for then-vice president Mike Pence, she was involved in the White House Covid-19 response. Fauci, who served as the director of the National Institute for Allergies and Infectious Diseases (Niaid), was also the chief medical adviser to seven presidents over three decades. Fauci described Miller warmly, writing that she was “great (tough, smart, but great)” on 25 March 2020, and that they “laugh at each other” in the Situation Room on 6 May 2020. When Miller tested positive for Covid, Fauci called to check on her several times a day. “She is very anxious about getting very ill since she is 10 weeks pregnant. Tonight she had an anxiety reaction. I calmed her over the phone,” Fauci wrote on 9 May 2020. Later, Fauci wrote that he had directly contacted Miller’s pediatricians to discuss the baby’s care. It is perhaps not surprising that Miller would turn to Fauci, as many others in the country also relied on his advice and insight during a deeply uncertain and terrifying time. But her actions contrast with the intensity and speed at which Covid was politicized – and the extent to which Fauci would draw conservatives’ ire, even years later. In February and March 2020, Miller was reassessing communications from the Covid taskforce, and Fauci was told to stand down on media appearances until he received clearance again. “That’s the episode that got tagged ‘muzzling Fauci’,” said Céline Gounder, editor-at-large for public health at KFF Health News and a member of the Covid transition team under Biden. Soon after “deciding how much of Dr Fauci the public gets”, Miller was getting regular check-ins from Fauci on her own health, Gounder pointed out. “The same expertise: she’s rationing public access, but it’s available to her in private.” By April 2020, the pandemic was already being heavily politicized. The administration released plans for states to reopen, and President Trump posted a series of tweets encouraging supporters to “LIBERATE” blue states such as Minnesota, Michigan and Virginia. In late April, nearly half of Republicans (47%) surveyed by Pew Research Center said the pandemic was “made a bigger deal than it really is”. By June, that figure was 63%, and it rose to 66% in September. Republican attention to pandemic coverage went from 48% in March to 43% in late April to 35% by early June, while Democrats did not see any such changes. Spring 2020 looked similar across America; schools, for instance, were closed at about the same rate in red and blue states. But that changed by the fall, when “local partisanship predicted which districts would remain remote better than local Covid incidence did”, Gounder said. Those decisions were made not by Fauci, as he has been accused, but by about 13,349 public school districts, she pointed out in her newsletter, Underlying Conditions. “The more interesting story to me is who had private access to federal scientific expertise, what that access was worth in 2020, and what those same people have said about that expertise since,” Gounder said. She also pointed to early access to experimental treatments for Covid for Trump and his inner circle, nearly two months before they were available to the public. “A president publicly minimized a virus he was privately treated for with a drug the public couldn’t get,” Gounder said. Even after conservatives began publicly opposing his recommendations, the Millers still turned to Fauci for support. Fauci recounted speaking with Miller multiple times in October 2020, after her husband tested positive for Covid and she was traveling. “Spoke to her at Houston airport and after she landed,” he wrote on 6 October 2020. “Am on phone frequently with Katie and Stephen,” Fauci wrote on 31 December 2020. Katie Miller has since come out forcefully against Fauci. On the Covid taskforce, “Fauci cared more about virtue signaling than science,” Miller wrote in September 2025 in an apparent reference to wearing a face mask. In June, she said “he should be in jail”. After Fauci’s notes were made public, Miller claimed Fauci used the pandemic to “maximize his popularity”, and she endorsed calls to prosecute him. She told Notus she kept Fauci close so that he “did not leak against me or my husband”, though she didn’t specify what Fauci might leak. “Dr. Fauci was neither my friend nor my doctor, but a work colleague who weaponized my pregnancy and child for his gain to aggrandize himself,” Miller posted on Thursday, adding that “this man should be in prison”. Fauci has led the US through epidemics and pandemics over the decades: anthrax attacks in 2001, HIV, Sars, Ebola, Covid-19 and more, and he co-authored one of the most esteemed internal medicine textbooks. “We lose a lot when we see Republicans vilify Tony Fauci,” Yamey said. The US wasn’t unsafe because of Fauci’s leadership, Gounder said. “It wasn’t safe to leave home because a novel airborne virus was circulating in a population with no immunity, no vaccine, and no treatment.” And the Trump administration’s politicization and mismanagement “raised the toll”, she added. The trials facing Fauci make it less likely that others will step forward to guide public health, now or during a crisis. There were 1,499 harassment events across 583 local health departments between March 2020 and January 2021, and 222 officials left the field because of the targeting, Gounder pointed out. About 71% of the public health workforce reported at least one symptom of burnout and 20% reported near-constant symptoms in a 2024 survey. Three senior CDC leaders resigned last August over politicization of the agency, and one was fired for refusing to “rubber-stamp” Robert F Kennedy Jr’s anti-vaccine policies. The same month, a man fired more than 180 rounds into the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) campus because of misinformation about the Covid vaccine. He killed a police officer, David Rose. “If you’re 40 and choosing between US government service and industry, that’s now part of the math, not just the vast differences in compensation,” Gounder said. Yamey said he worried “that’s going to put future public health leaders off”. And there is an overwhelming amount of work to be done in addressing current public health crises and decades of repair to come. “But we will get there,” Yamey said. “We will all roll up our sleeves and build back, and hopefully build back better.”

Even after conservatives began publicly opposing his recommendations, the Millers still turned to Fauci for support. Fauci recounted speaking with Miller multiple times in October 2020, after her husband tested positive for Covid and she was traveling. “Spoke to her at Houston airport and after she landed,” he wrote on 6 October 2020. “Am on phone frequently with Katie and Stephen,” Fauci wrote on 31 December 2020. Katie Miller has since come out forcefully against Fauci. On the Covid taskforce, “Fauci cared more about virtue signaling than science,” Miller wrote in September 2025 in an apparent reference to wearing a face mask. In June, she said “he should be in jail”. After Fauci’s notes were made public, Miller claimed Fauci used the pandemic to “maximize his popularity”, and she endorsed calls to prosecute him. She told Notus she kept Fauci close so that he “did not leak against me or my husband”, though she didn’t specify what Fauci might leak. “Dr. Fauci was neither my friend nor my doctor, but a work colleague who weaponized my pregnancy and child for his gain to aggrandize himself,” Miller posted on Thursday, adding that “this man should be in prison”. Fauci has led the US through epidemics and pandemics over the decades: anthrax attacks in 2001, HIV, Sars, Ebola, Covid-19 and more, and he co-authored one of the most esteemed internal medicine textbooks. “We lose a lot when we see Republicans vilify Tony Fauci,” Yamey said. The US wasn’t unsafe because of Fauci’s leadership, Gounder said. “It wasn’t safe to leave home because a novel airborne virus was circulating in a population with no immunity, no vaccine, and no treatment.” And the Trump administration’s politicization and mismanagement “raised the toll”, she added. The trials facing Fauci make it less likely that others will step forward to guide public health, now or during a crisis. There were 1,499 harassment events across 583 local health departments between March 2020 and January 2021, and 222 officials left the field because of the targeting, Gounder pointed out. About 71% of the public health workforce reported at least one symptom of burnout and 20% reported near-constant symptoms in a 2024 survey. Three senior CDC leaders resigned last August over politicization of the agency, and one was fired for refusing to “rubber-stamp” Robert F Kennedy Jr’s anti-vaccine policies. The same month, a man fired more than 180 rounds into the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) campus because of misinformation about the Covid vaccine. He killed a police officer, David Rose. “If you’re 40 and choosing between US government service and industry, that’s now part of the math, not just the vast differences in compensation,” Gounder said. Yamey said he worried “that’s going to put future public health leaders off”. And there is an overwhelming amount of work to be done in addressing current public health crises and decades of repair to come. “But we will get there,” Yamey said. “We will all roll up our sleeves and build back, and hopefully build back better.”

title: US to shut five consulates as critics fear China could fill diplomatic vacuum
body_text: The US state department is to shut five foreign consulates and missions across Asia, Africa, North America and the Caribbean, drawing criticism that it is leaving a diplomatic vacuum at risk of being filled by China. The US Congress has been served notice of the impending closures, which are being justified on cost grounds and follow a reassessment of the US’s bilateral relationships with a range of countries since Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025. According to a notice served to several congressional committees, missions will close in St George’s, Grenada; Nagoya, Japan; Medan, Indonesia; Douala, Cameroon; and Winnipeg, Canada. The closures will continue a process of cutbacks in US state department operations overseen by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state. Last year, the department fired more than 1,300 employees, including 246 foreign services officers and 1,107 civil servants. More than half of the US’s 195 ambassadorial posts around the world remain unfilled, including in keys locations such as Germany, Cuba, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan, according to the American Foreign Service Association. Democrats have criticized the latest planned closures, saying it risked leaving the field free for China. “China has a diplomatic presence in three of the five locations where the state department is closing shop and Beijing is going to exploit that new vacuum to undercut American interests,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate foreign relations committee. “The yearly operating costs of these diplomatic facilities represent a tiny fraction of the state department’s yearly budget,” Shaheen added. “Is that worth pulling back from these places where China is present?” The decision to close the consulate in Winnipeg has come in for criticism in Canada, on which Trump recently announced the imposition of 50% tariffs on a range of goods. Opened in 2001, the Winnipeg consulate has served to facilitate trade and investment issues mainly relating to the province of Manitoba, of which Winnipeg is the capital. Brad Kirbyson, a former political specialist who worked at the consulate for 20 years, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC the closure could harm US interests. “I’m sure it’ll save them a few dollars, but I think the net effect is to lose touch with a broad swath of Canada by not having a presence there,” he said. “The United States found that it was a very long way between the US consulate in Calgary and the [one] in Toronto. “It makes a lot of sense to have a consulate in the middle of the country that can cover issues in this part of the world.” A spokesperson for the Canadian embassy in Washington said: “Canada and the US have a long history of collaboration on areas of shared interest, including through our foreign offices in both countries.” China does not have a diplomatic mission in Winnipeg, but it has a presence in St George’s, Nagoya and Medan. The US mission in St George’s, the capital of the Caribbean island of Grenada, has full embassy status, while the Douala facility is defined as an “embassy branch office”. A state department spokesperson said: “The department is committed to following congressional notification procedures including post closures. We have nothing further to report at this time. “We are focused on ensuring our diplomatic footprint is efficient, effective and delivers results for the American people.” In a later statement, issued after this story was first published, a department spokesperson countered the assertion that the closures would benefit China. “Claims that China is filling a diplomatic vacuum is [sic] inherently false and we recommend that individuals who subscribe to this propaganda take a look at the so-called help China had in the recent earthquakes in Venezuela or to address the Ebola outbreak,” the spokesperson said. The White House’s office of management and budget has argued for a much more extensive closure program of up to 30 foreign missions. Democrats, supported by national security and foreign policy specialists, have countered that such moves will dangerously reduce the US’s diplomatic footprint and global influence, especially when combined with last year’s dismantling of USAID, the main overseas development body, which was drastically reduced in size before being bundled into the state department.

title: Trump denies US low on key munitions in war with Iran after reports of shortages
body_text: Donald Trump has lashed out at reports that the US is running short of key munitions in its war with Iran, threatening long prison sentences for officials who leak information about the military’s weapons stocks. The US president claimed on Thursday that the US had “massive amounts” of ammunition and said more was being manufactured and shipped to the region, as his frustration over the conflict spilled into a public attack on the media. “Defense companies are building the largest number of plants and factories in our country’s history,” Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform, without providing evidence or details about the specific weapons in question. His remarks came after a report that he had demanded answers from his defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, over alleged shortages at a cabinet meeting last Friday at Camp David, the US presidential retreat in Maryland. Trump told Hegseth he felt misled because he believed the problem “had been fixed”, according to the Washington Post newspaper, citing two unnamed sources familiar with the exchange. Hegseth defended himself and sought to shift blame to his deputy, Stephen Feinberg, the Post reported. The president responded angrily on Thursday, accusing the media of spreading “treasonous statements” and warning that those responsible would be pursued. “The ‘leakers’ of these treasonous statements are being hunted down,” he wrote. “Long term jail sentences will be sought!” The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that Trump had ordered investigations into the disclosures about US munitions stockpiles. CNN separately reported that shortages of long-range guided missiles and air defence interceptors had begun to constrain Trump’s strategy in the conflict. The US military had “nearly exhausted 80%” of its stock of Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (Thaad) interceptors, the network said. The Washington Post also reported that concerns over dwindling supplies had contributed to Trump calling off further strikes against Iran, despite his repeated threats to hit the Islamic Republic “very hard”. The White House and Pentagon rejected the claims. Karoline Leavitt, the White House press secretary, described the account of the Camp David exchange as “FAKE NEWS!” on X. She wrote: “I was at Camp David with President Trump and Secretary Hegseth. This literally never happened.” Seeking to quash speculation about Hegseth’s future, Leavitt insisted that “the President loves the Secretary and thinks he’s doing a tremendous job”. Sean Parnell, the chief Pentagon spokesperson, dismissed both the reports of a confrontation between Trump and Hegseth and claims of weapons shortages as “equally fictional”. Parnell added: “Secretary Hegseth isn’t going anywhere and he’s going to continue to work side by side with Deputy Secretary Feinberg to execute President Trump’s agenda, strengthen America’s defense industrial base, and ensure our warfighters have every capability they need to deter and defeat any adversary.” Trump himself weighed in later on Thursday. “I am extremely happy with the job that Pete Hegseth is doing,” the president said on social media, accusing outlets reporting otherwise of “spreading false and completely unfounded rumors”. The increasingly public dispute comes as Trump seeks to project confidence over the course of the war. On Sunday he claimed he had ordered and subsequently called off “the biggest attack since” the second world war, in the light of fresh negotiations over the strait of Hormuz. Iran’s foreign ministry denied that talks were taking place, despite Trump’s claim that Tehran was eager to reach a deal. The Pentagon has faced criticism for manipulating US casualty figures and failing to hold regular press briefings about the war. Hegseth, a former Fox News host who styles himself as the secretary of war, last month announced a screening programme for “testosterone deficiency” among US troops. Joe Scarborough, an MS Now host and former Republican congressman, posted on X: “When Hegseth attacks media questions on this extreme munitions shortage as ‘fake news’, he makes this unforgivable blunder worse. Congress needs to take action. Americans need the truth. Hegseth can’t give it. He needs to go.”

title: Trump is laying waste to the agency that keeps hospital patients safe
body_text: When I started my training in 1980, we accepted an arithmetic that would now be indefensible. Central lines, the catheters we threaded into the great veins of the critically ill, became infected, and some of those patients died. We recorded the deaths as complications. Almost no one thought of them as preventable, because no one had yet done the slow work of proving they were. That work got done, and federal money paid for it. Beginning in 2008, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, a small arm of the health department, funded a national effort in more than a thousand adult intensive care units: a checklist, a sterile insertion protocol, and a unit culture in which a nurse could stop a surgeon. Central-line bloodstream infections fell by 41%, from 1.915 to 1.133 per 1,000 catheter days. The agency estimates that effort alone averted between 290 and 605 deaths. Across its wider work on hospital-acquired harm, AHRQ’s own accounting credits 20,500 deaths prevented and $7.7bn saved in the four years from 2014 to 2017. Hardly any of my patients have heard of the agency. That was always rather the point. On 15 July, AHRQ sent researchers around the country nearly identical letters ending at least 104 grants, most of them aimed at making care safer. Congress appropriated $345m for the agency this fiscal year. It has spent under $15m on grants and has not issued a new one in more than a year. About three-quarters of the staff have been fired or have quit since Donald Trump took office, and the office that ran grant review was eliminated last summer. An agency with no grant managers cannot make grants, which tells you how long the closure is meant to last. Senator Tammy Baldwin, the ranking Democrat on the appropriations subcommittee that funds AHRQ, counts 150 awards cut off, worth $94m. If you have spent a night in a US hospital in the past 20 years, this agency was working on your behalf whether you knew it or not. It built the patient-experience surveys Medicare uses to help set what hospitals are paid. The quality indicators regulators rely on to spot a hospital that is harming people are its work. With the defense department, it produced the team-communication training now standard in operating rooms and emergency departments. The scientist who spent three decades building those Medicare surveys learned her funding was gone from an email that arrived around 5pm. Among the other grants killed this month: training for physicians, nurses and paramedics managing high-risk pregnancies, in a country where rural women die of pregnancy-related causes at two to three times the rate of women elsewhere; a study of how to spare children in community emergency rooms from unnecessary CT scans and the radiation dose that comes with them; work on catching lung cancer earlier; and telehealth projects serving rural patients. The stated rationale does not hold. AHRQ’s director, Roger Klein, told grantees the agency was redirecting resources toward patient safety, antibiotic resistance, overmedication of children and measurable health outcomes. When KFF Health News examined about 20 of the cancelled grants, nearly all of them pursued those objectives. One of the cancelled grants studied antibiotic resistance. The Michigan pediatrician who lost the last two years of her award said none of it makes any sense, and her field studies exactly what Robert F Kennedy Jr’s “Make America healthy again” agenda claims to champion. Klein has held no agency-wide meetings and published no plan. He has said little in public since January, when he co-wrote an essay in Newsweek arguing that “scientific neutrality” had given way to “moral signaling”. He has reportedly told staff that artificial intelligence can replace much of what his scientists do. A White House science report released on 22 July urged the government to back individual scientists over legacy institutions, to move past slow consensus peer review and to build the future on AI. I use AI tools daily. They are gifted assistants, and they have never placed a central line. I wrote this week in the Annals of Internal Medicine about patients who arrive holding a chatbot’s answer. The models are fluent and often correct, but they have no way of knowing what they were never told. That limit scales. A language model can summarize everything ever published about catheter infections. Someone still had to stand in the unit at three in the morning and notice that the nurses were quietly working around the protocol. Someone still had to design the study that found out why. None of that knowledge existed until people went and got it. Then there is the money. Congress decides how public funds are spent, a principle written into statute after Richard Nixon tried withholding appropriations he disliked. The Society of General Internal Medicine and the North American Primary Care Research Group sued Kennedy and Klein last August over the frozen grant-making, and the case is pending in Maryland. The Government Accountability Office is examining whether the agency’s conduct amounts to an unlawful impoundment. On 17 July a federal judge in Boston held that agencies may not cancel awards over priorities they adopted after making them. Now consider what the health department says about the AHRQ letters: nothing was terminated, and the grants were merely “not awarded continued funding”. That phrasing is doing work. It is an attempt to walk through the one door the court left open. After 45 years in medicine, I know this much about safety. When it works, no one notices. No patient wakes up grateful for the bloodstream infection she did not get, or for the dose a pharmacist’s protocol caught before it reached her line. AHRQ costs each American about a dollar a year, roughly 0.3% of the health department’s discretionary spending, and it is being dismantled in the confidence that the people it protects will never learn what they were spared. The deaths will arrive one at a time, in different hospitals, unlabeled. No letter from Washington will claim them. In 1980 we did not know how to prevent those deaths. We know now. That knowledge took 30 years and public money to build, and it is being discarded by people who have not said why. Robert B Shpiner is an internist and clinical professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA. He has practiced and taught intensive care medicine for more than 40 years

title: US unexpectedly lost 23,000 jobs in July as slump in growth continues
body_text: US employers unexpectedly lost 23,000 jobs in July and gains for the previous two months were revised down sharply by a combined 103,000 jobs, painting a weaker picture of the labor market than past data indicated. The unemployment rate, however, held steady at 4.1%. Economists had projected an unchanged unemployment rate and 83,000 new jobs for the month. The latest data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics illustrates the continued summer slump in job growth amid ongoing conflict in the Middle East. Pressure has been mounting within the US Federal Reserve to raise interest rates to combat persistently high inflation, but July’s job report and its latest revisions may cool those expectations at the central bank’s next meeting. July’s job losses were concentrated in local government education, with 50,000 jobs lost, and retail, which lost 19,000. The private sector, however, gained 30,000 jobs, with growth focused once again in healthcare. Hourly earnings of all employees changed little over the past year, increasing by 3.2% compared to last year. Next week’s consumer pricing data will reveal whether these gains have kept pace with inflation. Figures for May were revised to 63,000 jobs added, down from an initially reported 129,000 jobs, while figures for June dropped 37,000, to 20,000 jobs added. In total, job figures for May and June were revised down 103,000 jobs. In June, the US added 57,000 jobs, about half of what economists had predicted, with most of the growth concentrated in healthcare and social assistance. The unemployment rate had also dropped to 4.2% in June, down from 4.3% in May, driven by 720,000 people leaving the workforce. Other data had pointed toward a slowdown in July. Private employers added 44,000 jobs in July, according to the payroll firm ADP, a significant drop from the 98,000 jobs added in June recorded by the firm. Job openings decreased by 178,000 to 7.4m in June, according to the latest Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey. Job openings in healthcare and social assistance, key areas of job growth, declined by 147,000 in June, the largest decline since July 2025. Economists have long said the US labor market is in a “low-hire, low-fire” state, and recent data from outplacement firm Challenger, Gray and Christmas found that layoffs in July plunged compared with last year. US-based employers announced about 33,500 job cuts in July, the lowest month in two years. Though consumer spending has remained resilient, increasing by 0.3% in June 2026, the personal savings rate for Americans in June 2026 hit a four-year low at 2.7%, the lowest rate since June 2022, according to the US Bureau of Economic Analysis. “With immigration having largely been stopped – and possibly now a net negative – the labor force is growing very slowly,” wrote Dean Baker, economist and co-founder of the Center for Economic and Policy Research, in a post on what to expect from the July jobs report. “However, slower wage growth, even in the face of rising inflation, indicates it is not a very good labor market for most workers. That story does not seem likely to change any time soon.” Economists are closely watching the labor market and inflation as officials at Fed have become divided on whether to raise interest rates or leave them unchanged. Though the Fed held rates steady last month, officials indicated that they expect at least one rate hike before the end of the year to combat price increases. The annualized inflation rate in June was 3.5% – 0.8% higher than a year prior. title: Netanyahu rejects US-led 15-point Gaza peace plan in rare public break with Trump
body_text: Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan for Gaza in a rare public break with Donald Trump. In a statement on Sunday, Netanyahu said that he was confronting a “wave of rumours about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts” and rebuked US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in. On Gaza, he said: “Israel does not accept the 15-point document. The IDF will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is disarmed. And when I say the disarming of Hamas, it means heavy weaponry, lighter weaponry, all weaponry. And we are talking about genuine disarmament, not fictitious disarmament. Right now, we are talking with the Americans about this issue.” Trump’s Board of Peace in July proposed the 15-point plan, which mandated that Hamas disarm in exchange for providing a full Israeli military withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and an eventual transition of power to an independent Palestinian National Committee. Trump had said that the agreement would be implemented in stages, but Netanyahu on Sunday said that he wanted a full disarmament first in order to implement the deal. The Israeli leader’s main target in his remarks was the US. Israel has emerged as a key stumbling block in the Trump White House’s plans to broker peace in the region, in Israel’s conflicts in Gaza and Lebanon as well as in the war begun by joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran. And Netanyahu, who is facing tough elections in October and pressure from hardliners in his own government, appears ready to test his relationship with Trump in public in order to shore up his reputation as a defender of Israel at home. Israel had already signalled that it would reject the US-led plan. Soon after Trump announced it last month, Israel stepped up its bombing campaign in the Palestinian territory – strikes killed 18 people last Sunday. Netanyahu’s office had previously indicated it would not back the plan, saying: “The version that has been made public does not reflect Israel’s positions.” But Sunday’s rejection was far more forceful and direct, and appeared targeted at the Trump White House, as Trump and Netanyahu both face difficult elections. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said. The head of Trump’s Board of Peace hit back on Sunday, saying the plan remained the “only way forward”. Nickolay Mladenov, the board’s high representative for Gaza, told Israeli television: “The option we are offering today is the only way forward that ensures this tragedy does not happen again.” Netanyahu’s rejection is a blow to Trump’s desire to be seen as a broker of peace in foreign conflicts. With US midterm elections due in November, the White House is desperate to negotiate a peace in Iran in order to reopen the strait of Hormuz and help bring down oil and petrol prices. But the conflicts in the Middle East are interconnected and parallel US efforts have continued to bring peace to Lebanon, where Israel has occupied land in what it says is a buffer zone against Hezbollah, and Gaza, where Gulf allies of the US have decried what they say is an ethnic cleansing campaign being carried out by Israel. Like US presidents before him, Trump has found that Netanyahu can be a difficult ally. Bill Clinton, after meeting Netanyahu for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?” More recently, the Biden administration found that its concerns about the human toll in Gaza were ignored, but continued to publicly back Netanyahu and did not significantly suspend military aid to the country for fear of the political blowback that Netanyahu and his allies in the US could cause. In Trump, however, Netanyahu has found a far more unorthodox and unpredictable counterpart in the White House. Netanyahu is a natural ally for Trump, and he has attacked Democrats before the midterm elections for being weak on supporting Israel. Yet more broadly, support for Israel and its war in Gaza is eroding in the Democratic party, and the Republicans have a presidential frontrunner for 2028 in the vice-president, JD Vance, who is publicly sceptical of Israel and the war in Gaza. Trump will have to decide whether to increase pressure on Netanyahu, potentially alienating some pro-Israel allies, or to allow his efforts for a Gaza peace plan to stall, perhaps indefinitely. The answer will depend heavily on the US president’s own political instincts – are US voters hoping to see Trump emerge as a statesman capable of ending one of the world’s bloodiest recent wars in Gaza, or would a public clash with Netanyahu provoke a revolt among his base? With both countries entering tumultuous election cycles and a generational shift in support for Israel among US voters, the result could redraw the alliance between Israel and the US.
