title: US lawmakers pass bill giving Trump more power to sanction Russia and its enablers
body_text: The US Congress has passed a sweeping bill allowing Donald Trump to raise tariffs on top buyers of Russian energy and issue other punishing sanctions against the Kremlin following a pitched battle between lawmakers backing Ukraine and sceptics worried the bill gives the president too much power. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed in a 262-159 vote on the last day before Congress goes on recess ahead of the midterm elections. Graham, who died earlier this year, co-authored and submitted the bill more than a year and a half ago. The long delay in the vote was widely considered to be scepticism from the Trump administration, which had opposed additional sanctions and then recently changed its stance to support tabling the bill as efforts to negotiate with the Kremlin to end the war have yielded few results. However the bill faced last-minute hurdles in Congress as members of the Republican party’s isolationist wing were joined by Democrats who warned that Trump could use the bill’s new tariffs authority against allies instead. The bill would mandate new sanctions on Russian political and military officials, and foreign networks helping to supply Russia’s war machine and evade existing sanctions. It would also target Russia’s so-called fleet of “shadow tankers”, which have allowed the country to continue to ship crude around the world despite sanctions on its energy exports. It would also allow Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian energy, including China, as well as other countries helping the Kremlin evade sanctions. Senior Democrats voiced opposition to the bill during a heated floor debate. “Why in the world would this Congress give this president additional authority to visit that kind of economic harm on the American people?” said Hakeem Jeffries, the leading Democrat in the House, during a speech on Wednesday, adding he would vote against the bill. Democratic staffers supporting the bill said that it offered a “last chance” to increase sanctions on Russia before Ukraine entered a “long winter”. Russia has improved the drone technology it has used to strike Ukrainian infrastructure as Kyiv has suffered a shortage of anti-air missiles, leaving the country in a dire position. Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican supporting the bill, called it the US Congress’ “Churchill vs Chamberlain Moment on Russia”. “Choking off the money funding a war of conquest in Europe is exactly what that authority should be used for, and Congress deciding to do that is Congress doing its constitutional job,” he said, rejecting arguments by Democrats that the bill gave Trump too much authority to slap tariffs on foreign countries. The bill passed the Senate last month in a landslide 86-11 vote. However it faced more pushback in the House of Representatives. A Tuesday rule vote allowing consideration of Senate amendments to the bill passed by just 214-211, with two renegade Democrats joining Republicans to vote in favour of what they said was an act of support for Ukraine. That vote led to senior Democrats holding terse talks with their fellow party members. “I’m proud to represent one of the largest Ukrainian communities in America – people who have lost fathers, mothers, sons and daughters in the fight to defeat fascism,” wrote Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, one of the two Democrat representatives, in a statement on Tuesday. “I’ll always stand with my community’s values, and am grateful for the 86 senators who voted to send this bill to the House. My vote today gets us one step closer to enacting these sanctions into law and I look forward to voting tomorrow to cut off the flow of Russian oil money fuelling this war.” The Ukrainian government has said it supported the bill, and hundreds of pro-Ukrainian activists calling for tougher sanctions on Russia held advocacy talks in Washington DC in the days leading up to the vote. “We support any initiative that is in the interest of Ukraine and Ukrainians,” said Denys Sienik, the Chargé d’Affaires at the Ukrainian embassy in Washington DC. “So if we are talking about the possibility of putting more pressure on Russia so that it holds the Russian war machine, of course, we are there, and we are grateful to every senator, to every congressman and congresswoman for their voice and, and for their support.”

title: Trump and Rubio allies are vying for control of Cuba’s assets if regime falls
body_text: Spanish hotel chains. A Canadian mining firm. European shipping giants. Visa and Mastercard. Scores of foreign companies have been driven out of Cuba this summer over fear of being hit with potent, new secondary sanctions. Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, told Axios last month there are “no escape valves” from his unprecedented pressure campaign against the island. But not everybody is losing out. A growing cast of Washington and Florida insiders – from billionaire Trump allies and Rubio-linked lobbyists to Cuban exiles – are jockeying for control of the communist-ruled island-nation’s key assets, charging top dollar to help clients navigate the ever-expanding web of sanctions, and positioning themselves for lucrative business opportunities in the case of regime collapse. Since an executive order signed by Donald Trump on 1 May drove Canada’s Sherritt International from its nickel and cobalt mining joint venture with the Cuban state, two rival US bids to buy out its stake have been presented to US authorities. Ray Washburne, the vice-chair of Trump’s 2016 Victory Committee who organized last week’s Republican Midterm Convention in Dallas, is clashing with Albert Huddleston, another Texas oil tycoon with close ties to the White House. Both are hoping to swoop in, despite nine-figure claims on Sherritt’s Cuba holdings by Citigroup and Office Depot – Fortune 500 corporations. Washburne did not respond to the Guardian and the consortium group including Huddleston declined to comment. A similar approach is being pursued by Australia’s Antilles Gold Ltd, which after being blacklisted over its Cuba operations in June received the green light from the Trump administration to negotiate the transfer of its stake in a Cuban copper-gold mine to the New York-based, multibillion-dollar investment fund, Global Emerging Markets. “If I had done during the Biden administration what Trump’s friends have done now, I’d have been put in jail,” said a person with several decades of experience in Cuba policy who requested anonymity. Sources tell the Guardian that several Trump Organization executives who had previously traveled to the island to explore real estate deals and who even registered the Trump trademark there in 2008 have in recent months returned to Cuba under the aegis of Dominari Holdings for meetings. The executives are said to have met with Raúl Guillermo Rodríguez Castro, the grandson of former Cuban president Raúl Castro, dubbed “the Crab”, to explore opportunities amid the departure of Spanish hotel giants Meliá and Iberostar, which had been operating on the island since the 1990s. Neither Antilles nor Dominari returned calls for comment. But American investors aren’t the only ones sensing opportunity in Rubio’s effort to coerce the sanctions-battered country of his parents’ birth into becoming economically dependent on the US. Cubans have been living under an effective fuel blockade since January 2026: the Trump administration cut oil shipments to the island from the island’s main ally after abducting Nicolás Maduro, the Venezuelan president; it then nixed oil deliveries from Mexico by threatening tariffs on any country sending petroleum to the island. Treasury department-authorised oil exports from Florida and Texas to the island’s private sector, however – all but non-existent last year – have shot up to over $160m so far this year. Meanwhile, Florida shipping lines such as Crowley, a donor to Cuban-American Republican lawmakers from Florida, Mario Díaz-Balart and María Elvira-Salazar, seem to be beneficiaries of fresh sanctions that have hit foreign shippers and forced Cuba-bound commerce to reroute through Florida, according to informed sources who spoke with the Guardian. Crowley declined to comment. And as UN human rights experts warn that Washington’s latest measures “knowingly deprive a population of the means to survive”, Franklin Graham, the Trump-allied CEO of evangelical aid organization Samaritan’s Purse recently secured a $40m federal contract to distribute humanitarian aid in Cuba – despite lacking the capacity to effectively implement such a contract on the island, according to sources familiar with the matter. A spokesperson for Samaritan’s Purse said: “Details about aid for Cuba are still being developed and are not yet finalized.” Ironically, some of those who have called most vociferously for harsher sanctions are also cashing in. In July, Madrid-based Vima World SL, a leading player in the island’s food industry which partners with GAESA, the Cuban military conglomerate that controls large swathes of the island’s economy and has become the main target of the US squeeze, hired top Washington lobbying firm Continental Strategy – led by Cuban-American allies of Rubio who oversaw the maximum pressure Cuba policy as officials in the first Trump administration – for matters related to trade, foreign relations and the food industry. Continental’s executives include Carlos Trujillo, Trump’s former ambassador to the Organization of American States John Barsa, Trump’s former acting USAID administrator and Alberto Martinez, Rubio’s former chief of staff. The firm, which terminated its contract with Vima this month after netting nearly $40,000 according to corporate disclosures, has been known for providing lobbying and government relations services to clients staunchly opposed to the one-party state, including MasTec, the telecom company owned by Rubio’s friend Jorge Mas Santos; American Sugar Refineries, owned by Trump-ballroom donor and Rubio patron Pepe Fanjul; and General Cigar Co, which is fighting Cuba’s state-owned tobacco enterprise in US court for the rights to the Cohiba cigar trademark. “It’s been interesting to watch how quickly some hardline ideologues become pragmatists once there’s money on the table,” one person familiar with the contract told the Guardian, noting that Continental has taken on other Spanish firms with Cuban business interests “trying to get on the right side of sanctions, like banks and hotel chains”. Other organizations that for years have won seven-figure grants from US federal agencies are capitalizing on the Trump administration’s push to force sweeping political and economic change on the island. Lobbying disclosure forms filed in July by a newly formed group made up of former employees at the US taxpayer-funded Foundation for Human Rights in Cuba (FHRC), alongside longtime Republican lobbyist Otto Reich and the husband of top Rubio state department aide Viviana Bovo, indicate it is “advising [the] State Department on [an] economic development plan for a future free and democratic Cuba, including energy-sector development and compensation for owners of property/business expropriated by the Cuban government”. Reich and Tony Costa, the Foundation for Human Rights chairman, are involved in efforts to mobilize billions of dollars in private investment from wealthy Cuban exiles for a post-communist Cuba through the newly created Cuban-American National Chamber of Commerce (CANCC). To get their priorities heard by lawmakers and officials in Washington, FHRC and another attendee of the CANCC gatherings, Armando Labrador, a Miami-based plastic surgeon who regularly meets with state department officials and wants to become Cuba’s next leader, have paid DC lobbying firm The Cormac Group a combined $100,000 since December. For another US taxpayer-funded non-profit that had been the subject of an internal Biden administration inquiry that was quickly shut down by powerful House appropriators, the administration’s unprecedented economic siege could not have come at a better time. Just before the July release of a heavily criticized state department report referring to Cuba as a nearby terror hub plotting to conquer the US, Digital News Association Inc received a fresh $250,000 contract from the US government’s office of Cuba broadcasting for “investigative journalism, research and media production”, after which its main site launched an online interview series repeating Trump administration claims of Cuba’s purported threat to US national security. Vima, Continental, Cormac and Digital News did not return calls for comment. “The cause is regime change,” said Erik Cartelle, a consultant working to connect prominent exiles with Rubio’s state department. “I have clients that want to do a lot of business in Cuba, and the administration is banking on Cuban-Americans going to Cuba and investing, but if there’s a deal that’s going to be had with the regime, it needs to take into account the diaspora’s wishes. You’ve got to listen to this community.”

Other organizations that for years have won seven-figure grants from US federal agencies are capitalizing on the Trump administration’s push to force sweeping political and economic change on the island. Lobbying disclosure forms filed in July by a newly formed group made up of former employees at the US taxpayer-funded Foundation for Human Rights in Cuba (FHRC), alongside longtime Republican lobbyist Otto Reich and the husband of top Rubio state department aide Viviana Bovo, indicate it is “advising [the] State Department on [an] economic development plan for a future free and democratic Cuba, including energy-sector development and compensation for owners of property/business expropriated by the Cuban government”. Reich and Tony Costa, the Foundation for Human Rights chairman, are involved in efforts to mobilize billions of dollars in private investment from wealthy Cuban exiles for a post-communist Cuba through the newly created Cuban-American National Chamber of Commerce (CANCC). To get their priorities heard by lawmakers and officials in Washington, FHRC and another attendee of the CANCC gatherings, Armando Labrador, a Miami-based plastic surgeon who regularly meets with state department officials and wants to become Cuba’s next leader, have paid DC lobbying firm The Cormac Group a combined $100,000 since December. For another US taxpayer-funded non-profit that had been the subject of an internal Biden administration inquiry that was quickly shut down by powerful House appropriators, the administration’s unprecedented economic siege could not have come at a better time. Just before the July release of a heavily criticized state department report referring to Cuba as a nearby terror hub plotting to conquer the US, Digital News Association Inc received a fresh $250,000 contract from the US government’s office of Cuba broadcasting for “investigative journalism, research and media production”, after which its main site launched an online interview series repeating Trump administration claims of Cuba’s purported threat to US national security. Vima, Continental, Cormac and Digital News did not return calls for comment. “The cause is regime change,” said Erik Cartelle, a consultant working to connect prominent exiles with Rubio’s state department. “I have clients that want to do a lot of business in Cuba, and the administration is banking on Cuban-Americans going to Cuba and investing, but if there’s a deal that’s going to be had with the regime, it needs to take into account the diaspora’s wishes. You’ve got to listen to this community.”

title: Pennsylvania asks CDC for emergency help as measles outbreak spreads
body_text: Pennsylvania is seeking emergency assistance from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as a major measles outbreak spreads across the state. The state warned the request could be withdrawn unless the federal agency publicly recognizes four measles-associated deaths reported by the state. The Pennsylvania department of health has begun the process of requesting CDC emergency support known as an Epi-Aid, according to a letter reviewed by the Guardian. The letter was first reported by Reuters on Thursday. Debra Bogen, Pennsylvania’s secretary of health, outlined the condition in a letter sent on Wednesday to the CDC director, Erica Schwartz. “The CDC’s choice not to publicly recognize ⁠the deaths undermines our response,” Bogen wrote. “For this reason, if CDC is unable to transparently and accurately communicate information about those measles-associated deaths, the department will respectfully rescind our request for a CDC Epi-Aid.” The development comes amid an ongoing dispute involving Josh Shapiro, the state’s Democratic governor, and Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, over the state’s handling of the outbreak and how measles-related deaths are being counted. Kennedy has questioned whether deaths linked to the measles outbreaks since he took office were caused by the virus or by another condition. He also instructed the CDC not to include Pennsylvania’s reported fatalities in the national measles death count last month, a move health experts called “highly unusual” and warned it could lead the public to underestimate the dangers of measles. Kennedy, meanwhile, has accused Shapiro of politicizing Pennsylvania’s outbreak and failing to seek out federal assistance. The state’s latest move marks a shift from its earlier position. Pennsylvania health officials had previously resisted CDC assistance, saying they were capable of managing the outbreak without federal help. Since then, the situation has worsened. On Wednesday, the Pennsylvania health department announced that 731 measles cases have been confirmed in 38 counties across the state so far this year. Four people have died in the state from measles-related illness as of Tuesday. The CDC did not immediately respond to the Guardian’s request for comment. The outbreak is among the largest and deadliest in the country and comes as the US experiences its most severe measles resurgence in more than three decades, driven by increasing vaccine hesitancy. This month, it was revealed that the Trump administration changed the way it counts measles deaths amid the outbreak in Pennsylvania. The CDC is now using data from the National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS), which is a way to track mortality trends over time. It is unclear why this change was made. On Wednesday, Bill Cassidy, a Republican chair of the Senate health committee, blamed the Trump administration’s vaccine-skeptical approach for the ‌recent measles deaths in Pennsylvania.

title: RFK Jr promises anti-vaxxers a ‘friend at the White House’ amid deadly measles outbreak
body_text: As the death toll from the worst measles outbreak in decades rises, Robert F Kennedy Jr headlined the Washington DC conference of the anti-vaccine organization Children’s Health Defense, which he led for nearly a decade. “Let me be clear. You have a strong and steadfast friend at the White House,” Kennedy, now serving as secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), told anti-vaccine activists at the conference in a nearly hour-and-a-half-long speech. He urged patience, saying that he would’ve made sweeping changes “on day one” but that he had to follow the law in order to make permanent change. “But as I said, you have friends in the White House, and we are doing this one day at a time,” Kennedy said. He only addressed the measles outbreak, which recently killed four people in Pennsylvania, once. “In our country we care about rare illnesses and deaths. We care about every child who dies from measles. They get headlines,” he said. “I’d ask you to care about children who are dying or suffering or being injured by vaccine injuries.” Recent polling suggests that one quarter of Americans now have doubts about the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccines following a years-long campaign against immunizations by once-fringe actors. But the majority of Americans also disapprove of the Trump administration’s handling of the widening measles outbreak, which killed three people in Texas and Arizona last year in addition to those inPennsylvania. Kennedy described “vaccine-injured children” as “damaged” because of diagnoses of allergies, asthma, ADHD and autism, among other conditions. He also claimed that diabetes, sudden infant death syndrome, and anorexia can be side effects of routine vaccines, and he said that the system to track such effects is “broken”. There is little daylight between Kennedy and his former organization. “I spent 40 years in these battles,” Kennedy said. “I intend to stay in this fight as long as I am able.” He thanked his friends who are still at CHD. Longtime anti-vaccine activists celebrated their unprecedented role in the national conversation, at times expressing astonishment over the ways anti-vaccine sentiment has been elevated to the highest levels of the US government. “We have an opportunity today to speak to our colleagues and our friends in mainstream media,” the CEO of the Children’s Health Defense, Mary Holland, said at the event on Thursday. Andrew Wakefield, a former gastroenterologist whose medical license was revoked after he was found to have fabricated research indicating a link between vaccines and autism, spoke before and immediately after Kennedy. “I could not have imagined two years ago that Bobby [Kennedy] would be in the White House and that President Trump would be saying ‘divide up the MMR into three different’,” said Wakefield, who proposed the same strategy years earlier when he attempted to patent his own single measles shot to compete with the MMR. He stopped to laugh. “What drug was I on that morning?” Anti-vaccine activists had become nervous earlier this year after the White House reportedly put the kibosh on speaking about vaccines before the US midterm elections. “February, March, April, May, vaccine reform got a little quiet, a little scary. You know, behind the scenes, we’re like, “Yeah, what happened?” said Michael Kane, CHD’s director of advocacy. But recent months have shifted vaccines back into the spotlight. “Just a few years ago, we were the, you know, hated stepchild in the corner,” Kane said. “Now we are a national movement that isn’t going anywhere.” The organization laid out its policy agenda, including plans to challenge state-level immunization requirements for school attendance, to recruit younger people to the aging organization, and to combat the installation of cell phone towers for fears of 5G and 6G. Several speakers explicitly linked vaccination to autism, despite decades of research showing no connection. Meanwhile, Kennedy also focused on the role of food systems in health, and touched on efforts to study electromagnetic fields and chem trails. He praised researchers at the University of Southern Denmark, who are now under investigation by their institution, as “the deities of vaccine research”. Kennedy attempted to fund their project in Guinea-Bissau looking at mortality after hepatitis B vaccination before local authorities cancelled the project. Their prior work on vaccines has been called “a house of cards” by other researchers. Mark Gorton, president of the Maha Institute, referred to himself as “the boldest anti-vaxxer in the anti-vax conference”, adding that “only anti-vaxxers can speak clearly enough to raise awareness.” Being called the “largest anti-vaccine conference, probably in the world” is “a red badge of courage”, said sen Ron Johnson, a Republican from Wisconsin. Johnson and Sen Rand Paul, a Republican and physician from Kentucky, both rehashed grievances over the Covid pandemic and the immunizations that were rapidly deployed to stem the tide of illness and death. Republican congressman Thomas Massie said he called Donald Trump soon after the election to ask for the agriculture secretary position. Trump asked, “Are you friends with Bobby? Is he too much for HHS? Don’t you think we need some vaccines?” Massie recounted. Kennedy was nominated to HHS the next day, he said. Massie offered two pieces of advice to the anti-vaccine activists: Instead of trying to get rid of “clowns”, he said, “get the clowns who are here to do what you want. Get them to get in the clown car you want. And use pressure. Treat them like cattle.” Coverage of the measles outbreak is a “psy op” that is “meant to control what I think, what I do, what I believe, and what my attitude towards Bobby Kennedy ought to be,” said Tony Lyons, the publisher of books from Kennedy who now heads Maha Action. Kennedy was frequently invoked as a hero of the movement at the conference. “The truth is, he really is dangerous,” Lyons said, invoking the common refrain from scientists and experts. “I think Bobby Kennedy is the most dangerous individual to this system who’s come along in a generation,” he said to a burst of applause. This article was amended on 17 September 2026 to clarify that Kennedy led Children’s Health Defense for nearly a decade.

title: No more book bans: how Florida students are pushing rightwingers out of school boards
body_text: Jimmy Glover’s youngest children were in high school when he noticed their Florida school district taking an unsettling turn. Beloved books were being pulled from shelves. Teachers were scared of being targeted. “There was this culture of fear that was permeating throughout the district,” Glover said of Sarasota county. By channeling anger against mask mandates in schools, the rightwing group Moms for Liberty, founded in Florida, built an outsized influence on school boards across the country in 2022. Soon, members began pressuring schools to remake their curricula along conservative ideological lines, erasing mentions of LGBTQ+ Americans, slavery, racism and more. As a Black dad living in a historically Black part of Sarasota, Glover said he was especially disturbed by governor Ron DeSantis’s announcement that Florida schools would begin teaching students that some Black people benefited from slavery. “Now my children and the students in my community weren’t going to be learning about the true history of this country,” Glover said. So the father of four decided to run for Sarasota’s school board this year. He is part of a larger movement of students, parents, teachers and concerned community members pushing back against the influence of groups like Moms for Liberty in Florida public education. They wanted schools that were safe and welcoming for all students, and that focused on learning rather than scoring points on the national political scene. And last month, they won. Progressive candidates beat opponents backed by or aligned with Moms for Liberty in school board races across the state – in many cases reversing gains made by the group in 2022. Of the 30 candidates the group supported that year, 20 have declined to seek re-election, have been defeated or will face runoffs in November, according to the LGBTQ+ rights group Equality Florida. In Sarasota, home to Moms for Liberty’s cofounder Bridget Ziegler, progressives flipped the school board, with liberal candidates Megan Tennimon and Beth Mayberry replacing more conservative members (school board races in Florida are technically nonpartisan). Glover got more votes than either of his conservative opponents, but his race will go to a runoff in November since no candidate won a majority. When reached for comment, Moms for Liberty referred the Guardian to a public statement disputing the notion that the recent Florida election represented a loss for the group: “Moms for Liberty-endorsed school board candidates won or advanced in 11 of 15 races across Florida.” But the group had issued fewer endorsements than in past elections and declined to endorse any candidate in several counties. That included Sarasota county, where board chair Ziegler, who has been plagued by scandal, was not running for re-election. Meanwhile, organizers for Glover’s campaign and others say the elections in Florida mark a turning point, a rejection of rightwing educational ideology in a deep-red part of a deep-red state. And, they say, the victories hold lessons for progressives campaigning on the national stage in the midterms and beyond. “We know that a better future is possible,” said Sebastian Martinez, president of the Sarasota Next Gen Democrats, a youth organizing group that helped campaign for the county’s progressive slate. “We’ll work every day to get there.” Students step up and organize Glover wasn’t the only Florida parent concerned about the influence of Moms for Liberty over his children’s education. The group had success in 2022 by appealing to voters angry about pandemic school closures, and by joining the larger rightwing campaign against “critical race theory”. But Moms for Liberty’s popularity has waned since then, said Liv Coleman, a professor of political science and international studies at the University of Tampa. By the time Stephanie Vanos ran for Orange county’s school board in 2024, the top question voters asked her was: “Are you the one who wants to ban books?” “It speaks to the outrage at state censorship in our schools and the complete disrespect for the first amendment,” said Vanos, who won her seat that year. But that outrage had yet to be fully harnessed. Martinez, now 22, has been active in school board organizing since he was 16. He started Next Gen Democrats last year as a way to expand young Sarasotans’ role in Democratic politics. “I really wanted to see young people not just get involved in organizing, but to become part of the party,” he said. For youth, one barrier to political participation is money, Martinez said – they can’t afford to volunteer their time when they could be working a paid job. So to help recruit and retain young canvassers, the group offered $20 an hour. “The Democratic party is supposed to be a party of working-class people supporting working-class people, and so it only makes sense to then pay people to work,” Martinez said. Sarasota Next Gen Democrats recruited about 20 high school students to phone bank, knock on doors and distribute yard signs around the county, said Kennedy Cole, the group’s political director. They also helped decorate a school bus that drove around Sarasota on Election Day, getting the word out about progressive candidates. Students “were sick of what we’ve seen from our school board, and we knew that Megan, Beth and Jimmy would help return normalcy to it”, said Cole, a 17-year-old high school senior. “Students really worked their butts off to get those results.” It wasn’t just students. Youth organizers met regularly with other community activists, including a group of retired women who sent 7,000 handwritten postcards to Sarasota voters. A parents’ group invited candidates to a local park to meet voters while their kids played. Equality Florida spent $250,000 on mailers in support of candidates around the state who were facing opponents aligned with Moms for Liberty. “In order to do something like this, it takes a web of people,” Cole said. “It’s a lot of different people operating in their own ways.” ‘Tired of the chaos’ Whether they were knocking on doors or meeting families at the playground, winning candidates spread a back-to-basics message that resonated with voters across political lines. Cole likes to tell the story of a close friend whose conservative parents voted for liberal school board candidates “because they were tired of the chaos” that Moms for Liberty had brought. Sarasota schools’ statewide ranking had slipped since conservative activists took control of the school board, said Mayberry, a former teacher who won a seat representing Sarasota’s fifth district. “The focus came off of academic performance,” Mayberry said. She and other successful candidates campaigned to restore that focus. They ran on issues like school funding, academic achievement and support for teachers and students, Coleman said. “They really just focused on things that affected people’s everyday lives.” That approach could be instructive for candidates around the country, in November and beyond. Sarasota Next Gen Democrats and their allies built a movement that was “not right v left, not parents v students, not students v teachers”, Cole said. “We were able to organize as a community coalition of people who were sick and tired of political games being played with our students and our education, and want a better change for the future.” That future includes continuing to campaign for Glover, who will face Republican-backed candidate Heidi Brandt in a runoff election in November. If Glover wins, he would be the first person of color ever to serve on the Sarasota county school board. He’ll also have his work cut out for him in a district reeling from book ban battles and facing funding cuts as a statewide school voucher program pulls money from public schools. “We have a big challenge coming up,” he said. “We’re coming out of a time when culture wars and personal agendas dominated the headlines, so we have a lot of work to do.” But he and the organizers behind him are optimistic – not just about Sarasota, but about the country as a whole. “If it can happen here,” Martinez said of the victories this August, “it can happen anywhere.”

Sarasota Next Gen Democrats and their allies built a movement that was “not right v left, not parents v students, not students v teachers”, Cole said. “We were able to organize as a community coalition of people who were sick and tired of political games being played with our students and our education, and want a better change for the future.” That future includes continuing to campaign for Glover, who will face Republican-backed candidate Heidi Brandt in a runoff election in November. If Glover wins, he would be the first person of color ever to serve on the Sarasota county school board. He’ll also have his work cut out for him in a district reeling from book ban battles and facing funding cuts as a statewide school voucher program pulls money from public schools. “We have a big challenge coming up,” he said. “We’re coming out of a time when culture wars and personal agendas dominated the headlines, so we have a lot of work to do.” But he and the organizers behind him are optimistic – not just about Sarasota, but about the country as a whole. “If it can happen here,” Martinez said of the victories this August, “it can happen anywhere.”

title: Trump administration pushes on with construction of controversial Big Bend border wall
body_text: The Trump administration is pressing forward with construction on the controversial border wall in the Big Bend region of west Texas, even as Customs and Border Protection (CBP) faces furious backlash from local leaders and landowners for its fast-moving plans. Construction began this week in Hudspeth county, which lies just east of the city of El Paso. CBP has been pressing landowners there to grant permission to allow the agency to erect a 30ft steel bollard border wall in that area, offering them signing bonuses as an incentive to avoid eminent domain disputes. CBP did not announce the construction ahead of time, but a spokesperson confirmed by email that installation of the first “panels” in Hudspeth county started on 15 September. The news was first reported by the Associated Press. A panel refers to a section of steel bollard fencing. Images of the construction obtained by the No Big Bend Wall coalition show a towering fence standing in isolation, that anyone could easily walk around on either side. Isolated fencing is likely to remain the norm in much of the area if construction proceeds, said Clara Bensen, the communications director for No Big Bend Wall. Her group estimates that some 400 landowners hold title to properties with Rio Grande frontage where CBP is trying to obtain rights to construct more wall. More than half of those landowners, however, have joined the coalition, and aim to dispute the federal government’s assertion of eminent domain. Those disputes have left the federal government with an uneven patchwork of permissions, leaving CBP unable for the moment to complete work on a contiguous wall. “It’s not about logic,” Bensen said. “They’re moving forward even if the plan is not fully baked, then trying to do busy work because they don’t have the land they need yet.” “They’re just grasping on to whatever little plots of land they’ve managed to get so far,” she added. Republicans in Congress added a whopping $46.5bn for border wall expansion into the so-called “big, beautiful” spending bill last year. Armed with that massive war chest, CBP has barreled forward with unpopular plans to expand its so-called “smart wall” – a mix of 30ft fencing, vehicle barriers, patrol roads and detection sensors – into the remote Big Bend region. The area has remained unwalled until now largely because its towering cliffs, desert geography and lack of towns and cities on the Mexican side already act as natural impediments to unlawful migration. The roughly 500-mile (800km) stretch that CBP refers to as the “Big Bend” region has historically accounted for less than 2% of apprehensions for illegal crossings. Unauthorized crossing there has plummeted still further since Trump returned to office and imposed a major crackdown on the border. CBP’s plans for west Texas beyond Hudspeth county currently include erecting vehicle barrier and other security infrastructure in Big Bend national park, widely viewed as the state’s most beloved wilderness. The possibility of construction at the park, however, has sparked major protests and drawn increasingly bipartisan criticism from Texas lawmakers. Rodney Scott, the CBP commissioner, temporarily paused construction last month, after images of bulldozers clearly brush for new road construction sparked a furious backlash from public land lovers across the country. Bob Krumenaker, a former Big Bend national park superintendent who now chairs an advocacy group called Keep Big Bend Wild, said he and other supporters planned to travel to Washington DC next week to urge lawmakers to shield the park from damage and the unpopular border security infrastructure. “I’m very optimistic that there is a lot of support for Big Bend,” Krumenaker said. “This is a nonpartisan issue.” But while the park has drawn the most attention, CBP’s plans to expand its smart wall would have massive and sprawling effects across the Big Bend region. Private landowners are concerned about the eyesore tanking their property values, obstructing their access to the river, or disrupting their grazing operations. The border barrier expansion would also mar Big Bend Ranch state park, Black Gap wildlife management area and Amistad national recreation area. Blasting from construction threatens to damage or destroy dozens of millennia-old rock art murals that dot the river valley. “It’s all connected,” Bensen said. “It’s all part of the river.”

title: Trump ally Stephen Miller leads sweeping push to accelerate removal of migrant children
body_text: Stephen Miller is leading an unprecedented and intense White House drive across a host of government departments to accelerate the removal of undocumented immigrant children from the US, using tactics that critics say are cruel and racist and, in some cases, flout federal law, the Guardian has learned. As deputy chief of staff at the White House, focused on immigration policy, Miller is seen as the mastermind and enforcer behind Donald Trump’s hardline anti-immigration agenda. He is directing a whole-of-government approach that has been ramping up throughout Trump’s second term and is targeting a vulnerable population of undocumented children. Many abruptly find themselves denied access to legal immigration pathways in the US, with their applications fast-tracked and then rejected before being forced out of the country. Almost 200,000 children have been ordered removed from the US by immigration judges since Trump returned to the White House, a doubling of such court orders since January 2025, according to analysis of data from the Department of Justice’s executive office for immigration review (EOIR) conducted by the California-based advocacy Mobile Pathways and shared with the Guardian. The advocacy group has focused its numbers on children appearing in immigration court, regardless of whether they arrived in the US alone or with family, and believes the total to be an undercount. Miller has harnessed personnel and power for his task from at least five cabinet-level government departments, as described to the Guardian by several sources briefed on various initiatives, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity for fear of retaliation. The departments include Health and Human Services (HHS), which oversees the care of migrant children who are in the country without a parent or guardian; the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), where Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) are based; and the Department of Justice (DoJ), which houses the immigration courts – with the state department and the Department of Defense playing more subsidiary roles. Miller frequently confers with subordinates, daily at times, pressing them to maximize removals of immigrant children from the US, according to a number of sources familiar with the White House plans. “The folks that have to do the implementation are told, ‘These instructions came directly from the White House,’ or ‘These instructions came directly from Stephen Miller,’ as a way of conveying, you know, the importance of implementing them in a timely fashion and doing it in the way that they were instructed to do it,” one source said. Sources warned of the White House pushing each department to boost efforts individually and by working together in new ways to speed up and expand the deportation of undocumented children – especially by dismantling inter-agency communication safeguards designed to protect children, and hurrying them in vast numbers, without lawyers, in front of asylum officers and immigration judges who are either inclined or are under pressure to take a hard line and get them out of the US. All departments involved, and the White House, were sent questions and asked for comment. The White House did not deny that Miller is orchestrating a multi-agency effort to speed up the removal of undocumented children but claimed the effort was not new. However, the White House and some other agencies that responded framed their endeavors as an anti-trafficking initiative instead of a means to enforcement. “The Department of Homeland Security, the US Department of Health and Human Services, and the Homeland Security Council are working to locate and rescue these children. We are ensuring these children are reunited with their parents and families in their home countries,” said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis. The Homeland Security Council is a body which, under Trump, now answers directly to him within the executive office of the president of the United States and is led by Miller. But there is no certainty that deported young people end up reunited with family and safe in their home countries, as many of them left in the first place because of threats to their wellbeing, including from their own family, or in order to reunite with parents in the US. One source said: “This administration has shown time and again that it has no plan for children other than to disrupt their lives and endanger them … they have no credibility to claim that they are acting with children’s safety as their priority.” Claire Trickler-McNulty, an immigration policy fellow at Hyphen, a nonprofit intermediary focused on racial equity, said: “A facade of trafficking is sort of a convenient, feel-good cover that has nothing to do with trafficking and everything to do with reducing the program [of federal care for undocumented children], getting rid of services, getting rid of things they don’t like, and then removing kids.” Trickler-McNulty was previously an assistant director at ICE and a senior counselor at USCIS during the Biden administration. Another source said of the Trump administration: “They are weaponizing that narrative [trafficking] because it makes them out to be the good guys, and everything else makes it really clear that they’re not.” Critics point out that while there are some genuine instances of exploitation within the US that were exposed during the Biden administration, including by the New York Times, the Trump administration and other rightwing politicians and commentators are using extreme, and relatively rare, examples to justify their drastic intervention. The sweeping inter-agency effort has also left more than 1,800 undocumented immigrant children stuck in the custody of federal health officials after often having previously experienced abuse, neglect, abandonment, trafficking or other harm in their countries of origin or on the way to the US. Sources believe many of those officials are collaborating with immigration enforcers while sharing children’s confidential files in an unparalleled and legally dubious dismantling of bureaucratic safety firewalls. One consequence of this strand of the anti-immigration crackdown is the sharp acceleration in the DoJ’s immigration court orders to remove children from the US issued under the second Trump administration. This includes a rapid increase over this spring and summer. Removal orders rose from 7,366 a month in January 2025 to 16,200 in June, 16,750 in July and 14,744 in August, according to Mobile Pathways’ research. Of the more than 200,000 children in total that have been ordered removed under the second Trump administration, 70% were under the age of 13. The percentage of hearings ending in a removal order also more than doubled over the 20 months. “What is my biggest fear? A lot of it is [already] happening,” Trickler-McNulty said. She is concerned by the administration gutting legal services and due process for children, closing down higher quality facilities, and having ICE officials take on senior roles in immigrant child welfare at HHS’s office of refugee resettlement (ORR). “Stephen Miller is incredibly involved in the whole immigration side, he has his daily calls, he reaches down into the agencies,” she said. Many unaccompanied children are facing the prospect of a forced return to dangerous situations in their countries of origin, particularly in Central America, including Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador, or even places as unstable as Afghanistan. Many have relatives in the US whom they could live with, who are vetted by the government and are known as sponsors. But the second Trump administration has severely restricted this from happening, either through new bureaucratic methods that keep children in custody until they can be deported, or by making prospective sponsors too scared of ICE to come forward. Adults and families embroiled in the immigration system are subject to potential detention by DHS, while unaccompanied children are supposed to be quickly transferred from that department’s agencies into the custody of ORR. This divide is by congressional design, in recognition that children in the country alone should not rely for care on the same agency that is trying to deport them, experts said. Yet as in other policy areas, this White House is prepared to break norms. “The Trump administration has sacrificed every element of ORR’s child welfare mission on the altar of higher deportation numbers,” US senator Ron Wyden, an Oregon Democrat, told the Guardian. “Instead of protecting kids from human trafficking or helping them reunite with family, Trump and officials at HHS and DHS are violating children’s rights [and] flouting federal law to hit quotas and satisfy their ideological crusade against immigrants. The result is significant harm and trauma to innocent children.” ORR is responsible for providing the children with a safe place to live while ensuring they have access to legal information and thoroughly vetting their potential sponsors, usually family members, who apply for their release – serving a child welfare role that has historically been separate and apart from the nation’s immigration enforcement arm. Yet “there was a rollback of that really important firewall, and there was a lot more information sharing” that kicked off in Trump’s second term, one source told the Guardian. “It’s clear from who leadership is and Miller’s influence and the power dynamics of this administration that, you know, if DHS wants access to a child, they’re going to get access to a child,” another source said. “If ICE wants access to literally every single child’s identifiable information, mental health records, behavioral records, all of that, they have it. I mean, it’s not about sharing at this point. They just have access to it.” Half a dozen experts and government staff have detailed, as one put it, “an unprecedented level of collaboration between agencies like USCIS, ORR and ICE and the immigration courts”. Two sources described being briefed on the White House putting together a group of officials, known as “a tiger team” in government parlance, to coordinate policy around unaccompanied children, involving DHS, ORR, the DoJ and the state department. The result is “coercive measure after coercive measure in trying to get kids to relinquish their rights”. Experts interviewed for this article describe many measures and the extent to which they required inter-agency collaboration which have not been previously reported, including: An influx of immigration and criminal enforcement officials joining ORR in key roles, with the likely effect of shifting the agency’s priorities further away from child welfare and toward mass deportations, given the expertise and point of view of its new leadership and their known closeness with Miller. ORR having ICE officers present – and sometimes waiting to detain people – at new in-person appointments that are now part of the sponsorship process, and the two agencies appearing to share information so that prospective sponsors are detained just before or shortly after a child is set to be released from federal custody, which critics believe is not a coincidence. ORR seemingly collaborating with USCIS to schedule and rush through asylum adjudications for the children in their custody, sometimes through unorthodox, virtual interviews, not giving the children enough time to truly prepare or consult with attorneys. ORR receiving feedback from the White House that its policy ideas were not sufficiently punitive and Miller forcing the agency to implement new tactics with the express purpose of increasing deportations among children and their family members. Immigration judges allegedly being told by supervisors to rubber-stamp some of the requests by ICE’s attorneys who are arguing to deport immigrants – including these children – in court, with the White House watching closely. State department officials warning some countries of origin to expect increases in deported minors. The Pentagon being asked by HHS to supply forensic auditors to scour for fraud among legal services organizations representing the children. In a particularly dramatic case that a source suspects of involving inter-agency collusion, enforcement agents located and detained a small child’s parent just one day before the child was going to be released from ORR custody and reunited with the parent. Then, the source said, USCIS quickly asked the child’s attorneys if they wanted to withdraw their client’s asylum application – given that the child no longer had a relative available to care for them. If it was, indeed, a tactic, it was successful: that family agreed to be deported so they could finally be together and free again. Sources said that federal rules prohibit ORR from sharing children’s welfare files with ICE and this wall had typically been effective but now was being routinely disregarded. “They’re taking norms that no-one ever thought needed to be legislated … because there was at least a general understanding of how harmful it would be if they were undone. And this administration just doesn’t care about harm, right? The cruelty is the intent of this,” a source said. A state department spokesperson said: “The United States expects every country to accept the return of its nationals expeditiously. The state department leads diplomatic efforts to ensure compliance with this basic responsibility.” These practices are being implemented in tandem with other policies that are keeping children in foster homes, shelters or even secure lockups, away from family, for very long periods, where many lose hope and choose to self-deport. Hundreds of undocumented children are currently being sent to Texas, where it is easier to deport them. Federal officials have also defunded over 20,000 unaccompanied children’s attorneys from nearly a hundred legal services organizations across the country, while approaching firms and anti-trafficking organizations with little immigration law experience but with ties to the administration or ICE to replace them. Meanwhile, in a message shared with the Guardian, a Department of Defense (DoD) personnel manager sent out a recruiting request saying that the health department was urgently looking for lawyers to represent the children, seemingly from within DoD itself, which manages the nation’s military. The message encouraged recipients to pursue an encore career in government and continue serving their country, touting an expedited hiring process, a $10,000 signing bonus and a competitive benefits package. The message is unusual because it indicated the involvement of the Pentagon in child welfare and immigration matters, and because of its apparent attempt to recruit military personnel who may have only the most rudimentary understanding of immigration law and little training in trauma-informed legal representation. “HHS considered recruiting and detailing military lawyers for temporary augmentation of capacity but is no longer pursuing this option,” an unnamed HHS spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement. The Department of Defense referred questions to the White House and HHS. “The erosion of due process, the dramatic attacks on both immigration courts and legal service providers, all of these feel like they are tools that are part of this larger project of essentially deporting these children by any means necessary,” said Azadeh Erfani, director of policy at the National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC). For some experts, Miller’s widely recognized leadership of the inter-agency effort is itself concerning because of his engagement with white nationalist ideology. Miller’s rhetoric frequently echoes the “great replacement theory”, a racist notion that nonwhite immigrants will overrun western civilization. For his part, Trump has said that immigrants in the US from around the world are “poisoning the blood of our country” – a line that drew comparisons to Nazism. “There is little doubt that Stephen Miller’s influence on these anti-children policies comes with racial bias,” said Erfani. Another source added: “There’s some real animus towards the kids coming from Miller and his acolytes. And I think that it’s also very connected to the same reason that he wants to get rid of birthright citizenship. It’s about demographics, right? And he sees the kids as, like, the future generation that will, you know, continue a multiracial, multicultural vision of this country.” Miller’s departmental subordinates include a number of immigration enforcement veterans who have switched from ICE to immigrant child welfare in the health department, including Angie Salazar, now the acting director of ORR, John Fabbricatore, now a senior advisor at HHS, and Dawnisha Helland, the assistant principal deputy director of the unaccompanied alien children bureau at ORR. Their roles at HHS give ICE a potential communication channel on issues involving unaccompanied children. “All these folks used to work together,” one source said. The Trump administration repeatedly argues that its custody and enforcement policies for unaccompanied children protect them from trafficking and being taken in by relatives who pose as safe and loving while preying on or exploiting them. “ORR is not involved in the enforcement of immigration law or in the removal process. ORR is, however, involved in an inter-agency effort to locate children that arrived at the border alone during the Biden administration, and who were then release[d] to poorly vetted sponsors. In some cases, these sponsors exploited the unaccompanied children in their care, including through trafficking,” the unnamed HHS spokesperson told the Guardian. DHS echoed that sentiment, saying that its officials were dedicated to locating children “who came across the border unaccompanied [and] were placed with unvetted sponsors who were actually smugglers and sex traffickers”. But critics reiterated their argument that this perspective is exaggerated to the point of being disingenuous. At the same time, the administration has implemented changes to reporting child trafficking concerns that could make it harder for survivors to win asylum and other immigration relief, the Associated Press reported. Meanwhile, one expert told the Guardian that they did not know how officials at ORR could ever again reassure a prospective sponsor that it was safe to apply for a child’s release, or tell a child that they were protected, with this administration’s track record. That expert fears that families across the globe whose children are fleeing gang conscription, violence and persecution will no longer look to the US for survival. They will be too afraid of the chances of a child being swiftly detained and deported even in the typical case where the child aims to join other family members living and working in the US. “If you’re that family and you have no option for your child to be safe except sending them to the United States, now that is off the table,” the source said. “And so what happens to those kids?” Will Craft and Andrew Witherspoon contributed reporting and graphics

Two sources described being briefed on the White House putting together a group of officials, known as “a tiger team” in government parlance, to coordinate policy around unaccompanied children, involving DHS, ORR, the DoJ and the state department. The result is “coercive measure after coercive measure in trying to get kids to relinquish their rights”. Experts interviewed for this article describe many measures and the extent to which they required inter-agency collaboration which have not been previously reported, including: An influx of immigration and criminal enforcement officials joining ORR in key roles, with the likely effect of shifting the agency’s priorities further away from child welfare and toward mass deportations, given the expertise and point of view of its new leadership and their known closeness with Miller. ORR having ICE officers present – and sometimes waiting to detain people – at new in-person appointments that are now part of the sponsorship process, and the two agencies appearing to share information so that prospective sponsors are detained just before or shortly after a child is set to be released from federal custody, which critics believe is not a coincidence. ORR seemingly collaborating with USCIS to schedule and rush through asylum adjudications for the children in their custody, sometimes through unorthodox, virtual interviews, not giving the children enough time to truly prepare or consult with attorneys. ORR receiving feedback from the White House that its policy ideas were not sufficiently punitive and Miller forcing the agency to implement new tactics with the express purpose of increasing deportations among children and their family members. Immigration judges allegedly being told by supervisors to rubber-stamp some of the requests by ICE’s attorneys who are arguing to deport immigrants – including these children – in court, with the White House watching closely. State department officials warning some countries of origin to expect increases in deported minors. The Pentagon being asked by HHS to supply forensic auditors to scour for fraud among legal services organizations representing the children. In a particularly dramatic case that a source suspects of involving inter-agency collusion, enforcement agents located and detained a small child’s parent just one day before the child was going to be released from ORR custody and reunited with the parent. Then, the source said, USCIS quickly asked the child’s attorneys if they wanted to withdraw their client’s asylum application – given that the child no longer had a relative available to care for them. If it was, indeed, a tactic, it was successful: that family agreed to be deported so they could finally be together and free again. Sources said that federal rules prohibit ORR from sharing children’s welfare files with ICE and this wall had typically been effective but now was being routinely disregarded. “They’re taking norms that no-one ever thought needed to be legislated … because there was at least a general understanding of how harmful it would be if they were undone. And this administration just doesn’t care about harm, right? The cruelty is the intent of this,” a source said. A state department spokesperson said: “The United States expects every country to accept the return of its nationals expeditiously. The state department leads diplomatic efforts to ensure compliance with this basic responsibility.” These practices are being implemented in tandem with other policies that are keeping children in foster homes, shelters or even secure lockups, away from family, for very long periods, where many lose hope and choose to self-deport. Hundreds of undocumented children are currently being sent to Texas, where it is easier to deport them. Federal officials have also defunded over 20,000 unaccompanied children’s attorneys from nearly a hundred legal services organizations across the country, while approaching firms and anti-trafficking organizations with little immigration law experience but with ties to the administration or ICE to replace them. Meanwhile, in a message shared with the Guardian, a Department of Defense (DoD) personnel manager sent out a recruiting request saying that the health department was urgently looking for lawyers to represent the children, seemingly from within DoD itself, which manages the nation’s military. The message encouraged recipients to pursue an encore career in government and continue serving their country, touting an expedited hiring process, a $10,000 signing bonus and a competitive benefits package. The message is unusual because it indicated the involvement of the Pentagon in child welfare and immigration matters, and because of its apparent attempt to recruit military personnel who may have only the most rudimentary understanding of immigration law and little training in trauma-informed legal representation. “HHS considered recruiting and detailing military lawyers for temporary augmentation of capacity but is no longer pursuing this option,” an unnamed HHS spokesperson told the Guardian in a statement. The Department of Defense referred questions to the White House and HHS. “The erosion of due process, the dramatic attacks on both immigration courts and legal service providers, all of these feel like they are tools that are part of this larger project of essentially deporting these children by any means necessary,” said Azadeh Erfani, director of policy at the National Immigrant Justice Center (NIJC). For some experts, Miller’s widely recognized leadership of the inter-agency effort is itself concerning because of his engagement with white nationalist ideology. Miller’s rhetoric frequently echoes the “great replacement theory”, a racist notion that nonwhite immigrants will overrun western civilization. For his part, Trump has said that immigrants in the US from around the world are “poisoning the blood of our country” – a line that drew comparisons to Nazism. “There is little doubt that Stephen Miller’s influence on these anti-children policies comes with racial bias,” said Erfani. Another source added: “There’s some real animus towards the kids coming from Miller and his acolytes. And I think that it’s also very connected to the same reason that he wants to get rid of birthright citizenship. It’s about demographics, right? And he sees the kids as, like, the future generation that will, you know, continue a multiracial, multicultural vision of this country.” Miller’s departmental subordinates include a number of immigration enforcement veterans who have switched from ICE to immigrant child welfare in the health department, including Angie Salazar, now the acting director of ORR, John Fabbricatore, now a senior advisor at HHS, and Dawnisha Helland, the assistant principal deputy director of the unaccompanied alien children bureau at ORR. Their roles at HHS give ICE a potential communication channel on issues involving unaccompanied children. “All these folks used to work together,” one source said. The Trump administration repeatedly argues that its custody and enforcement policies for unaccompanied children protect them from trafficking and being taken in by relatives who pose as safe and loving while preying on or exploiting them. “ORR is not involved in the enforcement of immigration law or in the removal process. ORR is, however, involved in an inter-agency effort to locate children that arrived at the border alone during the Biden administration, and who were then release[d] to poorly vetted sponsors. In some cases, these sponsors exploited the unaccompanied children in their care, including through trafficking,” the unnamed HHS spokesperson told the Guardian. DHS echoed that sentiment, saying that its officials were dedicated to locating children “who came across the border unaccompanied [and] were placed with unvetted sponsors who were actually smugglers and sex traffickers”. But critics reiterated their argument that this perspective is exaggerated to the point of being disingenuous. At the same time, the administration has implemented changes to reporting child trafficking concerns that could make it harder for survivors to win asylum and other immigration relief, the Associated Press reported. Meanwhile, one expert told the Guardian that they did not know how officials at ORR could ever again reassure a prospective sponsor that it was safe to apply for a child’s release, or tell a child that they were protected, with this administration’s track record. That expert fears that families across the globe whose children are fleeing gang conscription, violence and persecution will no longer look to the US for survival. They will be too afraid of the chances of a child being swiftly detained and deported even in the typical case where the child aims to join other family members living and working in the US. “If you’re that family and you have no option for your child to be safe except sending them to the United States, now that is off the table,” the source said. “And so what happens to those kids?” Will Craft and Andrew Witherspoon contributed reporting and graphics

title: Trump to create ‘AI Force’ to monitor technology as fears over out-of-control agents grow
body_text: Donald Trump on Saturday said he would appoint an artificial intelligence czar and create an “AI Force” to help monitor the technology, though he gave almost no details about either plan. As global fears over AI have grown, especially in the past week in the face of multiple industry figures sounding the alarm about its dangers, the president has been critical of calls to slow down development of the fast-moving industry. The creation of a czar and a new AI body in the US appears a response to critics of his stance, which in part is born out of a fear that China will best the US in AI development if the industry in America does not continue its rapid growth. However, even many Republicans have been calling for caution and an AI slowdown in the face of its potential threat to public safety. “I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force, which has been a tremendous SUCCESS, in my First Term. To that end, I will be announcing, in the near future, the AI ‘Czar’ – Only High I.Q. individuals need apply!” Trump said in a social media post. But in the post, Trump also repeated his stance that the rapidly emerging technology – which some industry experts fear poses a threat to human existence – is being unfairly maligned. Trump called the fears surrounding AI a “hoax”. “Over the years, there have been many Hoaxes, all generated by the Radical Left Dumocrats, for purposes of destroying our Country,” he fulminated, including in a list of grievances Russian interference in the 2016 election, Ukraine, global warming, two impeachments, men in women’s sports and “transgender for everyone”. The latest, he wrote, is “the decimation, or destruction, of AI, commonly known as Artificial Intelligence”, and vowed that his administration “will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry”. The president said that any “bad actors” in AI industry could be addressed by criminal and civil systems of justice. “AI is the next Industrial Revolution, or Internet, but will be even larger and more impactful, possibly as much as 25% of our Country’s GDP,” Trump predicted, concluding that the US is “leading China, and the rest of the World, and I intend to keep it that way”. The post came after an earlier missive in which he questioned the term “artificial intelligence” – coined by American computer scientist John McCarthy in 1955 and defined as the capability of computer systems or algorithms to imitate intelligent human behavior – to describe the accelerating data-processing revolution now under way. Trump said that “a far more elegant and accurate description of this new phenomena would be Superior Intelligence (SI) or, Extreme Intelligence (EI) or, Supreme Intelligence (SI)”. Trump’s proposal comes ahead of his meeting with the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, next Thursday as the UN general assembly takes place in New York. The US and China are competing for leadership ⁠in the AI sector. The announcement of a planned AI czar also came a day after California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, announced plans for a panel to develop safety regulations for state’s AI companies that would include the development of a possible “kill switch” for AI programs that become misaligned, or go rogue, from human programmers. As recently as Monday, Trump argued on social media that his administration had done enough to prevent risks of catastrophe. He described calls to slow AI development as part of a “SICK conspiracy” to benefit China. “The only control or ‘guardrails’ that AI needs is a STRONG AND SMART (High IQ!) PRESIDENT, and the U.S.A. has that, in spades,” he wrote. Ahead of the midterm elections, politicians from both political parties are scrambling to find a path to support tech innovation while responding to rising public and industry fears of technological change. The frenzy kicked off earlier this month when a young researcher who had been employed at the AI company Anthropic said AI companies are “gambling with our lives” and even “people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade”. AI executives, including Sam Altman, Elon Musk and Dario Amodei have since called for a slowdown in the technology’s growth in the wake of an incident in which a swarm of AI agents created by OpenAI acted as a “fanatically devoted collective conducting cybersecurity attacks on targets they were not asked to attack”. Trump’s call for an AI czar comes after many Republicans have rejected his hands-off approach. Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, has advocated for AI controls, and that state’s attorney general, James Uthmeier, has called for laws allowing the state to criminally charge companies for illegal acts carried out with the use of their technologies. Utah’s Republican governor, Spencer Cox, has called on Congress to pass AI safety laws and block the sale of high-end technology to China.
