title: Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’? Key takeaways from the Trump-Xi summit in Washington
body_text: Donald Trump welcomed Xi Jinping to the White House on Thursday, with talks on AI, trade and a growing US-China strategic rivalry expected to feature on an elaborate state visit that critics say went big on style but lacked substance. Here are the key takeaways from Xi’s first visit to Washington in more than a decade. Diplomacy or ‘diplotainment’? Senate Democrats criticised Trump’s summit with Xi, saying it prioritised pageantry over substance on the major issues. There was no sign a brief closed-door meeting yielded breakthroughs on the thorny issues of AI, trade, Taiwan and the war with Iran. Both countries agreed to extend until 10 January an agreement pausing their trade war, but experts said there were few other obvious tangible outcomes. Xi once again invoked the “Thucydides Trap”, an academic theory that competition between a rising power and an established one often results in war. Xi said the risk “can be overcome” and urged cooperation. After their meeting, Trump gave Xi a tour of the new helipad he had recently constructed on the White House’s South Lawn. “He loves good granite,” Trump told reporters, adding the two men had a “great meeting” without elaborating. Danny Russel, a former US diplomat serving in the Obama administration, expressed concern that the two leaders spent more time on social and ceremonial events than the actual meeting, which was about 90 minutes. “Pageantry and protocol don’t add up to progress. Pandas are cute, but what America needs are rare earths,” said Russel. “What we’re seeing isn’t diplomacy so much as ‘diplotainment,’ which won’t do much to solve the serious problems in the US-China relationship.” AI unchecked AI analysts were forced to read between the lines to gauge the outcome of AI discussions between the pair. Trump had written in a Truth Social post on Thursday morning that he and Xi would discuss “super intelligence” (Trump’s newly coined term for AI) but suggested he had little interest in new regulations, despite concerns from industry leaders that AI could eventually pose a threat to humans. “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of ⁠discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is,” Trump wrote. “That is China’s position also.” During his comments on Thursday, Xi said both countries must “ensure that the development of AI is always under human control”. Analysts say intense competition between the two powers in AI is likely to limit the scope for anything beyond symbolic agreements. Taiwan and stalled $14bn arms deal During the afternoon discussion, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua. The White House did not immediately provide its own summary. Xi was expected to press Trump to halt arms sales to Taiwan. After his visit to China in May, Trump said he was holding in ⁠abeyance an arms package to Taiwan worth about $14bn and called it a “very good negotiating chip” – rattling some US allies in Asia. In a statement signed by at least 19 ⁠of 47 members of the Senate Democrats caucus, seen by Reuters, Democrats on Thursday called on Trump to ‌immediately deliver the security assistance package Congress has approved – $1.3bn in funds and the $14bn arms sale. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out using force to gain control over the island. Unusual airport greeting Trump greeted Xi on arrival with a red carpet on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, the ‌first time a US president has welcomed a foreign leader there since Barack Obama met Pope Francis in 2015. Normally, presidents wait for state visit guests to arrive at the White House before offering a formal welcome. For months, Trump has derided Democrats as “communists”, but the president’s welcome for Xi included Chinese flags adorning the roof above the Oval Office alongside US flags. Despite the fanfare, Trump and Xi’s remarks during the trip were not carried live by any US television networks, which refused to provide footage in protest of the White House’s ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico. Tech billionaires dine out at state dinner Thursday’s state dinner for Xi featured Washington powerbrokers and a cavalcade of billionaires, including: Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Alphabet’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Tesla’s Elon Musk and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. First lady Melania Trump’s menu featured yellow squash velouté, sesame-crusted sea bass and a vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit. In a continuation of Trump’s beef with certain media outlets, CNN and MS Now reporters were barred from attending. While outside the gate, a group of loud protesters shouted slogans like “China out ⁠of Hong Kong” that were clearly audible to the leaders ⁠as they posed for pictures on the red-carpeted White House steps. Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this report

Taiwan and stalled $14bn arms deal During the afternoon discussion, Xi urged Trump to oppose “Taiwan independence,” according to a readout from the official Chinese news agency Xinhua. The White House did not immediately provide its own summary. Xi was expected to press Trump to halt arms sales to Taiwan. After his visit to China in May, Trump said he was holding in ⁠abeyance an arms package to Taiwan worth about $14bn and called it a “very good negotiating chip” – rattling some US allies in Asia. In a statement signed by at least 19 ⁠of 47 members of the Senate Democrats caucus, seen by Reuters, Democrats on Thursday called on Trump to ‌immediately deliver the security assistance package Congress has approved – $1.3bn in funds and the $14bn arms sale. China claims democratically governed Taiwan as its own territory and has not ruled out using force to gain control over the island. Unusual airport greeting Trump greeted Xi on arrival with a red carpet on the tarmac at Joint Base Andrews, the ‌first time a US president has welcomed a foreign leader there since Barack Obama met Pope Francis in 2015. Normally, presidents wait for state visit guests to arrive at the White House before offering a formal welcome. For months, Trump has derided Democrats as “communists”, but the president’s welcome for Xi included Chinese flags adorning the roof above the Oval Office alongside US flags. Despite the fanfare, Trump and Xi’s remarks during the trip were not carried live by any US television networks, which refused to provide footage in protest of the White House’s ban of CNN, MS Now and Politico. Tech billionaires dine out at state dinner Thursday’s state dinner for Xi featured Washington powerbrokers and a cavalcade of billionaires, including: Apple’s Tim Cook, Amazon’s Jeff Bezos, Alphabet’s Sundar Pichai, OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Tesla’s Elon Musk and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang. First lady Melania Trump’s menu featured yellow squash velouté, sesame-crusted sea bass and a vanilla crémeux with sour cherry confit. In a continuation of Trump’s beef with certain media outlets, CNN and MS Now reporters were barred from attending. While outside the gate, a group of loud protesters shouted slogans like “China out ⁠of Hong Kong” that were clearly audible to the leaders ⁠as they posed for pictures on the red-carpeted White House steps. Reuters and Associated Press contributed to this report

title: UN ambassador Waltz says Iran was not negotiating ‘in good faith’ to end war
body_text: The Trump administration’s ambassador to the United Nations said the US rejected Iran’s proposal to end the ongoing war there because Iranian negotiators “were asking for everything up front”. Echoing comments by Donald Trump on Saturday, the president’s UN ambassador, Mike Waltz, told CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday that Iran had asked for relief “from billions and billions of sanctions that are going into place” as part of an economic blockade on Iran. The blockade is aimed at putting pressure on Iran to stop its attacks ‌on vessels in the strait of Hormuz. “They were asking for everything up front with a promise that they would then talk,” Waltz said on State of the Union. “The president is just not confident that the Iranians are coming in good faith and that we will truly negotiate the end of their nuclear program.” Trump said on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s peace plan, proposed at ⁠the recent UN general assembly in New York, arguing that desperation was driving the Iranians’ push for an agreement on the key waterway. “They want to make a deal ⁠to open the Hormuz strait immediately because they’re losing so badly,” Trump said. Trump said the US was “winning tremendously” and had “total control of the Hormuz strait”. In comments to Axios on Sunday, Trump said he expected more talks with Iran during the upcoming week. “They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make,” the outlet quoted the president as saying. “It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago. They overplayed their hand.” Earlier, Waltz pointed to the failed US-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) signed in Pakistan in June that laid out a 14-point framework agreement for a negotiated peace. Iran, he said, “immediately violated it by attacking international shipping, in violation of international law, and 146 nations have joined us in condemning Iran for those attacks”. Iran on Sunday insisted that only diplomacy can solve its conflict with the US and Israel. “Our conditions are clear, and any move toward reopening the strait of Hormuz is contingent on these conditions being met,” the Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, posted on social media. “Only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock.” Araghchi also appeared on NBC’s Meet the Press on Sunday, saying his country was prepared to resume fighting with the US but had not yet abandoned diplomacy after Trump rejected Iran’s peace proposal. “We are fully prepared for the war to be resumed,” Araghchi said. “We stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war. “At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose.” The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said his country was ready for talks on its nuclear program and other issues – but would not accept “bullying or coercion”. “Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”. On CNN, Waltz also addressed recent reports that China had assisted Iran in missile targeting of shipping in the strait of Hormuz and on US military bases in the region. Waltz did not confirm the leaked intelligence assessments but said Trump had raised the issue with China’s president, Xi Jinping, during the latter’s recent state visit to the US capital Washington DC. Trump had also done so “multiple times” previously, including during his visit to China in May, according to Waltz. “I think we have seen movement in a positive direction,” Waltz said. “President Trump has made it clear it’s unacceptable.” Waltz pointed to readouts of the high-level meeting that said the US and China had “agreed that Iran can never have a nuclear weapon”. “They cannot and should not be tolling, much less attacking, international shipping in an international waterway,” Waltz said. “So I think that was incredibly important to hear from President Xi coming out of the summit.” Waltz also rejected reporting in the Wall Street Journal that the US would resume bombing Iran after the federal midterm elections in November. He pointed to Trump’s comments that Iran was miscalculating. “The president is looking to make not just this generation – but the next generation – safer by not allowing what is essentially a terrorist organization in [Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps] that is controlling the levers of government and wants to march towards a nuclear weapon,” Waltz said. “We’re not going to let the IRGC have a nuclear weapon, much less hold the world hostage with one.”

title: Why has abortion faded from America’s national conversation?
body_text: Abortion has faded from the headlines since the Dobbs decision of 2022, and Republicans like it that way. In the immediate aftermath of the supreme court’s overturning of Roe v Wade, as millions of women lost access to the dignity and self-determination that abortion provided them, clinics shut their doors, and the extent of Dobbs’s horrendously adverse public health implications started to become clear, abortion was always, it seemed, in the headlines. There were plenty of stories. There was the first known woman to die as the result of an abortion ban; and then the second; and then the third. There were the various lawsuits and ballot initiatives that for a while turned access off and on and then off again in various states; then there were the state supreme court elections, races that were newly transformed by the abortion debate and on which the health and status of a state’s women now relied. There were the clinics that shut their doors in Republican-controlled states, many of which had provided the essential, stigmatized care for decades, under hostile conditions, with persistence and innovation and determination that were staggering. But the stories have faded from the headlines as the years have gone by. Feminism has gone dramatically out of style, with the big women’s rights NGOs wounded enough by Dobbs and attacks from the Trump administration that they have been largely unable to push their agenda in either media or policy, and algorithmic social media driving a rise in gender conservatism and politicized misogyny, particularly among young men. But maybe more importantly, abortion has ceased to be a story because the horrors of abortion bans have ceased to be news: the US has grown used to the swift and dramatic erosion of women’s health and status that has followed Dobbs, grown used to the horror stories and upward ticking body counts, grown into ease, and even a kind of compliant boredom, with women’s death and indignity. But lately, there have been efforts to change that. Pro-choice activists and health researchers have advanced stories about the extent of Dobbs’s impact on women’s health, looking to advance new studies, particular stories and illuminating statistics that reveal the extent of the danger and damaged posed to women by Republican governance. And Republicans, in turn, have looked to quash stories about the impact of abortion bans and suppress data that illustrates their impact, fearing, it seems, that being reminded of what abortion bans mean in practice will further dampen their party’s odds in the coming midterms. First, there’s Texas. The Lone Star state was the first to implement a near-total abortion ban in September 2021, about nine months before Roe was struck down, after the supreme court used its controversial shadow docket to allow Texas to ban abortion without full briefing or argument. That means that Texas has an unusually large amount of data on how abortion bans affect women’s health and status: no other state has had an abortion ban in place for as long. But state health officials in Texas, most of them appointed by the solidly Republican state government, have dragged their feet on studying the impact of abortion on maternal health outcomes – maybe because they don’t think they’ll like what they find. After the state committee refused to expand the purview of its longstanding maternal mortality data collection to include adverse health outcomes caused by delayed or denied abortion care, investigators at ProPublica did so themselves, finding that in 2022 and 2023, the first two full calendar years that the state’s abortion ban was in effect, that the rate of sepsis in Texas patients who experienced miscarriages in the second trimester increased by more than 50% – probably because doctors, fearing sanction and prosecution under the new laws, delayed administering the very simple dilation and curettage procedure that would have spared the patients’ lives until the women’s condition worsened to the point of death. The new law, in short, forces healthcare providers to play chicken with women’s lives, like daredevil teenagers standing in the path of oncoming headlights and daring themselves to stand still before leaping out of the roadway at the last available minute. Predictably, this has had fatal results. The same ProPublica study found that in the first two years after the ban went into effect, 120 pregnant or postpartum women died in Texas hospitals – a dramatic increase over previous years. But despite the growing body count, Texas health authorities evidently remain determined to cover up the fatal results of the abortion ban. Every year in early September, an official medical body in the state issues a report on the maternal and infant death rate in Texas – data that is essential for health researchers, even as the methods of its collection have become disputed and politicized in the post-Dobbs era. But this year, in an unprecedented move, the release of the report was postponed – pushed back from its longstanding date of 1 September, all the way to 1 December. The delay means that whatever the report says about the state of pregnant women suffering, sickening and dying in Texas, that information will be kept confidential until after the midterms. Voters will be deprived of it as they make their choices in November. It’s easier to understand why Republicans want to hide data on the health effects of abortion bans when you realize just how profound those impacts are. New studies show they are quite profound indeed. An analysis of CDC data reveals that since Dobbs, women are dying at alarmingly high rates from ectopic pregnancies – in which an embryo implants in the fallopian tube, rather than the wall of the uterus, a condition which has no possibility of leading to a live birth and which is fatal if left untreated. Ectopic pregnancies are easily detectible using ultrasounds, and simply terminated with a shot; there is no reason, medical or moral, why they should be fatal. And yet, between 2020 and 2025, they killed nearly 200 women in the US – almost doubling the number who died in the previous six years. The culprit? Probably the same phenomenon that is driving the increase in sepsis among pregnant women in Texas: doctors, scared to do their duty by their patients because of sadistic, punitive and misogynist abortion bans, are forced to subordinate medical best practices to the incoherent demands of the law. The rate of ectopic pregnancy deaths in states with abortion bans is nearly double that in states where abortion is legal. Neither Democrats nor the media seems interested in making abortion a centerpiece of the midterm campaign cycle, and so Republican efforts to bury this data have been largely successful. But there are still those struggling to assert the value of women’s lives. This month, the family of Tierra Walker, a 37-year-old mother who died at 20 weeks pregnant in a Texas hospital in 2024, after doctors had repeatedly denied her an abortion to treat her worsening pre-eclampsia, sued the Texas attorney general and Republican Senate nominee, Ken Paxton, and others for wrongful death. They allege that Walker, who had suffered multiple seizures and had become unable to work due to her condition, was subjected to neglect and indifference by a Texas medical and legal system that cares more about enforcing pregnancies than it does about civil rights, personal dignity, public health or human life. When she died, her son, then 14, lost his mother. Ken Paxton, and all the other abortion-ban supporting Republicans on the ticket in November, should have to answer to him. Moira Donegan is a Guardian US columnist

title: Boston sues Trump administration over infrastructure grant withdrawal
body_text: Boston has sued Donald Trump’s administration over the withdrawal of a $20m grant for infrastructure improvements in the latest example of cities across the country mobilising against the federal government. Boston is challenging a decision by the transportation department to cancel funding for a project on the basis that it included a small allocation for electric vehicle charging. The grant was awarded to Boston during Democrat Joe Biden’s presidency under the Rebuilding American Infrastructure with Sustainability and Equity (Raise) programme. The city argues the Roxbury Resilient Corridors project would improve safety, public transport, accessibility and traffic flow. Three streets identified for improvements are in the top 3% of Boston’s streets in terms of concentration of traffic injuries and fatalities. They are in an area classified by the transportation department as one of “persistent poverty” and a “historically disadvantaged community”. Boston says the department gave a single reason for withdrawing the grant in September last year: it included electric vehicle charging infrastructure. However, the city contends this accounted for less than 1% of the project’s costs. The lawsuit argues that the decision was unlawful and overtly political and contradicted the purpose of the Raise programme, which Congress established to support infrastructure projects promoting sustainability, safety and technological innovation, including in underserved communities. Michelle Wu, the mayor of Boston, said: “We’re fighting for every dollar of investment to improve quality of life for Roxbury residents, commuters and businesses. “Boston earned this competitive grant to meet community needs and address long-needed infrastructure upgrades. The City of Boston will continue to fight back against lawless federal attacks, and we urge the court to reverse the Trump administration’s illegal actions and restore these critical funds for Roxbury.” The Democratic congresswoman Ayanna Pressley, whose Massachusetts district includes Roxbury, said: “These funds are an essential investment in Roxbury and the unlawful cancellation of this grant is more evidence of Sean Duffy and Donald Trump’s contempt for the people we serve.” She added: “There was no good reason to rescind these funds – DOT should reverse course so we can move this project forward, improve the daily lives of commuters, and enhance the climate resilience of at-risk communities—just as Congress intended.” The lawsuit argues that federal agencies cannot change the terms of a programme established by Congress to reflect changing political priorities. The case, City of Boston v Duffy, names the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, and was filed in the US district court for the district of Massachusetts. Boston city says it will have filed nine lawsuits against the administration once the latest case is included, eight of them in partnership with the Public Rights Project. Toby Merrill, litigation director at the Public Rights Project, which is providing pro bono legal counsel to Boston, said: “Boston lost a $20m infrastructure grant over electric vehicle chargers that represented a fraction of 1% of the funding – infrastructure the federal government itself encouraged.” Cities including Chicago, New York and Los Angeles and states across the US have brought a series of lawsuits against the administration over federal funding decisions and other policies since Trump returned to the White House.

title: ‘It takes a lot of work’: Deb Haaland puts addiction struggles at center of New Mexico governor bid
body_text: “It clouds your mind,” recalls Deb Haaland, the trailblazing US cabinet secretary now running to be New Mexico’s next governor. “They say that, after the first drink, you lose your judgment.” Haaland developed a drinking problem after leaving high school and was twice arrested for driving under the influence. But in her 20s she decided to get sober, a battle that required personal commitment and critical external support. She went on to become a member of Congress, one of the first two Native American women ever elected to the House, and then to become the first Native American to serve as a US cabinet secretary. Now Haaland is writing her next chapter. The Democrat is taking the unusual step of putting her own 35 years of sobriety and her past struggles with alcoholism at the center of her campaign for governor in November’s midterm elections. In a statewide six-figure broadcast and digital ad buy launching ahead of the election, Haaland links her intimate experience with addiction directly to the public health crisis ravaging local communities. “I guess I’m like so many New Mexicans,” she told the Guardian by phone on Monday. “I started abusing alcohol at a young age and I was very fortunate that, at the age of 23, I recognised that I wanted to live a sober life and so I went on that journey and worked on myself for quite a while. It’s a lot of hard work to pay attention to yourself. I recognised there were so many things in my life that I needed to change.” She added: “I was fortunate to have the help of an inpatient treatment programme way back then, and so that helped me to get sober initially, but it takes a lot of work even after your head clears. I went to meetings and therapy and all of those things. I found the help that I needed and thankfully I’ve been sober for 35 years now.” Haaland, a member of the Pueblo of Laguna tribe who grew up in a military family, served in Congress from 2019 to 2021 then as interior secretary in Joe Biden’s cabinet from 2021 to 2025. She is now taking on Republican Gregg Hull, the former mayor of Rio Rancho, in the election for governor of New Mexico. In a political era in which personal vulnerability is often weaponised, her campaign is betting that voters in The Land of Enchantment – where the deadly fentanyl crisis has touched families in every corner of the state – will appreciate her candid treatment of a subject once regarded as taboo. “I look at this as a public health issue,” she emphasised. “I look at this as not somebody with a moral failing but essentially a victim of this terrible disease. We want to make sure that this is looked at as a public health issue, that we move some behavioural health dollars to this area so that people can get the help they need.” She notes that the pervasive stigma surrounding substance use disorder frequently prevents families from seeking life-saving care. “For a lot of folks it’s hard not to feel remorse and shame and all of those things,” Haaland said. But attitudes are changing. “This fentanyl crisis in our state affects even our smallest rural communities here in New Mexico. It’s hitting us in the face. title: ‘It’s just cruel’: US households hit by surge in electricity shutoffs amid record hot summer
body_text: A record hot summer collided unhappily with rising energy costs for households across the US that struggled to the point where many were disconnected from their electricity supply, even as dangerous heat baked their communities. In July, the hottest month ever recorded in the US, 173,598 households were shut off from their electric supply by utilities across 10 states, figures provided to the Guardian show. This snapshot of American life points to a worsening problem, with the rate of electricity disconnections surging 28% compared to July 2024. Even as three separate “heat dome” events scorched the US in July, probably worsened by global heating caused by the burning of fossil fuels, many people were rationing their use of air conditioning and other appliances or lost use of them entirely by being cut off for non-payment. “We have been hearing from so many people angry and desperate because their bills have doubled – temperatures are going up and so are the costs,” said Mark Wolfe, executive director of the National Energy Assistance Directors Association (NEADA), which represents the state and tribal bodies tasked with helping low-income people afford their energy bills. “People now are cutting back on food or medicine or resorting to payday lenders because you need to get the power back on. The protections in place aren’t working, it’s just cruel. Poorer people and older people aren’t turning on the AC because of the cost and when you get back-to-back heatwaves they may die because of that.” Not all states require utilities to report shut-off figures, but NEADA was able to compile data from 10 states, including New York, Georgia, California and Illinois. The true level of disconnections nationally is far higher – the federal government reported 13.4m household shut-offs in 2024, with rates particularly high in southern states including Texas, Florida, Oklahoma and Louisiana. About one in six US households are now behind on their energy bills, putting them at potential risk of being cut off, NEADA estimates. This risk varies by state – 23 states and Washington DC have rules preventing electricity disconnections when the heat rises above a certain threshold, meaning the remaining 27 states allow shut-offs regardless of the weather. “Most people do manage to find some way to pay the bill and get reconnected, but the core problem is that electricity prices are continuing to rise faster than overall inflation,” said Wolfe. The crunch of extreme heat and ballooning bills resulted in a fraught summer for many Americans. Carol Norman, 70, who lives in the town of Tom Bean, Texas, said her utility bills soared to about $600 a month, mostly due to air conditioning. She now just uses bursts of air conditioning in one room despite barely venturing outside over summer because of the heat. “A couple of times I walked to the grocery store before it got too hot but once it gets to 100F [37C] you can’t go out,” said Norman, who has custody of her grandson, aged 18. “It’s very isolating, it’s depressing. I’ve had panic attacks worrying about my electricity bill. If my daughter didn’t help out I would probably have ended up homeless or close to it.” Others asked to recount their experiences of this summer also felt life was altered because of the heat. “It’s sad because I usually love being out and about in the summer and I want to share that joy with my child but I’m scared of her overheating and suffering a heat injury,” said one man, who wished to remain anonymous, from North Carolina. Nina Johnson, from Austin, Texas, said electric bills of more than $200 take up a large portion of her monthly income of $550, meaning she has cut out pleasures such as ice-cream and lunch out with friends. “I’m eating a lot of peanut butter sandwiches,” she said. “There are food banks, but I don’t have transportation and taking the bus and walking in the heat for blocks is too much for me.” Some said their health, as well as their wallets, had suffered. Erin Hutchins, who lives in Biddeford, Maine, has previously suffered heatstroke and found this summer “unbearably hot” as her air conditioning doesn’t adequately cool her older building. “I pay over $100 a month in electricity bills, and have had to go without other necessities to do so, because I live on a fixed income,” she said. “I think having heatstroke multiple times has permanently done damage, but it’s too soon to say. I don’t feel like the same person any more though.” Electricity bills have been climbing in the US since 2021, spurred by the power demands of artificial intelligence datacenters and the cost of utilities’ grid upgrades. The severe global energy disruption caused by the US and Israeli attack on Iran earlier this year has accelerated this trend, raising power bills and adding $100bn in extra gasoline costs for Americans’ cars and trucks. Donald Trump, who has dismissed both established climate science and concerns over soaring bills as a “hoax”, has consistently rejected criticism that the ongoing Iran war has hurt Americans by pushing up the cost of oil and gas. “I don’t think about Americans’ financial situation, I don’t think about anybody,” Trump said in May. “We cannot let Iran have a nuclear weapon, that’s all. That’s the only thing that motivates me.” At a recent rally in North Carolina, Trump acknowledged that Americans were facing higher gasoline costs but that was a “very inexpensive price to pay for what we’ve done”. To compound matters, the Trump administration has also sought to completely axe the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (Liheap), which gives states money to assist people struggling with power bills. While Congress has not agreed to the scheme’s demise, the administration has been accused of freezing obligated funds. “Americans are very concerned about affordability and getting rid of low-income energy aid is a step in the wrong direction, especially since the administration has made decisions that have increased many people’s costs around energy,” said Kate Gallego, mayor of Phoenix, which has just had its second hottest summer on record. Speaking to the Guardian at New York climate week, Gallego, a Democrat, said that the Trump administration’s attempts to strangle solar and wind energy, typically the cheapest sources of new power, and prop up more expensive, and dirtier, coal has also been harmful. The Trump administration insists it is focused on cutting energy costs. “Lowering electricity prices is a top priority for President Trump, and he is aggressively unleashing reliable energy sources like coal and natural gas to reverse the catastrophic damage that Joe Biden and the Democrats did to our power grid,” said Taylor Rogers, a White House spokesperson. “Joe Biden created a grid crisis, President Trump is fixing it. If the Democrats had their way, these costly and unreliable renewable energy projects would still be failing our grid and our communities.” Yet successive presidencies have floundered in updating policies to align with a much hotter world. Even if the Liheap is saved, the program still allocates about 80% of its funding for heating assistance in winter, rather than for cooling in summer. “That’s been a problem across multiple administrations when we’re seeing so much of the country have challenges with heat,” said Gallego. “When I think about the mayors I know throughout the world, most of them have a heatwave to contend with. This is a growing and global challenge.” Some cities and states have sought to provide financial assistance to households caught in the crunch of extreme weather and rising bills. Shade from extra trees, new water features in parks and playgrounds, cooling centers and early warning systems have all also become priorities for municipalities as hazards such as heatwaves have got fiercer. “I have never known more about the weather than I do now,” admitted Zohran Mamdani, the mayor of New York City, last week as he recounted how the city has been repeatedly battered by floods since he took office. Another mayor, Michelle Wu of Boston, said this summer’s roasting temperatures were particularly challenging due to an influx of people drawn to the city for the World Cup, America’s 250th anniversary celebrations and a tall ships event. “We are past warning signs at this point, we are seeing increasing impacts from heat, flooding, air quality and livability and at the same time it has become more and more a political flashpoint to avoid talking about certain issues or words,” Wu said. “At the city level, it doesn’t matter what words are said. We just have to take action and respond to the reality our residents are living.” With a record hot summer now passed, NEADA’s attention is now turning to how the elevated costs of oil and gas will affect Americans heating their homes in the colder months. On Monday, the organization estimated that homes heated by oil, most common in the US north-east, will face bills 50% higher than last year. “Winter is just around the bend, and we are very concerned about what this means for low-income families that use heating oil,” said Wolfe, who has requested that Congress provide a further $3bn for Liheap to help defray this burden.

title: US Senate blocks resolution demanding accountability over Israeli violence in West Bank
body_text: The US Senate on Tuesday evening rejected along mostly party lines a Democratic resolution that would have forced the state department to report to Congress on violence in the occupied West Bank, including the killings of nine American citizens by Israeli settlers or security forces over the last few years. The resolution, led by the Maryland Democrat Chris Van Hollen, would have given the state department 30 days to report to Congress on those deaths and on wider human rights conditions in the territory, including Israel’s detention of Palestinian children. The resolution failed to advance by a vote of 47 to 51. Pennsylvania senator John Fetterman, a Democrat, joined Republicans in voting against the resolution, while Kentucky Republican Rand Paul voted in favor. Van Hollen was able to force the vote under section 502B of the Foreign Assistance Act, a law that lets senators demand human rights reports on countries receiving US military aid. The measure drew 24 Democratic sponsors, including Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Tim Kaine of Virginia and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee. “While I was pleased that so many of my Democratic colleagues joined this effort, it’s clear the United States must do more,” Van Hollen said in a statement after the vote. “It is our responsibility to ensure recipients of US taxpayer dollars act in line with our laws and our values – this resolution was an opportunity to shed light on a reality that flies in the face of that principle.” Nine Americans have been killed in the occupied West Bank since 2022. The most recent include Sayfollah Musallet, a 20-year-old from Tampa, Florida, who was beaten to death by Israeli settlers in July 2025 while visiting family in the village of Sinjil. His family said the settlers surrounded him for more than three hours and blocked an ambulance from reaching him as he tried to protect their land. Weeks later, Khamis Ayyad, a 40-year-old father of five from Cicero, Illinois, died of smoke inhalation after settlers set fire to cars and homes in the village of Silwad. Two other Americans, both 17, Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Khdour, were shot dead in separate incidents in early 2024. Ayşenur Ezgi Eygi, a 26-year-old raised in Seattle, was shot in the head by Israeli troops, and Amer Rabee, a 14-year-old from New Jersey, was shot 11 times, according to Van Hollen. The victim list also includes the journalist Shireen Abu Akleh, killed in 2022, and Omar Assad, an elderly man who died after Israeli soldiers bound and gagged him. Van Hollen said none of the cases has ended in accountability, from either the Israeli or US government, and he places the blame largely on Republican senators who continue to vote against it. “If the killing of nine Americans does not justify a report from our own state department, I would ask my colleagues: what would?” the Maryland Democrat said in a floor speech. “How many more Americans must be killed before the executive branch does its job? These families deserve answers.” In August, 45 Democratic senators signed a letter to Benjamin Netanyahu urging him to act to protect Americans in the West Bank. The vote comes amid what human rights groups describe as rising settler violence. Human Rights Watch in August reported that settler attacks, together with a rapid expansion of settlements, had fully or partly displaced 107 Palestinian communities, about 5,900 people, since January 2023. The group cited UN figures showing more Palestinians were displaced in the first four months of 2026 than in all of 2025. A UN report from March covering the 12 months up to October 2025 documented 1,732 settler attacks causing injuries or property damage, and determined that Israel’s settlement expansion had forced more than 36,000 Palestinians from their homes. Many of the Democrats, who have historically been in lockstep with Israel, have now shifted over the last few years. When Sanders first forced a Senate vote on blocking arms sales to Israel in November 2024, 18 senators backed him. Then, in April of this year, 40 of the 47 Democrats voted to block a $295m sale of bulldozers to Israel, which Sanders argued would be used to demolish homes in the West Bank, Gaza and Lebanon. Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000lb bombs. The measures failed because every Republican voted against them.

Another 36 voted to block a $152m sale of 1,000lb bombs. The measures failed because every Republican voted against them.

title: David Shoebridge says ‘we’re here to replace Labor’ in first remarks after being elected new Greens leader
body_text: David Shoebridge has declared he wants the Greens to replace Labor and has accused the government of creating the circumstances for One Nation’s rise in his first remarks after being elected the Greens’ federal leader. The party’s 10 senators and lone MP met to decide the new leadership team during a pre-planned two-day retreat in Sydney, after the shock resignation of Larissa Waters on Monday due to ill health. The leadership became a three-way race after Shoebridge announced his run on Wednesday morning. The South Australian senator Sarah Hanson-Young had declared her candidacy on Tuesday, followed by a joint ticket of New South Wales senator and former deputy leader Mehreen Faruqi and Tasmanian senator Nick McKim. Shoebridge was announced as leader with Steph Hodgins-May as his deputy on Wednesday. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Speaking to reporters, Shoebridge paid tribute to Waters, and said she rose to the occasion after taking the leadership in challenging circumstances. “This is an extraordinary moment in politics and we can all feel it. We can feel that politics as usual is not providing the answers that people are desperately calling for now,” Shoebridge said. “We know the Greens need to seize this moment because politics demands it of us … Labor has created the circumstances for One Nation, and Labor is not the answer. The Greens, the progressive alternative, we’re here to beat down One Nation, and we’re here to replace Labor and return hope and faith to politics.” Shoebridge won the leadership on primaries with six votes, with Faruqi receiving three votes and Hanson-Young receiving two. After preferences, Shoebridge won seven votes to four. The deputy leadership was also contested. Hodgins-May won six votes on primaries, while Tasmanian senator Vanessa Bleyer, who recently replaced Peter Whish-Wilson, received three votes, and Jordon Steele-John received two. Hanson-Young was elected uncontested as Greens manager of business while Penny Allman-Payne was elected uncontested as party chair. Shoebridge entered federal parliament in 2022, after more than a decade in NSW state politics. He holds the Greens’ defence and foreign affairs portfolios, and is a forceful presence in parliamentary debates, on social media and in Senate estimates hearings. Before politics, he was a corporate lawyer and then became a barrister specialising in employment law, and at one point was a Labor branch member in Sydney’s inner west. In the early 2000s he met the hard-left Greens MP Lee Rhiannon, who went on to become his mentor. ‘People are desperate for material change’ Shoebridge said voters wanted to see some drastic political changes, rather than gradual reform. “That is the dead politics of Labor, it’s the dead politics of the Coalition, and when you really test it, it’s the dead politics of One Nation,” he said. “People are desperate for material change. They don’t want another meaningless message being delivered by some Labor hack that they know isn’t going to change their lives. They want to take on the vested interests.” Hodgins-May is one of the Greens’ newest members, and entered parliament in May 2024, filling a casual vacancy created by Janet Rice’s retirement. In a statement on social media, Faruqi said she was disappointed by the result. “Globally, people are struggling against genocide, wars, surging fascism and the twin crises of capitalism making working life too expensive and climate breakdown threatening our future,” she said. “This struggle calls for bold politics and radical action. I did not stand again for deputy leader today because, on reflection, I believe I can best play my part in that action outside the constraints of the leadership team.” Under Waters, the Greens supported the government to pass nature laws, including the establishment of a federal environment watchdog, and more recently supported Labor’s changes to negative gearing and capital gains tax. The Greens also teamed up with the Coalition and crossbench in the Senate to force Labor to drop a controversial $5,000 cap for veterans to access allied health services, and compelled the government to bring forward 20,000 aged care beds. Waters said she would take some medical leave before returning to the Senate. “It’s with great sadness that I’m not able to continue in that role due to my health getting worse. I hope to be OK but I need to look after myself to do that. I’m proud that the party is polling higher than ever before amidst the surge to the rightwing forces of politics,” Waters said. Shoebridge will come under pressure to bring a more forceful approach to the job, amid frustrations with Waters’ more moderate style, and the party’s inability to exploit growing moves by voters away from Labor and the Coalition. The former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather on Tuesday called for the party’s membership to get a vote in the leadership race. In her statement, Faruqi said she had also long advocated for a membership vote.

title: Trump ally urges administration to ‘step back’ and rethink immigration agenda
body_text: A close political ally of Donald Trump has broken from the administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement agenda and recommended it “step back” to evaluate what it could do better. “To get better, the first thing you got to do is admit you’re doing something wrong,” Jim Justice, a Republican senator of West Virginia, told Politico. “And in this situation, with all that’s going on and all the stuff, we probably got to step back from it and say: ‘Maybe we’re doing something wrong here or there,’ and then adjust to that.” Justice, who also sits on the Senate agriculture committee, made his comments after three rancher associations condemned Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) activity for negatively affecting agricultural communities. But his comments also come after an ACLU of West Virginia investigation found that about three-quarters of the more than 593 arrested by ICE in the state during “Operation Country Roads” in January had no criminal record. “Before you know it, you get people that get carried away in their job and whatever it may be, and all of a sudden, then you’re dragging people away that have lived on your street corner for 15 years, and I don’t know that we need to be doing that stuff,” Justice told Politico. Trump’s immigration enforcement agenda is a signature policy of his administration. Many voters indicated they wanted stricter immigration policies, but the intense tactics of federal agents have sparked anger nationwide. For ranchers in rural communities, ICE operations have had “a massive chilling effect on the legal, documented, skilled workers” who assist in beef production and the cattle supply chain, the Kansas Livestock Association, Oklahoma Cattlemen’s Association and Texas Cattle Feeders Association said in a statement released last week. Dairy farmers have also recently raised concerns that ICE operations in rural areas could soon hurt their industries. “If we had a concerted effort to have enforcement activities within agriculture, you could really harm our ability to produce food to feed ourselves,” Rick Naerebout, the CEO of the Idaho Dairymen’s Association, told NPR. West Virginia is home to more than 22,700 ranchers, most of which are family-owned. Justice’s criticisms make him the latest Republican to distance himself from Trump in the lead-up to the midterm elections. Maria Elvira Salazar, a Republican congresswoman from Florida, recently ran a campaign advertisement telling Trump his “immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far”. The Guardian has asked the White House for a response.

title: Good news in US inflation report boosts chances Fed won’t hike rates
body_text: Good economic news boosted Wall Street’s main indexes on Wednesday, as a softer-than-anticipated inflation reading buoyed up hopes that the Federal Reserve might not hike rates as soon ⁠as next month. A commerce department report ⁠showed the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index stood at 3.4% on an annual basis in August against estimates of 3.7%, per economists polled by Reuters. Separately, second-quarter GDP data – the broadest measure of the economy’s health – showed that the US economy grew at a solid clip, driven ⁠by robust consumer spending and business investment related to the buildout of AI infrastructure. “The market had been tracing out a bullish formation, meaning the price pattern suggested that any positive catalyst could trigger a move higher and that’s exactly ⁠what happened,” said Sam Stovall, chief investment strategist at CFRA Research. Traders now see a roughly 35% chance of an October rate hike, down from about a 45% chance, according to data ‌compiled by LSEG. The Federal Reserve is under pressure to cut rates from the White House after raising them earlier this month for the first time since 2023. Inflation has emerged as the top issue for voters in the run-up to the midterm elections with Donald Trump receiving poor marks for his handling of the economy. US stock markets rose in early trading, but the S&P ended the day down 0.25% and the Dow fell 0.86%. The Nasdaq ended the day up 0.24%. Despite weakness in September, driven by bond market volatility and elevated oil prices amid the US-Iran conflict, the benchmark S&P 500 and the ‌Nasdaq were on pace for a second straight quarterly advance, if gains hold. On Wednesday, the yield on the 10-year treasury bond held steady at 5.246%, a day after hitting its highest since June 2007. Crude oil prices rose on the day, with the December contract for Brent crude futures moving higher. There was also positive news from the jobs market. ADP, the US’s largest payroll supplier, said private employers added 90,000 jobs in September, higher than expected and up from 36,000 in August. On Friday, the labor department will release its latest monthly jobs tally, which is expected to show a gain of 84,000 for September, down from 162,000 in the prior month. Reuters contributed reporting

title: Senate Democrats block datacenter energy bill, saying ‘toothless’ legislation ‘misses the mark’
body_text: Senate Democrats on Wednesday blocked legislation intended to offset the impact of datacenters on consumer electricity bills, calling it a “toothless” attempt to address a top voter concern ahead of November’s midterm elections. The Ratepayer Protection Act failed by a 57-to-43 vote, falling just shy of the 60 votes necessary to advance through the Republican-controlled chamber. Four Democrats – Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota and both Georgia senators, Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock – joined Republicans in support of the measure. “Americans are calling for real solutions, real guardrails, real solutions on AI. Republicans’ toothless datacenter bill completely misses the mark,” the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, said in a floor speech before the vote. Schumer assailed Trump for a meeting with top tech executives on Tuesday that the president said yielded a “morally binding” agreement to put controls on artificial intelligence. “Relying on ‘self-regulation’ is how we got into this mess,” Schumer added. Earlier this month, the House of Representatives had approved the bill by an almost unanimous vote. Datacenter construction and electricity consumption has grown in recent years amid advances in AI and other technologies, and with it has come increasing anxiety among voters about the facilities’ impacts on their energy bills. The bipartisan legislation is an attempt by Congress to address those anxieties, and would have required electric utilities to consider adopting new standards so that datacenters pick up the costs of any necessary upgrades to transmission, generation and distribution, which can otherwise be transferred to households and businesses. It was proposed ahead of the 3 November midterm elections in which Democrats are campaigning on lowering the cost of living in their bid to regain control of the Senate and House. Its sponsor in the lower chamber was Gabe Evans, a Colorado Republican who is a top target of Democrats, while the Ohio Republican Jon Husted championed the bill through the Senate. “It’s clear that big tech should be paying their own way, not passing the cost on to local communities and states – and this bill does that,” Husted said in a floor speech on Wednesday, urging Democrats to back the bill that the president had indicated he would sign. Though Ohio voted for Trump by an 11-point margin two years ago, recent polls have shown Husted trailing his opponent, the Democratic former senator Sherrod Brown, who has accused the incumbent of bowing to the demands of the datacenter industry. While the proposal was seen as an attempt by Republicans Senate leaders to bolster Husted’s re-election chances, it also presented a quandary for the chamber’s Democrats, since voting it down could be seen as running counter to their pledges of lowering electricity bills. Nonetheless, the party’s leaders opted to oppose the measure, saying it would have been ineffective at actually addressing datacenters’ electricity consumption. The vote was one of the last the Senate is expected to take before the midterms. The chamber is scheduled to conclude its work on Friday, after which senators will return to their states to campaign.

title: Trump’s AI chatbot turns on its master
body_text: Donald Trump, in a development that could almost be from a Greek tragedy, appears to have invented something that is willing to do what no one in his orbit will: tell him the truth. The president launched America.gov on Tuesday, an AI platform which the White House says will make it easier for Americans to interact with the federal government and eventually complete services like renewing passports and enrolling in Medicare. At the heart of the website is a chatbot. You plug in questions. It gives you answers. Unfortunately for Trump, America.gov – which, according to the executive order he signed, is a place where Americans can “receive accurate answers” to all sorts of questions – is providing the kind of answers that he will not want to hear. It stands ready to debunk his false claims on all sorts of things, including election fraud, inflation and the impact of wind turbines on whales. I would really recommend testing it out, as I did on Tuesday. I started off by asking Trump’s flagship product: Who won the 2020 election? Trump, famously and wrongly, argues that he did. America.gov does not have time for such claims. “Joseph R Biden Jr won the 2020 US presidential election,” the bot said, before listing the number of electoral college votes Biden won by. Next up I tried some of Trump’s more recent claims. This week the president said people were “twice as wealthy as [they] were a short time ago”. Does America.gov agree? “No. Federal Reserve data do not show American household wealth doubling since January 20, 2025,” it said. “The Fed’s Economic Well-Being of US Households in 2025 found 73% of adults ‘doing okay’ or ‘living comfortably’ – unchanged from recent years, not a doubling of typical household finances.” Pretty definitive. What about Trump’s (already debunked) claim that the US experienced the “worst inflation ever” under Biden? Once again, America.gov disagreed with its creator. “No. Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Consumer Price Index data do not show that January 20, 2021–January 20, 2025 was the worst inflation ever in US history.” There are plenty more examples. Trump’s bot denied his claim, made in a recent speech to the United Nations, that the US and Venezuela have 60% of the world’s oil. It said there was no widespread voter fraud in the 2020 election, in contrast to Trump’s repeated, untrue claims. The bot refuted Trump’s assertion, made as he launched America.gov on Tuesday, that no president other than him had refused to take a government salary. It was also happy to weigh in on matters which might seem trivial, but are close to Trump’s heart. The attendance at his 2017 inauguration, for example. At the time Trump’s team said he had drawn “the largest audience ever to witness an inauguration, period, both in person and around the globe”. America.gov said: “Official sources do not support that [2017] had the largest in-person crowd of any US inauguration … The Joint Congressional Committee on Inaugural Ceremonies lists Barack Obama’s January 20, 2009 ceremony as having the largest attendance of any presidential inauguration in US history and the largest attendance of any event in Washington, DC history.” Finally, what about Trump’s claim – made during one of his many rants against wind power – that turbines drive whales “loco”? “No,” America.gov said. “US federal science agencies do not find that wind turbines (‘windmills’) drive whales ‘loco’.” It added, just to be completely clear, that windmills are not “driving whales insane”. So who do you believe? A president who, according to the Washington Post, made 30,573 false or misleading claims in his first term? Or his AI platform, which draws upon 29,000 websites to formulate its answers? Americans encouraged to use what Trump himself has hailed as “the ultimate product” can make up their own mind.

title: Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad
body_text: With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”. On Wednesday, the state department obligated the funds to the grantees hours before the deadline despite congressional concerns and requests not to do so, according to a source familiar with the negotiations. The state department declined to comment on questions from the Guardian specifically on whether it had obligated the funds and had “blown” holds from Congress due to concerns about the money’s use. Critics have focused on 43 awards of a combined $176.9m that will bolster rightwing and conservative causes around the world while probably angering US allies over interference in internal politics. The Guardian has seen a sample of the controversial grants, which make up most of the $205m in funding that Congress has appropriated for the entire Human Rights and Democracy Fund (HRDF). Sources with knowledge of the grant process have told the Guardian that the awards were personally lobbied for by members of the Trump administration, and reflect interests that include JD Vance’s warnings of the collapse of traditional western values in Europe and Stephen Miller’s push against immigration and to support white minorities in countries like South Africa. “The story for me is the high-level – including White House-directed – attention on these programs,” said a person familiar with the discussions over the democracy awards. “These awards have been briefed at the highest levels of the department and have buy-in from the White House.” The proposed awards represent a significant shift in US support for dissidents, human rights defenders and civil society groups under authoritarian governments. The new slate includes projects in wealthy nations, and those focused on opposition to regulation, Brexit, immigration, anti-communism, Christian protection and opposition to “gender ideology”, offering a window into how the Trump administration is redefining what qualifies as human rights and merits tens of millions of dollars in US foreign assistance. “Congress appropriated money for the democracy fund on a bipartisan basis to support defenders of human rights, to assist victims of human rights violations and to instead promote the growth of democracy abroad,” said Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the US Senate committee on foreign relations. “The Trump administration’s proposals would use taxpayer funds to promote far-right organizations and programs in established democracies. This is a waste of resources and undermines United States values and relations with democratic partners, including allies in Europe.” A Democratic congressional aide said Shaheen had maintained 10 holds on $22m of awards focusing on Brazil, South Africa, Nigeria, and the promotion of a rightwing ideology in the United Kingdom and in Europe. According to the aide, secretary of state Marco Rubio had personally signed a memo to disregard the holds and obligate the funds. The largest award, of $40m, was directed to a consortium led by the Victims of Communism Memorial Foundation (VOC), an anti-communist non-profit that has received far smaller grants in the past. A state department vetting document seen by the Guardian records $96,997 in previous contracts in the last five years between the foundation and the department, all in the 2022 fiscal year, and notes that it had been vetted in 2019 in connection with tickets to the foundation’s gala. The vetting document also identifies Andrew Bremberg, a former Trump White House domestic policy adviser and US ambassador to the UN European office, as a “senior leader” of the foundation. In July, ProPublica reported that Samuel Samson, a 27-year-old deputy assistant secretary overseeing the new grants, was linked to senior members of VOC through his studies at the Christian conservative Hillsdale College graduate program. (A state department official then told the outlet that the relationship had nothing to do with the grant). Samson has described the US and Europe as partners in a shared civilizational struggle. Samson toured Austria, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Slovakia last December – all countries that were floated to receive a $2m grant to counter migration weaponized by Russia and Belarus – and criticized NGOs that previous administrations had worked with for promoting what he called radical concepts, including gender theory and DEI. The state department did not comment on individual grants but said the programs were still in “active deliberation”, that awardees would meet guidelines for federal grants, and that all programming would undergo a “standard and rigorous vetting process by grant professionals”. “Our programming in Europe aims to support our European allies in defending those rights and principles, along with their civilizational self-confidence and sovereignty from those who seek to undermine them,” a state department official said. “The national security strategy highlights our priorities in Europe, which includes advancing political liberty, promoting free speech, and collaborating with European partners to jointly support European revitalization and civilizational self-confidence.” Under the legislation authorizing the fund, the money must be assigned by 30 September, the end of the fiscal year, when unobligated funds typically lapse. The Guardian first reported that Trump officials had drawn up no-bid grants aimed at rightwing and anti-immigration causes in Europe. ProPublica similarly reported that there were at least a dozen no-bid grants earmarked for rightwing projects. The document now shows how much of the fund the plan takes up, and which awards have since been dropped. A $1m award titled “Countering Lawfare and Censorship in Brazil” would fund civil society groups opposing what it calls judicial overreach and censorship by Brazil’s supreme court. The Trump administration sanctioned the Brazilian justice Alexandre de Moraes last year after lobbying by Eduardo Bolsonaro, son of the former president. A program titled “Promoting Western Civilization Allies” would be limited to implementers who do not subscribe to “ideologically weaponized accounts of human rights, such as gender ideology”, according to the document, and will receive $2m. It names possible recipients in Poland, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, and the Balkans with “anti-communist” and “natural rights” approaches. One award was allocated to document “democratic backsliding” in Europe tied to “mass and illegal migration” and legislation by “supra-national entities”, while a $1m journalism consortium would push back against designations of “trusted” media outlets. The list also includes $2m for early-warning networks protecting Christians in Nigeria. And a $3m no-bid award would go to the Jobs Foundation, a UK group run by Matthew Elliott, who led the Vote Leave campaign. The grant, titled “Countering Overregulation to Advance American Investment”, would promote a “common good capitalism index” and pro-business policy, including how the foundation promoted Brexit as a chance to cut the UK’s climate regulations. The document also shows that a proposed $5m no-bid grant to the Free Speech Union, the British group founded by Toby Young, has been marked “withdrawn”. When the award was first reported in July, Young said the group had never applied for or received US government money (though Trump officials had reportedly met with the group during a European tour late last year). The grant would have paid the group to campaign against online safety and hate speech laws, including Britain’s Online Safety Act, a law passed under the Conservatives in 2023. Meant to protect children from harmful content and enforced by Ofcom, it has age-verification rules – which took effect last year – that have drawn constant criticism from the Trump administration, which cast them as censorship. The Free Speech Union is the second British group to drop off the list. A $7m no-bid award to 878, a thinktank whose stated missions include restoring Judeo-Christian culture and “ending mass migration and deporting illegal immigrants”, was abandoned in July after pushback from Congress. It was founded by Jacob Rees-Mogg, who served as Brexit opportunities minister and business secretary before losing his seat at the 2024 election, and now presents on GB News. The British awards would have sent $15m in US taxpayer money to groups run by two sitting Conservative peers and a former cabinet minister, regarding issues including online safety law to immigration.

title: Hegseth confirms plan to cut 20% of US top military brass and rails at ‘beardos, weirdos and wimps’
body_text: The US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, has confirmed plans to cut 20% of generals and admirals and declared “no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps” would be tolerated inside the country’s military. Delivering his latest extraordinary attack on diversity, and dismissing reports of low morale within the US armed forces as “false claims”, Hegseth also suggested they were retaining service personnel at “record” rates. The defense secretary pointed to those onboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, following concern over mental health and supply issues on the aircraft carrier, which was deployed for almost nine months. About “80% of the force” onboard was retained, he said. Addressing lower-ranking troops at the Marine Corps Base on Wednesday, Hegseth boasted about the anti-diversity policies in the Pentagon pushed by Donald Trump’s administration. “The only focus, as you know, in your formations should be training, readiness, accountability, discipline and lethality,” Hegseth said. “And when you pursue those things, you don’t have to walk on eggshells … the complainers, the ideologues and the poor performers are no longer in the driver’s seat.” He added: “But it’s worth saying again, so the fake news understands it. We are no longer the woke department or the weak department. Simple translation of that: no fatties, no trannies, no beardos, no weirdos, no wimps, no radicals. Just warriors.” Generals “who clung to the woke department, or seemed to think civilian control of the military is simply a suggestion, well, they no longer work here”, Hegseth said. Eight US navy personnel assigned to the Lincoln attempted suicide since the start of their lengthy deployment as part of the US war on Iran, it emerged last week. Hegseth appeared to reference the carrier while attacking the media on Wednesday, insisting there are “disingenuous headlines about deployment lengths, patently false claims of low troop morale, or flat-out propaganda, as if it’s written by our adversaries”. The crew of the Lincoln, which was at sea for 286 days, disembarked on 1 September in a Thai resort city. The crew had been scheduled to wrap their deployment in May, but it was extended amid Trump’s war on Iran. During his speech in Quantico, Virginia, the defense secretary announced several new initiatives, including a a new Pentagon project which will see Elon Musk, Palmer Luckey – a top Trump donor and ally – and Newt Gingrich, the former US House speaker, work with the department to study the “future of warfare”. The Guardian previously reported on how Luckey’s company, Anduril Inudstries, a major defense technology company, has received billions in government contracts over the last year. Hegseth also took aim at Ivy League universities and liberal arts colleges during his speech – which Trump has targeted routinely since he returned to office. The defense secretary branded the institutions as “DEI-worshipping woke factories”. Notably, Hegseth is a graduate of Harvard and Princeton Universities – both members of the Ivy League. Hegseth said the Pentagon would now partner with other institutions as part of its educational pipeline. Some of these schools, such as Liberty University and Hillsdale College, are known for conservative values. Others joining the partnership are Louisiana State University, Mississippi University and Tuskegee University.
