title: Trump suggests Iran could ‘take out’ Los Angeles or San Diego
body_text: Leaders in California have denounced Donald Trump as “reckless” and “deranged” after the US president suggested Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego – two liberal cities in the blue state that has been a frequent target of his administration. At a rally in ruby red Nebraska on Monday night, Trump told supporters that he hoped to see a “tremendous victory” in the fast-approaching November midterm elections. He then suggested high prices due to the war with Iran were a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”. “They can take out a city,” Trump said in Grand Island. “Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” The crowd applauded. “It’ll be over very soon,” Trump said of the war. The governor and the cities’ mayors quickly condemned the comments. “After sending the National Guard and Marines to occupy California, Donald Trump is now saying our foreign enemies should ‘take out’ Los Angeles and San Diego,” the California governor, Gavin Newsom, said on X. “He is deranged and dangerous.” Newsom, a Democrat who has repeatedly clashed with Trump over his two terms, said from his press office account: “Let’s be clear: The President is advocating for an attack on 10+ million U.S. residents in two of America’s largest cities. This is not normal. None of this is. And we will continue to remind folks of that every day.” Karen Bass, the mayor of Los Angeles, assailed the president for making what she called “irresponsible threats” that “could potentially compromise” the safety of America’s second-largest city. “The role of a president is to protect the country, not to actively threaten it and encourage attacks on American lives,” she said in a statement. Todd Gloria, the mayor of San Diego, said his city was “not collateral damage” in the president’s war. “We are not expendable. And we are never a “small price to pay,” he wrote on X “Keep our city out of your reckless war talk.” San Diego, the nation’s eighth-largest city, is home to critical US military infrastructure. Online, the comments – part of a rambling, nearly hour-and-a-half speech – set off a debate about what the president actually meant. Was it a crude joke about two blue cities or had he, accidentally perhaps, disclosed confidential intelligence about potential Iranian targets? Some conservative activists argued that Trump, in his elliptical way of speaking, was referring to high gas prices when he argued that it was a “small price to pay”, and not the capacity of Iran to “take out” a US city. The White House on Tuesday sought to downplay the remark, calling the backlash a “media freakout” and “not rooted in reality”. In a social media post, the White House communications director, Steven Cheung, said the president was “clearly stating US cities would have been threatened if a nuclear Iran hadn’t been stopped”. “America is safer because of the President,” he added. “Iran has no nuclear, no navy, no air force, and no money.” US defence officials have previously stated that Iran currently lacks the capability to launch a direct missile attack on the US mainland. Trump has argued in previous speeches that allowing Iran to develop a nuclear weapon would threaten US cities. In his last state of the union speech he claimed that Iran was working to build missiles that would “soon” reach US soil. In Nebraska, where an unexpectedly close Senate race has rattled Republicans, Trump insisted that he was “doing great” and urged supporters to pretend like his name was on the ballot when they vote in November. But in California, where Steve Hilton, the Republican gubernatorial candidate endorsed by Trump, is seeking an upset, the president’s comments were met with furious denunciations. “Thirteen million Californians call LA and San Diego counties home,” said Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor who has sought to take up the anti-Trump mantle carried by the outgoing Newsom. “Their lives are not a ‘small price to pay’ or a punchline for Donald Trump.” • This article was amended on 6 October 2026. Trump suggested that Iran could “take out” the two cities, but did not suggest that it do so, as the original headline indicated.

title: ‘Spit on our sacrifice’: Canadian veterans fume after Trump and allies take jibes at military
body_text: On the morning of 11 September 2001, Perry Chalmers was running drills for the Royal Canadian Regiment’s specialised mortar platoon in New Brunswick when he heard the news: America was under attack. Word quickly spread across the base. “I went inside to watch the news,” the former corporal recalls. “And there was a huge feeling of – and you’re going to have to excuse me – holy shit. What the fuck just happened?” Chalmers called his wife, who informed him that, just before 10.30am, the second of the World Trade Center towers had fallen. With that, his battalion was put on notice: dispatched to nearby airports to assist in the forced landings of commercial aircraft after the shutdown of North American airspace. The Canadian troops went to retrieve their rucksacks and any other necessities, should they need to spring into action at a moment’s notice. As Chalmers recalls: “Things started to happen really quickly.” Chalmers would deploy to Afghanistan, on a nine-month tour of combat duty, where he saw combat alongside US troops. He put his mortar platoon training to good use, as a counter-IED engineer, dealing with the threat of improvised explosives in conjunction with the US army’s 10th Mountain Division. He was one of more than 40,000 members of the Canadian armed forces who served in Afghanistan, supporting US and Nato operations. The Canadians lost 158 lives. In 2007, a stretch of Ontario’s highway 401 was rechristened the “Highway of Heroes” to commemorate the convoys of fallen soldiers ferried between the military base in Trenton, Ontario, and the coroner’s office in Toronto. This response to 9/11 was consistent with the longer history of Canadian-US military cooperation. About 14,000 Canadians landed on Juno Beach in Normandy on D-day during the second world war. More than 26,000 Canadians served in the Korean war. While Canada did not officially participate in the Vietnam war, an estimated 30,000 Canadians headed across the border to volunteer for the US military. Over the course of the war in Afghanistan, Chalmers can count 35 fellow Canadian troops who lost their lives. But he never really brooked any regrets, or bad feelings, about his role in the US-led war. “My experience was that we were participating in an operation to help our brothers and sisters in the United States,” he says. “None of them ever snubbed their noses at us. We were treated as equals, and respected, for what we brought to the table.” But no longer. While calling Canada “a state”, the US vice-president, JD Vance, recently commented that it “had underinvested in its military that quite literally would get invaded by a foreign country were it not for the umbrella of protection provided by the United States of America”. Going one step further, Donald Trump’s transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, told Fox News that Canada “doesn’t have a military”. Self-styled “secretary of war” Pete Hegseth has spent time on X, mocking Canadian cadets and criticising a Canadian coast guard detachment for taking part in a Pride celebration. Trump himself was criticised earlier this year for claiming that Canadian and other Nato forces in Afghanistan were “never needed”, claiming these allies “stayed a little back, a little off the frontlines”. The remarks have been condemned at the highest level of the Canadian government. The defence minister, David McGuinty, described Hegseth’s social media posts as “below the dignity of the office he holds”. Amid a serious diplomatic dispute between the two countries, the prime minister, Mark Carney, accused Trump and Hegseth of “doing memes”. “It’s disrespect and betrayal,” Chalmers says. “It makes me very angry.” “It’s really hard to hear how ungrateful they are, especially Vance, who served,” said Chris Banks, a retired Canadian army sergeant with nearly two decades of experience. “To hear him spit on our sacrifice is insulting, it’s hurtful, and it’s disrespectful to the dead. On the other hand, these men have proven themselves nothing more than children. So when I heard JD Vance say it, it’s like, ‘Oh, good. Dumbass said something else.’” Banks deployed to Afghanistan in 2008, where he was part of a Canadian platoon that laid down cover fire for Americans under attack from the Taliban. To this day, he still has vivid memories of taking cover in a ditch near Pashmul, alongside an American platoon, looking up as the trees overhead were shredded by shrapnel. He says he was proud to serve. But when he came home to Ontario in 2009, he felt something had changed. He began drinking heavily – sometimes as much as a litre of vodka a day – and struggling with suicidal thoughts. All hallmarks of PTSD. He received treatment, and now advocates for the mental health and wellbeing of other Canadian veterans. Still, a tinge of bitterness remains, when he thinks back on fighting on behalf of the US. “I lost a part of myself,” he says. “In that war we fought, for them.” *** Nancy Payne still remembers exactly where she was when she found out her son had died. Cpl Randy Payne served with a military police unit, stationed in Wainwright, Alberta. He was part of a specialised close protection team, charged with safeguarding high-ranking officers, government officials and other VIPs, in war zones. On 22 April 2006, an armoured vehicle triggered a roadside bomb outside Kandahar airbase, killing Payne and three other Canadian soldiers. It was the deadliest attack on Canadian forces since 2002 – when four Canadian soldiers were killed by a US bomb after a disastrous friendly fire incident at the Tarnak Farms training facility in Afghanistan. Nancy was at home, alone, when the phone rang in the dead of the night. It was her son’s commanding officer. “When you get a call at three in the morning from Randy’s boss, you know it’s not good news,” she recalls, speaking over the phone from her home in Lansdowne, Ontario. “I just kept saying ‘Not my Randy … not my Randy’.” In 2025, the Canadian government awarded Nancy a Silver Cross, a commendation for Canadian military mothers. That’s all changed, now.” Nancy is not the only military mother who feels this way. title: ‘Using the presidency to line his pockets’: could claims of corruption fuel backlash against Trump?
body_text: In Donald Trump’s telling, he’s a model of incorruptible self-sacrifice. “I’m the only president that donated his salary,” he told a group of cheering supporters at a Hispanic heritage month celebration in the White House last week, before conceding that George Washington – “a very wealthy person” – might have beaten him to the punch. “They pay me $550,000 a year, and in my first term, I donated it,” he continued. “In my second term I donated it too. I donated it to fixing the White House. I donated the salary into the White House preservation.” Trump’s ethical self-depiction was undercut in startling fashion a day later when the crypto company that runs his memecoin offered “the most exclusive dinner in the world” at the president’s members-only Trump National club in Washington. “Join three legends and featured speaker Donald J Trump,” gushed the invite to the 185 biggest investors in the Trump coin. The top 29 buyers were promised an invitation to an additional “VIP reception with your favourite president and one of the legends”. For the top four donors, a Trump 18-karat gold watch lay in store. The aim appeared to be to boost sales of the memecoin – called $Trump – over the next two months. Trump personally profits from the coin, and disclosures show he made about $636m from it last year. With just over a month to go before November’s midterm elections, Democrats seized on the dinner invitation as a political gift as they try to convert concerns over Trump’s perceived corruption into a groundswell of outrage. They theorize it will power a “blue wave” that could enable the party to retake control of the House of Representatives and the Senate on 3 November. “Donald Trump is vying to become the most corrupt person to ever walk the face of the earth,” posted Chuck Schumer, the Democrats’ leader in the US Senate. With the US president’s approval ratings already at record lows amid discontent over rising living costs fueled by the unpopular war with Iran, ethics experts say “unprecedented” levels of corruption engaged in by Trump, his family and close associates are sufficiently serious to make him vulnerable to a popular backlash. The question is whether the myriad of accusations – many of them technical in nature – are straightforward enough to carry popular resonance. The administration vigorously rejects the assertions, which a White House spokesman, Davis Ingle, called “irresponsible” and likely to “reinforce the public’s distrust in what they read”. “President Trump only acts in the best interests of the American public – which is why they overwhelmingly re-elected him to this office, despite years of lies and false accusations against him and his businesses,” he said in a statement. “There are no conflicts of interest. “The only special interest guiding President Trump’s decision-making is the best interest of the American people. President Trump has taken on a broad swath of entrenched special interests: negotiating most-favored-nation pricing deals with major pharmaceutical companies, launching TrumpRx.gov to lower drug prices, ending unfair trade practices that international corporations have exploited to offshore jobs, and implementing schedule F to fire unelected bureaucrats who actively subvert a democratically-elected president’s agenda. “Through these actions, President Trump is delivering on his promise to empower the forgotten men and women of our country by finally putting their interests first.” Recent surveys, however, indicate American voters are more concerned than ever before about government corruption. A Gallup poll published in September recorded 89% of both all adults as saying the problem was widespread. Only Lebanon, Peru, Ghana and Nigeria have registered higher levels of public concern in the past three years. Analysts insist the US public has ample cause for complaint. “We’re facing an ethics crisis which starts and ends with a president who is constantly using his office to find new ways to personally profit,” said Jordan Libowitz, communications vice-president with Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a non-partisan watchdog. “With a new story every day about Donald Trump using the presidency to line his pockets, it’s no surprise that Americans are losing faith in their government.” Trump’s own filings show he earned $2.2bn from his various business dealings in his first year back in the White House – including $1.4bn from his family’s cryptocurrency enterprise, World Liberty Financial. Observers identify at least three main areas of potential abuse; crypto, a venture which Trump denounced as a “fraud” just five years ago; stock trading by government officials, including the president himself; and the predictions markets, represented by companies such as Kalshi and Polymarket, both of which have links to Donald Trump Jr, and which have raised concerns about well-connected figures profiting through putting bets on government decisions and the content of official speeches. There are also concerns about the growth of “pay to play” practices that have seen wealthy donors being granted special access and favorable decisions, including dropped criminal investigations, in exchange for donations to Trump’s campaign and political Super Pac. Presidential pardons and sentence commutations have been doled out to those who have contributed to the president’s re-election effort. As Schumer’s post indicates, Democrats have increasingly tried to make corruption a campaign issue. A 30-second advertisement from Chris Pappas, a New Hampshire representative running for re-election, reflects a more widespread mood in favor of putting it center stage. The question is whether the message on rampant graft is cutting through with an electorate that may find inflation and higher living costs easier issues to grapple with. Dylan Hedtler-Gaudette, director of government affairs at the Project on Government Oversight, another watchdog group, acknowledged that many voters were confused by the complexity of the accusations leveled at Trump. “Support for the Trump administration and for President Trump himself is declining pretty rapidly,” he said. “But it’s hard to disentangle. Is it about the corruption? Or is it about the affordability crisis continuing and in some ways getting worse? “Corruption tends to be in the eye of the beholder. And if you ask different people about the word corruption, they say, ‘Yeah, it’s a problem.’ But if you ask them to define what they mean by corruption, it can diverge wildly depending on how they affiliate and how they identify in terms of their partisanship and their political identity.” Brendan Fischer, director of strategic investigation at the Campaign Legal Center, said the public had been overwhelmed and “numbed” by a “fire hose” of corruption emanating from Trump’s second presidency which, experts agree, has greatly exceeded that of his first administration. “It can become overwhelming trying to keep up with each of the latest examples,” said Fischer. “I think the Trump’s crypto dealings are incredibly concerning. His investments in the crypto industry open up new avenues for wealthy special interests to channel money to the president. But It’s potentially harder for the public to grasp. So it hasn’t broken through in the way that it that it probably should.” Easier to grasp, he believed, was Trump’s acceptance of a $400m plane from Qatar, which the president has said he will use in place of the existing Air Force One. The scale and brazenness of Trump’s cavalier disregard for ethical considerations creates a danger of apathy among voters, who may feel they are powerless to change the situation as they grapple with more quotidian cost issues. “It’s easy to just throw your hands up and say, ‘Everybody’s corrupt, nobody’s representing my interests, and my life is just not getting any better,’” Fischer said. “That is a dangerous situation for democracy. We need voters to cast their ballots and then remain engaged in the political process to make sure our elected officials are representing the interests of voters and not just their own or the interests of their donors.” Richard Painter, a former White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, said Trump’s decision to go war with Iran opened up further corruption avenues – citing reports that both Donald Trump Jr and his brother, Eric Trump, have invested in drone manufacturers that have secured government contracts. “Whenever there’s a war, there’s an enormous amount of money to be made. People say there are those who die in a war, and those who become millionaires, or maybe in this case billionaires,” said Painter, now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota. “This is what President Eisenhower talked about with the military-industrial complex back in 1961, but we’ve never had a president whose family actually made money from the military-industrial complex.” Painter predicted that conditions were ripe for “an enormous public backlash” but said the Democrats had to adopt a credible anti-corruption message after losing the public’s confidence by failing to speak out against Hunter Biden’s attempts to leverage his White House access when his father Joe Biden was president. “The Democrats had their chance in 2021 when Biden took office, when we should have had our reawakening on ethics, and they failed,” he said. “If they want to win races not only in 2026, but in 2028, they’d better get their act together and focus on ethics.” One historical model, Painter suggested, was the anti-corruption crusade championed by Jimmy Carter in his successful 1976 presidential campaign, which took place amid lingering anger at Richard Nixon over the Watergate scandal that drove him from office and his failure to quickly end the war in Vietnam. Democrats have invoked a more recent inspiration: Hungary’s recently elected prime minister, Peter Magyar, who mobilized rising resentment over government corruption in April this year to unseat the incumbent, Viktor Orbán – a close ally of Trump – in an election landslide. Steven Levitsky, a political scientist at Harvard University and co-author, with Daniel Ziblatt, of How Democracies Die, said the key similarity between the US and Hungarian circumstances was the sense of corruption further undermining an already failing government. “Orbán was successful in part because the economy was pretty good for much of his period in office,” Levitsky said. “But eventually it slowed down, and corruption became a major factor. “It’s sad but true that in many, many cases in democracies around the world, if incumbents are perceived to be delivering – if the economy is going well, if they brought down inflation, etc – voters will turn a blind eye to corruption. It’s only when you combine poor performance with corruption that it becomes salient. “Unfortunately, in the United States, one of the things that’s benefited Trump is the perception that all of politics is corrupt, mainly because of the extraordinarily outsized role of money in politics. “There are a lot of reasons why Trump is unpopular now. Corruption is one of them but I don’t think it’s the principal one.”

title: California to ‘actively monitor’ for possible threats after Trump said Iran could ‘take out’ LA and San Diego
body_text: California’s governor, Gavin Newsom, on Tuesday directed the state’s emergency preparedness center to “actively monitor” possible threats to the state after Donald Trump suggested Iran could “take out” the cities of Los Angeles and San Diego. Trump has faced a chorus of condemnation from Democratic leaders in California after his comments at a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, which the White House has suggested were being taken out of context. At the president’s rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, Trump claimed that high prices due to the war with Iran are a “small price to pay for keeping the world safe – keeping our country safe”. He went on: “They can take out a city. Let them take out Los Angeles. Let them take out San Diego.” The crowd applauded the line. “Donald Trump’s remarks were dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs,” Newsom said in a post on X, adding that the state’s threat-assessment center would be on heightened alert “in the event that foreign actors interpret the President’s remarks as an invitation to target California”. From the governor’s press office account, he taunted California Republicans for their “radio silence” in response the president’s bombastic remark. But one Republican House candidate, Jim Desmond, who is running in a competitive San Diego-based seat, pushed back. “America must stand up to Iran and defend our interests, but the first responsibility of our commander in chief is to protect the American people and our homeland,” Desmond, a former mayor of San Marcos, said in a statement. It is a notable rebuke from a Republican in a closely watched contest that could help the party retain their razor-thin majority in the lower chamber. Desmond is set to face Marni Von Wilpert, a lawyer and member of San Diego’s city council, for the state’s 48th congressional district – which was redrawn in response to Proposition 50. Desmond, also a navy veteran, said that he “served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war”. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage,” he added. He joined a string of prominent Democrats who called out the comments. Hakeem Jeffries, the House minority leader, said: “The nuclear annihilation of an American city is no laughing matter.” Xavier Becerra, the Democratic nominee for governor vying to succeed Newsom, said he wasn’t surprised by the president’s comments. “Donald Trump is a known commodity – you know how he acts, you know how he behaves,” Becerra told reporters at a campaign event in Los Angeles on Tuesday. But he took a jab at Republicans who “profess that they should be the leaders of our state” but were. not willing to “stand up to Donald Trump”. Becerra’s Republican rival, Steve Hilton, did not return a request for comment. But many Trump supporters dismissed the uproar. Blake Marnell, who wears a brick-patterned suit to resemble Trump’s border wall, lives in San Diego and was at the rally in Nebraska. He said by phone on Tuesday: “I defend his comments absolutely. It is not inappropriate to mention something like that now because you have to take it in the context in which it is spoken. title: S&P 500 and Nasdaq surge to record highs after AI chipmaker rally
body_text: The S&P 500 and Nasdaq closed at a record high after a rally around AI chipmakers and a dip in US treasury yields. At market’s close, the S&P 500 was up 0.58%, topping 7,800 for the first time in its history. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index rose 0.45%, while the Dow, which is slightly down from its record high in August, climbed 0.49%. Investors appeared optimistic after recent developments for chipmakers including Marvell Technology, Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom that showed growth in the markets for the chips used to power AI. Wall Street has also grown more optimistic that the US Federal Reserve will leave interest rates unchanged at its next board meeting in October. Job figures from September showed underwhelming growth in the labor market, and multiple Fed officials have said the next interest rate increase can probably wait. The optimism in the stock market, largely coming from continuing investment in AI, has defied other signs of instability in the US economy and global politics. The US bond market, typically seen as one of the safest investment vehicles, has been in turmoil in recent weeks. US bond yields, or the return an investor receives when a bond matures, reached recent highs amid concerns over high inflation and interest rates. The yield for 10-year US treasury bonds on Monday reached 5.349%, the highest since April 2022, before dipping back down on Tuesday. For American consumers, higher energy prices continue to be a major pain point. While gas prices have dipped over the last week, prices are still about $1.20 a gallon on average higher than a year ago. Diesel, which is used to fuel trucks, buses and trains, has also gone down from record high but is still over 40% higher than a year ago. The economy is expected to be a top issue in the upcoming midterm elections, with many voters expressing frustration over high prices. Donald Trump, who has been stumping for Republican candidates across the country, has been trying to paint a different picture for voters. At a rally in Nebraska on Monday night, Trump said that “our nation is doing better now than it’s ever done” and that gas prices would fall below $1.85 a gallon “in no time”.

title: LA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump suggesting Iran bomb them
body_text: Donald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked condemnation across the political spectrum. As residents of the two major west coast cities awoke on Tuesday to another sweltering day in a record-breaking heatwave, the president’s comments sent blood boiling even higher. Jessica, a 28-year-old Los Angeles hair stylist, was scrolling through social media early on Tuesday morning and was shocked to see that Trump had just suggested Iran should decimate her home town. For Jessica, who declined to be identified by her full name because she fears for the safety of her Mexican-born parents, the comments marked a new low for a president who had already spent years attacking immigrant families like hers. “I was just thinking what the fuck is wrong with him?” she said while waiting for a Waymo outside grocery store in LA’s Koreatown neighborhood. “He hates us. He hates LA. He hates any Democratic state ... It’s just a really sad situation.” In southern California, Trump’s unprecedented musing before a cheering crowd at a Nebraska rally on Monday night – that perhaps a foreign power should decimate two of the country’s best-known cities – has been met with reactions ranging from deep hostility to dismissive incredulity. Gavin Newsom, the state’s governor, called the remarks “dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs”. Perhaps most of all, California residents see it as a sign of the president’s fixation on tearing down west coast progressivism and diversity, most visibly through the deployment of national guard troops in Los Angeles during a series of brutal ICE raids in 2025. During a bustling lunch service at Grand Central Market, a food hall in downtown LA, tourists and residents milled between taco stands and dumpling stalls. Many had yet to hear of the president’s threats, until asked by a reporter. One of those who had was Jens Midthun, a downtown resident who often stops at the market for coffee. “Trump has tried to paint Los Angeles as a dystopia despite it being a wonderful place,” said Midthun, sipping an iced coffee under a shaded outdoor table as the temperature approached the triple digits. (Midthun serves as the president of the downtown LA neighborhood council, but was speaking in a personal capacity.) “It reminded me that the president is obsessed with us – obsessed with California, obsessed with Los Angeles,” Midthun said. “We try not to think about him and yet, here he is with Los Angeles’s name right there in his mouth.” Trump’s remarks have sparked a particularly strong reaction in San Diego, which is home to roughly a quarter-million veterans and has one of the largest concentrations of military personnel in the US. “His statement was so irrational, it’s hard to explain exactly what he was saying, but it sounded like he was willing to give us up,” said Gil Field, communications director for San Diego Veterans for Peace, a group that opposes the war. “It’s horrible and we’re horrified.” The military supports nearly 357,000 local jobs in the region, representing $61.3bn of San Diego county’s economy, according to a report released last year. Defense spending accounts for 22% of San Diego’s gross regional product and the area is home to multiple naval bases and Marine Corps stations, with one out of four active-duty marines based in San Diego. “This is a military town, so you’ve got bipartisan objections to his comments,” said Field, who noted that there were always concerns that San Diego could be targeted in war due to the heavy military presence. “So for him to say this about San Diego is particularly galling. He did San Diego a disservice.” Jim Desmond, a Republican naval veteran running for a congressional seat in San Diego, also offered a pointed rebuke. “I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war. Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality,” Desmond said on X. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.” Back in Los Angeles, far from the negative fantasies that Trump spins in his speeches, Midthun sees an economic powerhouse and vibrant cultural center sandwiched between the beach and the mountains, and enriched by some of the largest diaspora communities from across the world – South Korea, Mexico, El Salvador, Armenia and even Iran. “The president keeps talking about us, and talking about us,” Midthun said. “He’s got a lot of issues to solve. He should work on those issues instead of obsessing over the beautiful, great people of Los Angeles.”

title: Skepticism mires Trump’s Iowa steel plant project: ‘Promises are not the same as jobs’
body_text: Donald Trump has long sought to portray himself as a man of steel, from the White House photoshopping Trump to look like Superman, to enacting tariffs on steel and approving the sale of US Steel to Japan’s Nippon Steel with a ”golden” share given to the US government. Most recently, the Trump administration announced plans to construct the largest steel plant in the US, a $15bn plant in Lee county, Iowa, to be built by India-based Mesabi Metallics. But the project and claims surrounding it have incited skepticism over whether the plant will be built and delivered as promised, given Trump’s record and the financial history of Mesabi Metallics’ parent company, Essar Global. The plant had originally been scheduled to be built in Minnesota, a state that usually votes for Democrats. The shift to Iowa – where Republicans are struggling in the midterms – has also attracted attention. Doug May, who worked for 43 years as a steelworker at a mill in Granite City, Illinois, characterized the announcement as “political pandering” given the timing and how tariffs are hurting Iowa farmers. “He pulled the same thing in 2018, just before an election, when he announced that $10bn Foxconn project,” May said. That project, in swing state Wisconsin, failed to produce the jobs Trump and Foxconn had promised. May argued Trump was using the steel industry as a campaign strategy, while ignoring the work the United Steel Workers have done to push to save the industry, including filing more than 150 trade cases over the past decades to combat unfair trade practices that harm US workers. More than 40 domestic steel producers in the US filed for bankruptcy in the late 1990s. “We, the steel workers in Granite City, served as the best foot soldiers lobbying Congress, holding rallies and campaigns, to raise awareness to the cheating of foreign steelmakers and the need for stronger trade enforcement during that era,” added May. “Arguably, we played a very important role in saving domestic steel.” Essar Global first proposed building a steel plant with a $1.65bn investment in the Mesabi iron range in north-east Minnesota when they purchased Minnesota Steel in 2007. By 2016, Essar Steel Minnesota had filed for bankruptcy, following construction delays and financing issues at its Nashwauk, Minnesota, project, where its iron ore mine, which is supposed to fuel the Iowa steel plant, is located. In efforts to get rid of its debt, Essar Global sold off assets, including the completion of a sale of Essar Oil for $12.9bn to a Russia-controlled energy company. Mesabi Metallics briefly changed ownership to Virginia billionaire Thomas Clarke, before he lost control of the company in 2018, with Essar Global regaining control, but then losing its mining leases in 2021 when the state of Minnesota revoked them after a missed deadline. “This plant that has been 20 years in the making,” said Mark Dayton, former governor of Minnesota who dealt with Mesabi Metallics in the state through their bankruptcy proceedings. “I had, a decade ago, a very bad experience with Essar Steel because they started this plant, raised lots of expectations and hopes up north, and then went into default and went into bankruptcy and the like,” he said. Dayton said it did look like the plant was “actually proceeding, which is great if they’re going to actually complete building this plant”. But he added: “I’m skeptical of the announcement in Iowa this close to the election. That’s going to require $15bn of investment. I’d like to see that money on the table from Essar before they start to bring a shovel.” Some, including May, see echoes of Trump’s Foxconn announcement in June 2018. Ahead of the 2018 midterm elections, Trump described plans by the Taiwanese electronics contract manufacturer to open a gargantuan site outside Milwaukee as “the Eighth Wonder of the World” and said the plant “will provide jobs for much more than 13,000 Wisconsin workers”. Trump’s promises came as his approval ratings with the public were low, with Democrats poised to take advantage and regain control of the House. The site currently has about 1,100 employees and became an albatross around the necks of its backers as Foxconn’s ambitious plans failed to materialise. This time around, Trump’s approval ratings are even lower than they were in 2018 and Democrats are expected to regain control of the House and possibly the Senate. Trump has claimed “they’ve already started building” the plant, though a local NBC news affiliate in Iowa reviewed county records and disputed this claim. “The review found no major property purchases tied to the project this year. County officials say they don’t have details from the company about its plans. No permits have come before supervisors,” TV6 Investigates reported. A site location has not been disclosed by elected officials or Mesabi Metallics, with steel production aimed to begin in 2030. Mesabi Metallics did not respond to multiple requests for comment. In Iowa, the state’s Sierra Club chapter criticized the special state legislature session called for by the Republican governor, Kim Reynolds, to expand government subsidies the state can provide to Mesabi Metallics for the project. The state government is experiencing budget shortfalls, with more than $1bn in deficits the past two years. “Any time we step up incentive programs above and beyond what we’re giving, our revenues are going to be downgraded. And I understand there’s going to be jobs and economic activity around this, but the state is hurting financially,” said Pam Mackey Taylor, director of the Iowa chapter of the Sierra Club. “Do we need to really double the incentives that other large projects get to support this steel project?” The Iowa governor’s office did not respond to multiple requests for comment. In a special session, the Iowa legislature approved $1.36bn in tax incentives over 10 years to Mesabi Metallics. The steel plant is projected to create 1,750 permanent jobs and support up to 6,000 construction jobs. The White House did not comment directly on the steel plant’s move to Iowa or on White House senior communications strategist Jason Miller’s past work as a registered foreign lobbyist for Mesabi Metallics. Mesabi Metallics paid at least $240,000 SHW Partners, a government relations firm led by Miller, according to lobbyist disclosure records. The government of India also paid his firm $150,000 per month for “strategic counsel, tactical planning and government relations assistance on policy matters before the US government”, with the contract beginning in April 2025. Miller said the contract with India stopped in June 2026 and claimed the lobbying for Mesabi Metallics was domestic, not foreign, and ended in July 2026. “Taking a lobbyist who’s on the payroll of a foreign government and companies with huge government contracts and putting him inside the White House will create a three-headed beast of divided loyalties,” said Jon Golinger, democracy advocate at Public Citizen, in a statement on Miller’s appointment to a White House role. In response to Miller’s lobbying work and criticisms of it, Miller said: “Public Citizen is a bunch of America-hating fake news soy boy losers who prefer new investments go to China and not the US, and respectfully, they can get rekt. Not only did I deregister from Mesabi Metallics months ago, I took the additional step of recusing myself from having anything to do with their announcement at the White House.” A White House spokesperson, Kush Desai, said in an email: “No president has done more to revive American steelmaking than President Trump, whose 50 percent Section 232 tariffs on steel is driving record investments into this key sector. Those tariffs, along with the Administration’s other pro-growth and pro-investment policies, are not going away anytime soon.”

Miller said the contract with India stopped in June 2026 and claimed the lobbying for Mesabi Metallics was domestic, not foreign, and ended in July 2026. “Taking a lobbyist who’s on the payroll of a foreign government and companies with huge government contracts and putting him inside the White House will create a three-headed beast of divided loyalties,” said Jon Golinger, democracy advocate at Public Citizen, in a statement on Miller’s appointment to a White House role. In response to Miller’s lobbying work and criticisms of it, Miller said: “Public Citizen is a bunch of America-hating fake news soy boy losers who prefer new investments go to China and not the US, and respectfully, they can get rekt. Not only did I deregister from Mesabi Metallics months ago, I took the additional step of recusing myself from having anything to do with their announcement at the White House.” A White House spokesperson, Kush Desai, said in an email: “No president has done more to revive American steelmaking than President Trump, whose 50 percent Section 232 tariffs on steel is driving record investments into this key sector. Those tariffs, along with the Administration’s other pro-growth and pro-investment policies, are not going away anytime soon.”

title: Electric-shock gloves ICE plans to use inflicted intense pain in army study
body_text: The electric-shock gloves immigration agents could soon use to control detainees and protesters worked so powerfully during a military exercise that participants felt intense pain, stopped fighting immediately and feared additional exposures, according to a previously unreleased army study. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) leaders were aware of the findings before signing a $16.7m contract in August to purchase 6,000 pairs of shock gloves, according to records obtained by the watchdog group American Oversight and shared with the Associated Press. The shocks had a profound impact on army employees who played the role of combative prisoners during the exercise, which took place at the military prison at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas in October 2024 – as the Biden administration was in its final months. The participants, several of whom were large-statured men, stopped resisting seconds after officers applied shocks by touching the gloves to their skin, and were left with “fatigue, soreness and excessive apprehensiveness to being shocked again”, the study found. The gloves carry the brand name G.L.O.V.E., which stands for Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter, and are manufactured by Compliant Technologies, a company owned by military veterans and based in Lexington, Kentucky. When it emerged that the second Trump administration was ordering the devices for ICE, amid a hardline anti-immigration crackdown and record arrests and detention of immigrants the government wants to deport, experts expressed alarm and pointed to some high-profile lawsuits over their use in local correctional facilities. In one extreme case, a 43-year-old man died after allegedly being shocked 40 times by officers with a combination of the gloves and a Taser in a county jail in Kentucky, and the man’s widow is suing authorities. In the previous military exercise, the authors of the study shared with AP said: “After experiencing the effects of the GLOVE … participants stated just seeing the GLOVE was enough to make them want to comply.” ICE has called the gloves “distraction and de-escalation devices” that will be safer than other non-lethal options to subdue targets for arrest and deportation and protesters who create civil disturbances. The agency has argued the rapid compliance they cause will keep officers safer and prevent incidents from requiring potentially lethal force. But critics have warned the gloves will give ICE another weapon to intimidate and brutalize people even as the agency is under fire for excessive force that has left a trail of deaths and injuries across the nation. “The military assessment in ICE’s own files shows that these gloves can cause ‘intense pain’ and force compliance. It does not establish that they are safe,” said Chioma Chukwu, executive director of American Oversight. “Everyone should be alarmed that ICE is preparing to deploy a tool designed to inflict, at best, intense pain, without showing that it is safe for the people who will be subjected to it.” ICE released the study and other documents to American Oversight as part of the group’s Freedom of Information Act lawsuit against the agency seeking records related to its use of force. The military prison study assessed whether the gloves could be used effectively to forcibly remove combative prisoners from their cells, to respond to disturbances in common areas and to transport uncooperative inmates. Role-playing employees conducted several scenarios with and without the gloves to test their impact, including violent encounters in which inmates were to fight as hard as they could. The study found that using the gloves “increased the efficiency” of teams carrying out forced cell extractions and responding to disturbances by reducing the length of physical encounters, keeping guards from becoming exhausted and preventing injuries. They did not “significantly change” the time it took to control inmates during escorts but required less effort. “GLOVE provides a boost in confidence to smaller or less trained members,” the study found. “Inmate compliance was immediate” compared with other methods, it added. The electric jolt does not cause the body to freeze like a Taser shock does, but instead “works by overloading the peripheral nerve endings” of the skin to cause pain, the study said. Participants who were wet or had oil on their skin described even more powerful shocks, with one reporting discomfort for 30 minutes afterward. ICE’s contract requires the manufacturer to deliver the gloves within six months. The company owner, Jeff Niklaus, declined to make himself available for an interview. The White House border czar, Tom Homan, has said it could “be a while” before the gloves are in the field because ICE is still ironing out training and policy issues. A statement released on Tuesday by ICE did not address questions about the study and the status of the rollout, but said “officers are highly trained in de-escalation tactics”. Senator Catherine Cortez Masto of Nevada said ICE had not responded to a 27 August letter in which she and 15 other Democratic Senate colleagues called for ICE to abandon its plan to buy the gloves or explain how they would be used and managed to avoid abuse. She said she still wanted answers. “Without ICE’s responses to legitimate questions from 16 United States senators, the American public is being left in the dark about how these electric-shock gloves are being deployed and what, if any, training the agents who use them have received,” she said.

title: Trump backs away from top aides who reportedly advised pro-Russia government
body_text: Donald Trump distanced himself from two top advisers on Wednesday, claiming he did not have “any idea who else they work for”, after it was reported they spent the weekend assisting a pro-Russia government in the Balkans. On Truth Social, Trump wrote that Chris LaCivita, the co-manager of his 2024 presidential campaign, and James Blair, a campaign adviser and White House deputy chief of staff on leave of absence, “are outside consultants” and “do not work for me other than as outside consultants”. “They are allowed to do work for others, just like all consultants in Washington, D.C.,” Trump wrote. “I do not have any idea who else they work for but will, on reflection, ask them and, if there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!” The president’s comments came after the New York Times reported that LaCivita and Blair traveled to Republika Srpska, an autonomous entity in Bosnia and Herzegovina, to assist the government ahead of elections over the weekend. Sources told the newspaper that each adviser was paid hundreds of thousands of dollars. LaCivita and Blair are meanwhile working with Maga Inc, the Trump-backed SuperPac assisting Republican candidates in November’s US midterm elections. Both men have long histories with Trump, and the US president has praised them separately on social media. LaCivita joined Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign in 2022, after leading a pro-Trump Super Pac called Preserve America. In 2024, Trump wrote on Truth Social that LaCivita was “THE BEST” co-campaign manager alongside Susie Wiles, who now serves as the White House chief of staff. Blair worked for Trump’s 2020 campaign in Florida and was the political director of Trump’s 2024 campaign. He joined the president at the White House as deputy chief of staff for legislative, political and public affairs. In April, Trump called Blair “one of the brightest political minds” while announcing that Blair would leave his White House position, briefly, to join Maga Inc and assist Republicans in the midterms. Trump said Blair would return to the White House after the midterms. Trump’s statement distancing himself from the two advisers comes as Maga Inc prepares to ramp up efforts to assist Republican candidates in next month’s elections. Public polls indicate Democrats are leading Republicans in several key competitive races. That is largely attributed to widespread disapproval over Trump’s handling of the economy and cost of living. A spokesperson for Maga Inc told the New York Times that Blair and LaCivita remained engaged with midterm efforts while traveling, saying the two “hosted a team call with race captains on Saturday morning to go over recent survey data”. The Guardian has contacted Maga Inc for comment. Despite polling showing waning voter enthusiasm for Republicans, the party has a cash advantage over Democrats. At the end of August, Maga Inc had more than $415m cash on hand. Several Super Pacs tied to Maga Inc have begun launching multimillion-dollar ad blitzes.

title: ‘System is rigged’: Democrat Sherrod Brown puts datacenter danger at heart of populist Senate bid
body_text: Sherrod Brown, the Democratic former senator from Ohio hoping to return to office in November’s midterm elections, has spent the past year traveling across his home state explaining to voters about all the ways the “system is rigged” against them. Recently, he’s been telling people about a trip he took across the north-west Ohio countryside. “You’re driving on what looks like really good farmland, driving past fields, driving past barns, driving past milking parlors, and you see, all of a sudden, you see these huge cranes and you see these trucks coming,” Brown told a crowd of dozens at a coffee shop in the city of Lima earlier this month. The construction site was for a datacenter, Brown said, a component of the AI boom in which Ohio is a national leader. Brown believes the massive installations that pop up without warning do little good for the people around them. “Nobody knows they’re there,” Brown, speaking in shirtsleeves and without notes, said in his gravelly voice, as the crowd murmurs in agreement. “They eat up our land. They swallow up our water … then once they’re built, our electricity prices go up.” It was the latest iteration of an argument that Brown has been making his whole political career: that the most powerful people in the United States do not have the interests of Ohioans at heart. That message helped him win seven terms in the US House of Representatives and then three in the Senate, even as Ohio grew increasingly dominated by Republicans, and the working-class voters Democrats once relied upon deserted the party. In 2024, Brown lost his bid for a fourth term in an election in which Ohio voters backed Trump by an 11-percentage-point margin. “It’s not, I promise you, the last time you’ll hear from me,” he said in his final speech on the Senate floor, and months later, he announced another run for the Senate. Now 73, Brown has made standing up to datacenter developers a centerpiece of this campaign, calling his Republican opponent, Senator Jon Husted, “the face of datacenters”. A report from Ohio’s chamber of commerce found the state gave $2.5bn in tax breaks for the facilities from 2017 to 2024, a period during which Husted was lieutenant governor. “John Husted, I mean, he’s the guy that – he’s talking like he didn’t know – but he’s the reason these datacenters are here – 200 of them,” Brown said. Whether the former senator’s message lands with voters is central to Democrats’ hopes of retaking the Senate and blunting Trump’s abilities to get bills passed and judges confirmed for the final two years of his presidency. Democrats must win at least four Senate seats to return to the majority, most of which will come from states that voted for Trump by double digits in 2024 – like Ohio. ‘The anchor hanging around Husted’s neck’ Brown has wrapped concerns over datacenters’ impacts into the broad message of affordability that many congressional Democrats are campaigning on nationwide. He peppers his speeches with references to the Iran war, tariffs, Medicaid cuts approved by the Republican Congress and rising prices for Affordable Care Act plans brought on by their inaction. Asked in Lima to name an idea to lowercosts if he wins, Brown proposed a new expansion of the child tax credit, which reduced the poverty rate among children during its single year of enactment under Joe Biden. As the election has drawn closer, Brown has intensified his efforts to tie datacenters to Husted, who the Republican governor, Mike DeWine, appointed in 2025 to the seat JD Vance vacated when he became vice-president. Whichever candidate wins will serve out the remainder of his term, which expires at the end of 2028. This week, Brown’s campaign announced a volley of billboards reading “See that datacenter? Jon Husted did that” and a website critical of the senator that offers voters a map of the facilities in the state. Amy Natoce, a campaign spokesperson for Husted, accused Brown of lying, saying that while serving as lieutenant governor under DeWine from 2019 to 2025, Husted “did not have the authority to grant tax breaks”. She also noted his championing of the Ratepayer Protection Act in the Senate, which would have required electric utilities to consider standards that would make datacenters pay for their impacts on the grid. Though it passed the House with wide, bipartisan support, Senate Democrats called the proposal ineffective, and last month blocked its advancement. “Sherrod Brown and his friends like to talk about affordability, but when the rubber meets the road, they’d rather play politics than actually lower Ohioans’ energy bills. It’s disgusting,” Natoce said. There’s evidence that Brown’s attacks could be effective. Last week, the New York Times and Siena University released polling that found voters believed Brown would do a better job than Husted would managing the development of datacenters, by an 11-percentage-point margin. The race otherwise remains tight, with the Democrat leading the incumbent by three percentage points, within the survey’s margin of error. In August, a memo emerged from the GOP’s Senate campaign arm, the National Republican Senatorial Committee, warning that the issue could sink Husted. “More than any other thing in this race, datacenters are the anchor hanging around Husted’s neck,” the memo read. “If he loses and datacenters get the blame, politicians across the country will take notice – and they will not go near the next one.” DeWine and his predecessor have sought to encourage the development of datacenters. But political winds have shifted rapidly on the issue – nearly 140 communities in the state have put moratoriums on new constructions, according to the Ohio Capital Journal, and in May, DeWine announced a pause on tax exemptions for the buildings. Last year, Democrats campaigned against datacenters to gain power in elections in Virginia, New Jersey and elsewhere, and are this year lumping their perceived impacts on electricity prices with the Iran war’s upward pressure on gas prices to argue that Republicans have failed to accomplish Trump’s promise of fighting inflation. “Husted has been involved in datacenters prior to this election year, and … he’s just more exposed,” said Dan Birdsong, a senior lecturer in political science at the University of Dayton. It also offers Brown a way to appeal to rural voters who typically do not vote for Democrats, but are sensitive to the possibility of the datacenters being built nearby. “He has a bipartisan voting base that he can appeal to with this issue that’s different than other issues in the state,” Birdson said of Brown. Powerful enemies An Ohio native who received a bachelor’s degree from Yale University, Brown had been in office almost without interruption from 1975 until he lost in 2024 to Republican Bernie Moreno. By the end of his time in the chamber, he was something of an outlier – the last Democrat holding statewide elected office in Ohio and still describing himself as a champion for workers even amid abundant evidence that they had soured on his party. Brown argues that he has the accomplishments to back up his record. As a House member, he voted against implementing the North American Free Trade Agreement, concerned about its impact on Ohio manufacturers, and one of his last votes in the Senate was to pass legislation that boosts social security payments to public employees. Brown has been in politics so long that when Bowling Green State University polled the Senate race last month, a quarter of respondents incorrectly thought Brown was the incumbent. He has long courted the alliance of unions, many of whom have backed his comeback attempt this year, though some who supported him in 2024 are now behind Husted. His stances have also earned him deep-pocketed enemies: as chair of the Senate banking committee, he was an adversary of cryptocurrency, and this year, Fairshake, a Super Pac linked to that industry, plans to spend $30m against him, after helping Moreno to victory in 2024. “We will be outspent for sure,” Brown acknowledged to reporters in Lima, echoing a reality for many Democratic campaigns in a year when Republicans are generally seen as having the fundraising advantage. His campaign against datacenters also runs up against their own benefits to building trade unions, for which they have provided significant employment opportunities. Lee Daher, the senior business representative at north-west Ohio’s Carpenters Local Union 351, said datacenters were “a really good source of employment for us”. “It means a lot of work for our members, not only today, tomorrow, but for the years to come,” he said. His local is backing Brown this year, as they did in 2024, and Daher said his comments about datacenters had not dampened that support. “They’re coming one way or another, and is there some regulation that’s needed? I think so, but I think big tech is hearing what is being asked of them,” he said. Asked to reconcile this tension, Brown insisted it was his emphasis on costs that would convince some of the same workers who turned their backs on him two years ago to give him another chance. “Those unions support me in large part because their members don’t like higher electric bills. Their members don’t like having no say on these datacenters coming to their towns,” Brown said. “I don’t think very many union members want the state to give these huge tax breaks to these out-of-state billionaires that are building these datacenters.”

Their members don’t like having no say on these datacenters coming to their towns,” Brown said. “I don’t think very many union members want the state to give these huge tax breaks to these out-of-state billionaires that are building these datacenters.”

title: Oil prices jump 5% on Middle East tensions and US hurricane threat
body_text: Oil prices have risen sharply amid fears about escalating tensions in the Middle East and a squeeze on production from the threat of a hurricane off the US coast. Brent crude, the international benchmark, rose by 5% to $105.3 a barrel on Thursday, triggering a wave of selling in the global bond and stock markets. In the UK, the yield – or interest rate – on the 10-year government bond hit its highest level since July 2007, rising by six basis points to 5.515%. Investors appear concerned that rising oil prices could stoke higher inflation. The yield on the 30-year bond – the UK’s benchmark cost for its long-term borrowing – rose by three basis points to 6.0117%, after touching 6.036% on Wednesday, the highest since January 1998. The climbing cost of government borrowing places further pressure on John Healey, as he prepares to deliver his first budget, on 28 October. The market swings came after the Atlantic reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options for strikes against Iran before the US midterm elections. The report cited unnamed officials in Donald Trump’s administration who said the size and targets of potential strikes, and whether they would go ahead, were still being debated. The report has weakened hopes that Trump will refrain from escalating the conflict with Iran before the midterm polls next month. A “limited operation” could be followed up with more substantial action after the midterms, it states. Another wave of strikes against Iran represents further risk to oil supply from the Middle East, with the US-Israeli war against Tehran now entering its eighth month. Attacks on tankers in the strait of Hormuz have reached their highest levels of ⁠the war, ⁠cutting traffic through the waterway and deepening fears about supply. The latest attack came ⁠on Wednesday, when a tanker was hit by projectiles off the north coast of Qatar, causing casualties, according to United Kingdom Maritime ‌Trade Operations. Oil prices also rose in response to a squeeze on production in the Gulf of Mexico, after Tropical Storm Isaias strengthened to become the first hurricane of the Atlantic season. Shell and Chevron said they were shutting down production as the storm approached the region, forecast to make landfall on Friday or Saturday. The Danish shipping group Maersk added to worries around rising energy prices on Thursday after it said it was increasing its emergency fuel surcharge on all its export collections and import deliveries. The rise in energy prices has fed fears about inflation, reinforcing expectations that central banks will have to raise their interest rates in order to control rising prices. A sell-off in global bond markets continued on Thursday. In France, which has been hit particularly hard over worries about its rising debt and growing spending, the 10-year yield rose by six basis points to 4.931%, just behind the 24-year high of 4.994% it hit last week. Yields rise when prices fall. The German 10-year yield, the benchmark for European debt, rose by two basis points to 3.504%. The yield on the US 10-year treasury, which is widely considered the best quality government debt on the market, rose by five basis points to 5.331%. Global stocks also fell, with Japan’s Nikkei share index falling 1.4% and the South Korean Kospi down 2.6%. In Europe, the Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, dropped 0.9%. The UK’s FTSE 100 slipped by 0.4% in early trading on Thursday.

title: Democratic senator says Hegseth trying to hide costs of Iran war from US public
body_text: Senator Chris Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from a major US base in Qatar, yet saw enough damage on the US embassy in Saudi Arabia to conclude that an Iranian strike would have been deadly had it happened during the day. The Connecticut Democrat, who sits on the Senate foreign relations and appropriations committees, described the destruction he witnessed in Riyadh as “extraordinary” and much more damaging than the public has been led to believe. “Had that attack happened during the daytime, there’s no doubt that there would have been many, many Americans killed,” he told reporters on a call after returning from Qatar and Saudi Arabia. He also accused the Pentagon of trying to prevent Congress from seeing the costs of the war first-hand, saying the Pentagon secretary, Pete Hegseth, was “determined to hide the cost and the consequences of this war from the American public”. Two drones hit the compound in the early hours of 3 March, days after the US and Israel launched the war on 28 February, setting off a fire and sending black smoke over the district. The building was reportedly empty at the time and no injuries were reported. Saudi Arabia’s defense ministry initially described the damage as minor. But, according to Murphy, the drones caused extensive damage across several floors. The strike, he explained, hit “an area of the embassy in which there are a lot of people” and said that “part of that space is uninhabitable and will likely remain uninhabitable”. Murphy said some of it would not be repaired because the embassy is moving soon. In Qatar, the senator visited Ras Laffan, the gas complex where Iranian drone strikes halted LNG (liquefied natural gas) production early in the war. Murphy said 17% of Qatar’s exports had been eliminated, probably for at least three years of repairs. He also said he saw just one LNG tanker in port, compared with the usual six, and about one a day leaving rather than 10. Murphy said the Pentagon blocked him from seeing more. He said he gave notice of his visit weeks in advance and submitted a written request for access to Al Udeid air base, the largest US military installation in the region. He also said he raised it with Adm Brad Cooper, the commander of the US Central Command, who appeared surprised that military leaders had also been barred from speaking to him. On arrival, Murphy said, he was told he would not have access to the base and no contact with military leadership. In response, a senior Pentagon official told the Guardian that Murphy’s office “was informed before his trip” that he would not receive department support to access Al Udeid air base, as per Hegseth’s 3 March directive on travel restrictions in the region. “That decision was communicated in advance by the office of the secretary of war for legislative affairs,” the official said in a statement. “The department applies the secretary’s guidance evenly.” Murphy said he would draft language in the coming days requiring the Pentagon to give members of Congress access to overseas bases, which he would seek to include in next year’s appropriations and defense authorization bills. If the war is still going by early next year, he said Congress should withhold defense funding unless it includes a provision to end the conflict, and vowed accountability and investigations if Democrats win one or both chambers in next month’s midterm elections. The administration, he said, was “giving its middle finger to the Congress, pretending as if we are totally irrelevant”. “We will potentially have power of both the House and the Senate,” Murphy said of Democrats, “and we should make the end of the war a priority.”
